Week 3 · Hands-On
Kinetic Theory & Effusion Problem Set
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: the kinetic-molecular theory, average kinetic energy and absolute temperature, Graham's law of effusion, and the conditions where real gases deviate from the ideal gas law.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work — nine problems (plus a short “explain in words” warm-up) that turn the theory into numbers, predictions, and a data-based argument. No spreadsheet needed; a calculator with a square-root key is enough.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Given two gases at the same temperature, can I predict which moves faster, by how much, and where the ideal model can — and can't — be trusted?
🧮 YOUR TOOLKIT (USE THESE EXACT VALUES)
Graham's law of effusion: rate1 / rate2 = √(M2 / M1)  —  the lighter gas (smaller M) is faster
Average kinetic energy ∝ absolute temperature (K): at one temperature, all gases share the same average KE
Molar masses (g/mol): H2 2.016 · He 4.00 · CH4 16.04 · N2 28.02 · O2 32.00 · CO2 44.01 · Cl2 70.90
Real gases deviate most at: high pressure and low temperature
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
In the Canvas text-entry box, number your responses 1–9 (and include the short “explain before you calculate” note at the top). For calculation problems, show your setup (the ratio under the square root, or the reasoning), not just the final answer.
2
Work each problem before you open its ▶ Check your thinking box. Carry at least 3 significant figures; round sensibly at the end.
3
For every Graham's-law answer, run the quick sanity check: the lighter gas wins, so its rate-over-the-other should be a number greater than 1. If it isn't, you flipped the masses.
🧪 PART A · GRAHAM'S-LAW RATIOS (problems 1–4)
✎ EXPLAIN BEFORE YOU CALCULATE (do this first)
Before you touch the formula, write one or two sentences in words (no equation): for two gases at the same temperature, why does the lighter gas effuse faster? Naming the reason before you compute keeps the numbers meaningful — you should always be able to say what a calculation means.
▶  Check your thinking
At one temperature, every gas has the same average kinetic energy. Since kinetic energy is ½mv², a lighter molecule must move at a higher speed to carry that same energy — so it reaches and slips through the pinhole more often. The formula rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁) just puts a number on that idea.
1. How many times faster does helium (He) effuse than oxygen (O2)? Let He be gas 1.
2. How many times faster does hydrogen (H2) effuse than carbon dioxide (CO2)? Let H2 be gas 1.
3. How many times faster does methane (CH4) effuse than oxygen (O2)? Let CH4 be gas 1.
4. How many times faster does nitrogen (N2) effuse than chlorine (Cl2)? Let N2 be gas 1.
▶  Check your thinking — Part A answer key
Use rate1/rate2 = √(M2/M1) — masses flip relative to the rates.
1. √(32.00 / 4.00) = √8.00 = 2.83 → He effuses 2.83× faster than O2.
2. √(44.01 / 2.016) = √21.83 = 4.67 → H2 effuses 4.67× faster than CO2.
3. √(32.00 / 16.04) = √1.995 = 1.41 → CH4 effuses 1.41× faster than O2.
4. √(70.90 / 28.02) = √2.530 = 1.59 → N2 effuses 1.59× faster than Cl2.
Each answer is greater than 1 because the lighter gas (gas 1) wins — the sanity check holds every time.
🧬 PART B · RANK THE SPEEDS (problems 5–6)
5. These gases are all at the same temperature: O2, He, CO2, H2, N2. Rank them from fastest to slowest average molecular speed, and state the single rule you used.
6. Two flasks at the same temperature hold helium and chlorine (Cl2). (a) Which gas has the higher average kinetic energy? (b) Which gas has the higher average speed? Explain how both answers can be true at once.
▶  Check your thinking — Part B answer key
5. At one temperature, lighter = faster. Order the molar masses: H2 2.016 < He 4.00 < N2 28.02 < O2 32.00 < CO2 44.01. So fastest → slowest is H2 > He > N2 > O2 > CO2. Rule used: at the same temperature all gases share the same average kinetic energy, so the lightest molecules move fastest.
6. (a) Equal — same temperature means the same average kinetic energy for both. (b) Helium has the higher average speed. Both hold because KE = ½mv²: helium is far lighter than Cl2 (4.00 vs. 70.90 g/mol), so it must move faster to carry the same energy.
🔥 PART C · KINETIC ENERGY & TEMPERATURE (problem 7)
7. A sample of neon gas is warmed from 200 K to 400 K. (a) What happens to the average kinetic energy of its particles, and by roughly what factor? (b) Explain, using the kinetic-molecular theory, why warming the gas in a rigid sealed container raises its pressure. (c) Why must temperature be in kelvins, not Celsius, for the kinetic-energy relationship to work?
▶  Check your thinking — Part C answer key
7. (a) Average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature, and 400 K is twice 200 K, so the average kinetic energy roughly doubles (the particles move faster). (b) Faster particles strike the rigid walls harder and more often; since the volume can't change, the pressure rises (this is Gay-Lussac's law explained by the theory). (c) The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the point of zero molecular motion, so kinetic energy is truly proportional to it. Doubling 200 K to 400 K doubles the energy; doubling a Celsius value has no such meaning because its zero is arbitrary.
❄️ PART D · IDEAL vs. NON-IDEAL (problem 8)
8. For each condition below, predict whether the gas will behave nearly ideal or will deviate noticeably from PV = nRT, and give a one-line reason for each.
  (a) Carbon dioxide compressed to very high pressure at room temperature.
  (b) Helium at low pressure and high temperature.
  (c) A gas cooled to a temperature just above where it would condense to a liquid.
  (d) Then name the two ideal-gas assumptions that fail in non-ideal conditions.
▶  Check your thinking — Part D answer key
8. (a) Deviates noticeably — very high pressure crowds the particles so their own volume and attractions matter. (b) Nearly ideal — low pressure and high temperature keep particles far apart and fast-moving; this is the model's home turf. (c) Deviates noticeably — near condensing, slow particles feel one another's attractions strongly. (d) The two failing assumptions: that particles have no volume of their own (fails at high pressure) and that particles have no attraction for one another (fails at low temperature). Van der Waals corrected for each.

Check yourself: did your reasons connect “crowded” to particle volume and “cold/slow” to attractions?
📊 PART E · ANALYZE THE DATA, THEN WRITE (problem 9)
9. An unknown light gas and oxygen (O2) are released through identical pinholes under the same temperature and pressure. Measured effusion times:

  •  unknown light gas: fully effuses in 30. s
  •  oxygen (O2): fully effuses in 85 s

(a) Use the times to find the rate ratio (ratelight / rateO₂). Remember: the faster gas takes less time, so rate is inversely proportional to time.
(b) In 2–3 sentences, interpret the data: what do these times tell you about the light gas's molar mass compared with oxygen, and — using Graham's law — argue whether the light gas could be helium. Support your claim with the number you found.
▶  Check your thinking — Part E answer key
9. (a) Because rate is inversely proportional to time, ratelight/rateO₂ = tO₂/tlight = 85 / 30 = 2.83. The light gas effuses about 2.83× faster than oxygen.
(b) A sample write-up: “The light gas is 2.83 times faster than oxygen, so by Graham's law it must be much lighter. Setting 2.83 = √(MO₂/Mlight) gives 2.83² = 32.00/Mlight, so Mlight = 32.00 / 8.0 ≈ 4.0 g/mol. That matches helium (4.00 g/mol), so the data are consistent with the light gas being helium.” Notice how the measured ratio (2.83) is the same number as the He-vs-O₂ ratio you found in problem 1 — the experiment and the theory agree.

Data-analysis habit: you turned raw times into a rate ratio, then used it as evidence to support a claim about identity. That "claim → evidence → reasoning" move is exactly what a lab report does.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All 9 problems attempted, plus the “explain before you calculate” note. The four Graham's-law problems (1–4) show the ratio under the square root, not just a final number.
☐
Each Graham's-law answer passes the sanity check (lighter gas faster → ratio greater than 1).
☐
The reasoning problems (5–8) give a stated rule or cause, not just a yes/no; and problem 9 shows the rate ratio computed from the data and a 2–3 sentence interpretation that uses it as evidence — all attempted before checking.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
Graham's-law ratios (1–4)
8 pts		 All four set up as √(M₂/M₁) with the ratio shown and sanity-checked. Some missing setup, flipped masses, or unattempted. 8
Reasoning problems (5–8)
6 pts		 Each gives a stated rule/cause, not just an answer. Answers present but reasoning thin or missing. 6
Explain-first note + data write-up (9)
4 pts		 Reasoning stated in words before calculating; problem 9 computes the ratio from the data and interprets it in 2–3 sentences. Write-up missing, number-only with no interpretation, or unattempted. 4
Honest self-check
2 pts		 Attempted before checking; corrections noted where needed. Little evidence of an honest first attempt. 2
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer keys above let you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M5 W3 Hands-On — Kinetic Theory & Effusion
Type your numbered, worked responses directly into the Canvas text-entry box (or attach a photo of your paper work). No separate file is required.
Due: By the end of Week 3.
If you get stuck, submit what you have with a note on where you got stuck — that's useful information, not a penalty.

🧘 PREFER NOT TO USE A HEADSET?
A full non-VR alternate — “See the Particles Move (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the exact same objectives and earns the same credit. Do one pathway, not both.
📚 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
You're on the third week of your module-long project: the Gas & Energy Lab in OptimaXR, which you'll narrate on camera at module's end. In Week 1 you built the gas-law apparatus (piston/cylinder with P, V, and T gauges); in Week 2 you added a measured-amounts station with a partial-pressure jar. This week you make the kinetic-molecular theory visible: spawn a swarm of moving particles inside the apparatus, annotate it with two sticky notes capturing the heart of Lesson 5.05, and set up a small diffusion/effusion observation that shows lighter particles outrunning heavier ones. Today's question: what are the particles actually doing that makes every gauge in your apparatus read the way it does?
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your notes from Lessons 5.05 and 5.06 (KMT postulates; Graham's law; where real gases deviate).
▶  Your saved Gas_Wk2_YourName progress from last week.
▶  About 35 minutes in one sitting.
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (your placed objects stay between visits all module)

Location: Gas & Energy Lab
Spawn point: Gas-Law Apparatus
When you arrive: the gas-law apparatus and measured-amounts station you built in Weeks 1–2 are waiting where you left them. A Whiteboard IFX by the apparatus shows this week's task — bring the gas to life by filling the cylinder with moving particles and explaining what they are doing. A sticky note reads “Start here.”
📝 YOUR INVESTIGATION, IN ORDER
Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend — the same arc a scientist uses at the bench.
OBSERVE
1
At the Gas-Law Apparatus, look at the P, V, and T gauges you built in Weeks 1–2 and read the Whiteboard IFX. Notice that the gauges give you numbers but no reason.
QUESTION
2
Place a sticky note above the apparatus with today's driving question: “What are the particles doing that makes these gauges read the way they do — and why would a lighter gas escape faster?”
PREDICT
3
Before you build anything, add a second sticky note with your prediction: if you release a light gas and a heavy gas at the same time, which one spreads and escapes faster? Commit to an answer now — you'll check it against what you build.
INVESTIGATE
4
Spawn 10–15 small particle spheres inside the cylinder and spread them far apart, to show that a gas is mostly empty space. Use the IFX motion/animation tool (or hand-place and nudge them) so they appear to be in constant, random motion.
5
Set up a small diffusion/effusion observation beside the cylinder: spawn two clusters — a few light particles (label “He”) and a few heavy ones (label “O₂” or “Cl₂”) — with a small pinhole or gap they can spread through. Make the light cluster spread/escape faster than the heavy one.
ANALYZE
6
Compare what you built to your prediction. Then capture the explanation on two sticky notes: one reading “avg KE ∝ T (Kelvin)” with a 3D-pen arrow to the swarm, and one on the diffusion/effusion setup reading “lighter molecule = faster, Graham's law” with rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁). Sign the second note.
DEFEND
7
Lock the swarm and notes so they aren't bumped, save a snapshot named Gas_Wk3_YourName, and take one screenshot that clearly shows the particle swarm, both sticky notes, and the diffusion/effusion setup — the evidence for your explanation. (You'll defend it in words in the CER reflection below.)
EXTEND
8
Add one last optional sticky note connecting the kinetic picture beyond the apparatus — e.g., “same particle motion drives atmospheric mixing” or “real gases have size + attractions → PV = nRT strains at high P, low T.” Then leave open floor space beside the apparatus for next week's calorimetry setup and the final recording.
Need to stop partway? Because the Session is persistent, your placed and locked particles and notes will be waiting when you return. Save the Gas_Wk3_YourName snapshot before you log out so nothing is lost — next week you'll add the calorimetry setup and record the full narrated walkthrough.
📝 REQUIRED · CER REFLECTION
In the Canvas comment box (or a short typed note), defend what you built with a three-part Claim–Evidence–Reasoning reflection:
▶  Claim: Which of your two labeled gases moves faster at the same temperature?
▶  Evidence: What did you observe in your diffusion/effusion setup, and what does Graham's law give for that pair's ratio?
▶  Reasoning: Why does the kinetic-molecular theory predict this? (Tie it to equal average kinetic energy at one temperature and to ½mv².) Did the result match your PREDICT-step guess?
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
1. Upload your in-headset screenshot of the particle swarm, both sticky notes, and the diffusion/effusion setup to this Canvas assignment.
2. In the comment box, write your CER reflection (the Claim–Evidence–Reasoning block above): which labeled gas moves faster, your evidence, and the kinetic-molecular reasoning behind it. (Your reflection may be used when your work appears in the class gallery walk later this module.)

About 35 minutes in the headset.

📝 YOUR INVESTIGATION, IN ORDER

1

Week 4 · Hands-On (Excel)
Calorimetry & Enthalpy Data Analysis
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: q = m·c·ΔT (5.07), the calorimetry rule that heat lost by the metal = heat gained by the water (5.07), and conservation of energy (the first law) — now run across several trials in Excel, where the spreadsheet does the repetitive arithmetic so you can focus on the chemistry and on identifying each metal.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work, and it rehearses exactly the calculations your module calorimetry lab report asks for.
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
A chemist ran the same calorimetry experiment three times with three different mystery metals. Each time, a 50.0 g piece of metal was heated to 100.0 °C in a boiling-water bath and then dropped into 100.0 g of water at 20.0 °C in a coffee-cup calorimeter. Only the final equilibrium temperature differed. In Excel, you'll build a table that computes the heat the water gained, the heat the metal lost, and each metal's specific heat — then identify the metal by matching that value against a short reference table. Finally you'll analyze what the data reveals about conservation of energy.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
From nothing but a few temperature readings, can you measure how much energy moved — and use it to name a metal you never touched?
🔢 CONSTANTS & REFERENCE YOU'LL NEED
Specific heat of water: c = 4.184 J·g−1·°C−1.   Conservation rule: heat gained by water = heat lost by metal (qmetal = −qwater).
Metal (reference) Specific heat (J·g−1·°C−1)
Aluminum0.897
Iron0.449
Copper0.385
Lead0.128
📊 YOUR DATA · THREE METAL-IN-WATER CALORIMETRY TRIALS

Every trial uses 50.0 g of metal at 100.0 °C dropped into 100.0 g of water at 20.0 °C. Only the final temperature changes. Type this data into Excel exactly as shown.

Trial Mass metal (g) Metal start (°C) Mass water (g) Water start (°C) Final temp (°C)
150.0100.0100.020.023.5
250.0100.0100.020.024.1
350.0100.0100.020.027.7
✎ FIRST · REASON IN WORDS, BEFORE ANY FORMULA
A calculator can only check thinking you have already done. So before you build a single Excel formula, look at the data and write one or two sentences in your spreadsheet (or notebook) answering this: all three trials use the same mass of metal, the same starting temperatures, and the same 100.0 g of water — only the final temperature differs (23.5, 24.1, 27.7 °C). Which trial's metal do you predict has the largest specific heat, and why? Reason it out in words using q = m·c·ΔT — do not compute anything yet.
▶  Reveal a model answer after you have written your own
Trial 3 should have the metal with the largest specific heat. Its water rose the most (20.0 → 27.7 °C), so its water gained the most heat — and by conservation that metal gave up the most heat. Since every metal has the same mass and cooled from 100 °C by a similar amount, the one that released the most energy per gram per degree must have the highest c. In words: bigger water temperature rise → more heat delivered → larger specific heat. (Your Excel work will confirm it points to aluminum.) The point of predicting first is that when your spreadsheet agrees, you understand why; when it disagrees, you have caught either a formula error or a gap in your reasoning.
📝 WHAT TO DO IN EXCEL
1
Enter the three-trial table with headers in row 1: Trial, Mass metal (g), Metal start (°C), Mass water (g), Water start (°C), Final temp (°C).
2
Add a ΔT water (°C) column: final temp minus water start, e.g. =G2-E2 (adjust the column letters to match yours). Fill down all three trials.
3
Add a q water (J) column — the heat the water gained: mass water × 4.184 × ΔT water, e.g. =D2*4.184*H2.
4
Add a q metal (J) column — the heat the metal lost. By conservation it's the negative of q water: =-I2 (point at your q water cell).
5
Add a ΔT metal (°C) column: final temp minus metal start, e.g. =G2-C2 (this will be negative — the metal cooled).
6
Add a c metal (J·g−1·°C−1) column: rearrange q = m·c·ΔT to c = q ÷ (m × ΔT). Use absolute values so the sign cancels, e.g. =ABS(J2)/(B2*ABS(K2)) (q metal ÷ (mass metal × ΔT metal)).
7
Add an Identity column: compare each computed c metal to the reference table and name the metal (the closest match). You can type it by eye, or use a lookup if you're comfortable with one.
8
In cells or a text box below the table, answer the three Analysis Questions below.
❓ ANALYSIS QUESTIONS (answer in your spreadsheet)
A. In every trial the water started at the same temperature and gained heat, yet the three metals reached very different final temperatures. Why does the metal with the smallest specific heat cause the smallest rise in the water's temperature? Tie your answer to q = m·c·ΔT.
B. Your q metal column is the exact negative of your q water column. Which law of nature guarantees that, and what does it mean in plain words for this experiment?
C. A coffee-cup calorimeter is not perfectly insulated — a little heat always escapes to the cup and the air. If some of the metal's heat leaks to the surroundings instead of the water, would your calculated specific heat for the metal come out a little too high or a little too low? Explain, and say what that tells you about trusting a single measurement.
▶  Check your thinking — answer key
Computed results (rounded):
• Trial 1 — ΔT water = 23.5 − 20.0 = 3.5 °C; q water = 100.0 × 4.184 × 3.5 = 1,464 J; q metal = −1,464 J; ΔT metal = 23.5 − 100.0 = −76.5 °C; c metal = 1,464 ÷ (50.0 × 76.5) = 0.383 → copper (ref 0.385).
• Trial 2 — ΔT water = 24.1 − 20.0 = 4.1 °C; q water = 100.0 × 4.184 × 4.1 = 1,715 J; q metal = −1,715 J; ΔT metal = 24.1 − 100.0 = −75.9 °C; c metal = 1,715 ÷ (50.0 × 75.9) = 0.452 → iron (ref 0.449).
• Trial 3 — ΔT water = 27.7 − 20.0 = 7.7 °C; q water = 100.0 × 4.184 × 7.7 = 3,222 J; q metal = −3,222 J; ΔT metal = 27.7 − 100.0 = −72.3 °C; c metal = 3,222 ÷ (50.0 × 72.3) = 0.891 → aluminum (ref 0.897).

A. For a fixed mass and a fixed starting temperature, a metal with a smaller specific heat carries less energy for each degree it cools. Even though all three metals cool by roughly the same amount, the low-c metal (copper) releases the least total heat, so by q water = m·c·ΔT the water's ΔT is smallest. Specific heat is the metal's “energy density per degree” — lower c means less heat handed to the water.
B. The first law of thermodynamics — conservation of energy. Energy is never created or destroyed, so every joule the metal loses must reappear in the water (assuming negligible loss to the cup and air). In plain words: the metal didn't make the water's heat appear from nowhere — it handed over exactly the energy it gave up.
C. The calculated c metal would come out a little too low. We assume all of the metal's heat went into the water, so we set |q metal| = q water. If some heat actually leaked to the surroundings, the water gained less than the metal truly lost, so our q (based only on the water) underestimates the metal's real heat output — and dividing a too-small q by (m × ΔT) gives a too-small c. That is exactly why the trial-1 value (0.383) sits just below copper's true 0.385: a real reminder that one imperfect measurement can mislead, and why we repeat trials and improve insulation.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Build this in Microsoft Excel from your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_CalorimetryData_CHEM1H, save it to your Optima → Science OneDrive course folder, and submit through Canvas. New here? See the pinned “M365 Setup & File Organization Guide” page in this module.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: filling formulas down a column & using ABS to handle a signed temperature change (Excel).
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Data entered, with working ΔT water and q water columns filled down all three trials.
☐
q metal, ΔT metal, and c metal computed for each trial, and each metal identified from the reference table.
☐
All three Analysis Questions answered, then checked against the answer key.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
Heat columns
8 pts		 ΔT water, q water, and q metal columns present, with formulas filled down all three trials. Some columns missing or numbers typed by hand instead of formulas. 8
Specific heat & identity
6 pts		 c metal computed and the metal correctly identified for all three trials. Computed for some trials, or a recurring formula error. 6
Analysis + self-check
6 pts		 All three questions answered, then checked and corrected. Some questions missing or not checked. 6
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer key lets you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice for your lab report, not a test.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M5 W4 Hands-On — Calorimetry & Enthalpy Data Analysis (Excel)
Upload your Excel file (.xlsx) through Canvas (OneDrive tab or file upload).
If a formula gives a result you don't trust, submit what you have with a note about where you got stuck — that's useful information, not a penalty.

100 pts
Module 5 Writing Assignment
Calorimetry — A Lab Report
Word (.docx) · 100 pts · teacher-reviewed
📚 THE TASK
Energy is invisible, but it is never lost. When a hot object meets a cooler one, heat flows from the hot to the cold until both settle at one shared temperature — and every joule the hot object gives up is a joule the cold object takes in. That bookkeeping is the first law of thermodynamics, and a calorimeter is the simple instrument that lets us watch the energy move and add it up.
In this investigation, a hot piece of metal is dropped into cooler water in a coffee-cup calorimeter, and the whole system drifts to one final temperature. You are given the masses, the starting temperatures, and the final temperature. Your task is to write a lab report that works the energy all the way through:
From the data below, calculate the heat gained by the water, determine the heat released by the metal, find the metal's specific heat (and identify the metal), and account for energy with the first law — explaining why the heat lost should equal the heat gained, and why a real measurement comes out a little off.
You'll write it in Microsoft Word, organized into the standard lab-report sections listed further down.
🧪 THE INVESTIGATION · YOUR DATA
A student heated a piece of metal in a boiling-water bath, then quickly dropped it into water held in an insulated coffee-cup calorimeter and stirred until the temperature stopped changing. The principle is conservation of energy — the heat lost by the metal equals the heat gained by the water:
q = m · c · ΔT   and   qmetal = −qwater
(specific heat of water, c = 4.184 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹)
Quantity Value
Mass of metal50.0 g
Initial temperature of metal (boiling-water bath)100.0 °C
Mass of water100.0 g
Initial temperature of water20.0 °C
Final equilibrium temperature (both metal and water)23.5 °C
For identifying the metal, compare your calculated specific heat to these reference values (J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹): copper 0.385 · iron 0.449 · aluminum 0.897 · lead 0.128.
⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS
This lab report is one of only two teacher-reviewed pieces in Module 5 (the other is your Gas Behavior & Energy Lab VR project). Your teacher reads it personally and responds to your reasoning and your error analysis — so make it your careful best, and show every step of your math.
🧠 YOUR REASONING TOOLKIT (the path through the calculation)
Use these steps in your own words and show the arithmetic for each — don't just copy the headings.
Step 1 — Find the heat gained by the water.
Use qwater = m · c · ΔT, where ΔT = Tfinal − Tinitial for the water. Keep the sign: the water warms up, so its q is positive.
Step 2 — State the heat released by the metal.
By conservation of energy, qmetal = −qwater. The metal loses exactly what the water gains, so its q is negative and equal in size.
Step 3 — Find ΔT for the metal.
ΔTmetal = Tfinal − Tinitial,metal. The metal cools, so this value is negative.
Step 4 — Solve for the metal's specific heat & identify it.
Rearrange q = m · c · ΔT to c = q ÷ (m · ΔT) using the metal's q, mass, and ΔT (use magnitudes so c comes out positive). Compare your value to the reference table to name the metal.
Step 5 — Account for the energy (first law).
Explain why the heat lost should equal the heat gained, then discuss why a real measurement comes out slightly off — where could energy have gone that the simple model ignores?
📝 STRUCTURE: WRITE THESE LAB-REPORT SECTIONS
1
Purpose. One or two sentences: what question is this investigation answering? (e.g., how much heat moves from a hot metal to cooler water, and what does that tell us about the identity of the metal?)
2
Procedure & Given Data. Briefly describe the coffee-cup calorimeter method and present the given data in a small table (the two masses, the three temperatures, the specific heat of water, and the q = mcΔT relationship).
3
Calculations (q = mcΔT). Show all work: the heat gained by the water, the heat released by the metal, the metal's ΔT, and the metal's specific heat. Label every number with its units and keep the signs straight.
4
Conservation / Energy Analysis. State your specific heat, identify the metal from the reference table, and explain how the first law of thermodynamics (qmetal = −qwater) governs the whole experiment — the energy books must balance.
5
Error Sources. Give at least two realistic reasons a real calorimetry result deviates from the ideal — and say, for each, whether it would make your calculated specific heat come out too high or too low. (Think: heat lost to the cup and the air, the metal cooling slightly during transfer, an imperfectly read thermometer, evaporation.)
6
Conclusion — make your argument (Claim → Evidence → Reasoning). Don't just restate numbers — argue from your data. Claim: name the metal and state its specific heat. Evidence: cite your own results — the heat gained by the water, the heat released by the metal, the metal's ΔT, and the specific heat you computed. Reasoning: use conservation of energy to link the evidence to the claim — explain why |qmetal| should equal qwater, why your calculated specific heat comes out close to but a little off from the accepted value because some heat left the system to the cup and the surrounding air, and what the whole experiment reveals: energy is never created or destroyed; it only moves, and the books must close.
✎ LENGTH & STYLE
Aim for roughly 500–700 words across the six sections, plus your worked calculations (which can be handwritten and photographed in, or typed). Use correct terminology — heat, specific heat, q = mcΔT, conservation of energy, first law of thermodynamics, exothermic/endothermic. Carry units through every step, keep your signs straight (the water gains, the metal loses), and keep a sensible number of significant figures (three is plenty here). The chemistry and the clear, complete math are what's graded — not polished prose.
⚠️ A NOTE ON USING AI TOOLS
An AI tool will happily produce a specific-heat number for this data — and it can quietly use the wrong ΔT, flip a sign, or apply water's specific heat to the metal, and still sound completely confident. If you consult one, treat it as a draft to check, never an answer to paste: re-run q = mcΔT yourself, confirm that qmetal = −qwater, and make sure its arithmetic matches yours before you trust a single digit. The instrument proposes; your calculation verifies. That is exactly the skill this report is built to grow.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Write your lab report in Microsoft Word from your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_CalorimetryLabReport_CHEM1H, save it to your Optima → Science OneDrive course folder, and submit through Canvas. New here? See the pinned “M365 Setup & File Organization Guide” page in this module.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: building a labeled data table in Word and laying out worked calculations (typed equations or a photographed work page) inside a structured document. If your teacher returns comments for revision, turn on Track Changes before revising.
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED (TEACHER RUBRIC — build natively as a Canvas Rubric)
Criterion Full marks Developing Pts
Procedure & data presentation Clear Purpose; the calorimeter method, given data, specific heat of water, and the q = mcΔT relationship are presented in an organized table or section. Purpose or data incomplete; relationship missing; disorganized. 15
Calorimetry calculations (q = mcΔT) Heat gained by water, heat released by the metal, the metal's ΔT, and the metal's specific heat are all computed correctly with units and correct signs; all work is shown. q values or specific heat are wrong; signs flipped; steps or units missing. 30
Conservation & metal identification The metal is correctly identified from the specific heat, and the first law (qmetal = −qwater) is explained as the reason the energy balances. Metal misidentified, or conservation of energy stated but not explained. 25
Error-source discussion At least two realistic error sources, each correctly tied to whether it would raise or lower the calculated specific heat. Fewer than two sources, or sources are vague / not connected to the result. 15
Conclusion: argument from data (Claim–Evidence–Reasoning) Conclusion is a genuine argument from the data: it names the metal (claim), cites the student's own q and specific-heat results (evidence), and uses conservation of energy to link them (reasoning) — including why |qmetal| ≈ qwater and why the small gap points to heat lost to the cup and air. Correct terminology, clear lab-report form. Conclusion just restates numbers or gives an answer with no Claim–Evidence–Reasoning argument; conservation reasoning missing; terms misused or disorganized. 15
Total: 100 pts
The calculation and conservation analysis carry the most weight — a correct specific heat with no shown work, or an answer that ignores the first law, earns little. Account honestly for where the energy went.

Submit your Word .docx through Canvas (OneDrive tab or file upload). If your teacher returns it with comments, revise with Track Changes on and resubmit as a _Revision1 file.

Type

Points
Assignment
20 pts
Week 1 · Hands-On
Intermolecular Forces & Boiling-Point Prediction
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: the three intermolecular forces and boiling-point reasoning (6.01), surface tension / viscosity / capillary action and water's special properties (6.02), and the phase transitions and heating curves (6.03).
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work. Nine items: identify forces, rank boiling points with justification, explain properties from the forces, read a phase transition, and — last — a short data-analysis writing step where you predict in words before you read a boiling-point data table, then interpret the trend.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Given only a substance's structure, can I reason out the forces between its molecules — and from those forces, predict the physical properties I'd actually measure?
🧮 YOUR TOOLKIT (USE THESE EXACT IDEAS)
The three IMFs (weakest → strongest, comparable size): London dispersion < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding. (Full ionic/covalent bonds are stronger still.)
Hydrogen bonding requires: H bonded to N, O, or F.
London dispersion: present in all substances; stronger with more electrons / larger molar mass.
Key rule: stronger forces → higher melting and boiling points.
Cohesion = pull of a liquid for itself · Adhesion = pull of a liquid for a surface.
Heating curve: temperature plateaus during a phase change (energy breaks forces, doesn't raise temperature).
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
In the Canvas text-entry box, number your responses 1–9. For ranking and explaining items, show your reasoning (which force, and why), not just the final answer.
2
Work each part before you open its ▶ Check your thinking box. The keys are there to confirm your reasoning, not replace it.
3
Always name the strongest force present, and remember London dispersion is in everything.
🧪 PART A · IDENTIFY THE INTERMOLECULAR FORCES (problems 1–3)
1. Name the strongest intermolecular force present in each: (a) O2 (nonpolar), (b) NH3 (polar, H bonded to N), (c) HCl (polar, H bonded to Cl).
2. A classmate says water (H2O) and methane (CH4) should have similar boiling points because both are small molecules. Name the strongest force in each, and explain why this reasoning is wrong.
3. Which intermolecular force is present in every one of the substances above — and why is it found in all of them?
▶  Check your thinking — Part A answer key
1. (a) O2 → London dispersion only (nonpolar). (b) NH3 → hydrogen bonding (H on N). (c) HCl → dipole-dipole (polar, but H is on Cl, not N/O/F, so no hydrogen bonding).
2. Water's strongest force is hydrogen bonding; methane's is London dispersion only. Size alone doesn't set boiling point — the type of force does. Water's hydrogen bonds are far stronger, so it takes much more energy to separate water molecules. (Water boils at 100 °C; methane at about −161 °C.)
3. London dispersion forces. They come from the motion of electrons, and every substance has electrons — so dispersion is present in all of them (it is the only force in nonpolar O2, and acts alongside the stronger forces in NH3 and HCl).
🌡️ PART B · RANK THE BOILING POINTS, WITH JUSTIFICATION (problems 4–5)
4. Rank helium (He), methane (CH4), and water (H2O) from lowest to highest boiling point. State the strongest force in each and justify the order.
5. Ethane (CH3CH3) and ethanol (CH3CH2OH) have nearly the same molar mass, yet ethanol boils far higher (about 78 °C) than ethane (about −89 °C). Which boils higher, and what single structural feature explains the huge difference?
▶  Check your thinking — Part B answer key
4. He < CH4 < H2O. Helium — a tiny nonpolar atom with the weakest possible London dispersion — is lowest. Methane is also nonpolar (dispersion only) but larger, with more electrons, so its dispersion forces are stronger — middle. Water hydrogen-bonds, the strongest of the three forces — highest. (You can rank these from the forces alone, with no temperatures.)
5. Ethanol boils higher. The one difference is ethanol's –OH (hydroxyl) group, which lets it form hydrogen bonds; ethane (only C and H) has just weak London dispersion. The functional group sets the physical property through the force it enables.
💧 PART C · EXPLAIN A PROPERTY FROM THE FORCES (problems 6–7)
6. A water strider rests on a pond's surface, and a gently placed paper clip floats on water in a glass. Name the property responsible and explain it in terms of the forces on a surface molecule.
7. Explain, at the molecular level, why ice floats on liquid water — and why that is unusual compared with most substances.
▶  Check your thinking — Part C answer key
6. Surface tension. A molecule deep in the liquid is pulled equally in all directions, but a surface molecule has no neighbors above, so the net pull is inward. This makes the surface behave like a stretched skin that resists being broken — strong enough (thanks to water's hydrogen bonding) to support a light, gently placed object like a strider or a paper clip.
7. When water freezes, its hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open, spacious lattice with gaps, so solid ice is less dense than liquid water and floats. This is unusual: most substances pack closer when they freeze, so their solids are denser and sink. The floating ice insulates the water below.
🔥 PART D · READ A PHASE TRANSITION (problem 8)
8. A sample of ice is heated steadily. On the heating curve, the temperature climbs, then goes flat at 0 °C for a while, climbs again, then goes flat at 100 °C. (a) What is happening during each flat plateau? (b) Why does the temperature hold constant even though heat is still being added? (c) Name the two phase transitions occurring (in order), and say whether each absorbs or releases energy.
▶  Check your thinking — Part D worked answer
(a) The first plateau (0 °C) is the ice melting to liquid water; the second plateau (100 °C) is the liquid water boiling (vaporizing) to steam.
(b) During a phase change the added energy goes into breaking intermolecular forces (pulling the molecules apart) rather than raising their kinetic energy, so the temperature stays constant until the change is complete.
(c) In order: melting (fusion), then vaporization — both absorb energy (endothermic).

Check yourself: did you reason from the forces in every item, and name the strongest force present (remembering dispersion is in everything)?
✍️ PART E · DATA-ANALYSIS WRITING: PREDICT IN WORDS, THEN READ THE DATA (problem 9)
9. Below are the measured boiling points of five molecules of similar or increasing size.

(a) Before you look hard at the numbers — in words (no calculating, no sorting yet) — predict which molecule will boil lowest and which will boil highest, and name the one force that decides it. Write one or two sentences.

(b) Now study the data table and write 3–4 sentences analyzing the trend: which molecules rely only on London dispersion, which add dipole-dipole, and which can hydrogen-bond — and describe how the measured boiling points line up (or don't) with the strength order. Point out one place where molar mass (dispersion) and force type both matter.
Substance Formula Boiling point (°C)
methaneCH4−161
ethaneC2H6−89
formaldehydeCH2O−19
methanolCH3OH+65
ethanolC2H5OH+78
▶  Check your thinking — Part E model answer
(a) Prediction (in words): Methane should boil lowest — it is small and nonpolar, so only weak London dispersion acts. Ethanol should boil highest — its –OH group lets it hydrogen-bond, the strongest of the three forces. The deciding force is hydrogen bonding (present in the molecules with an –OH).

(b) Analysis of the data: The table confirms the prediction. Methane (CH4) and ethane (C2H6) are nonpolar, so they feel only London dispersion — and they boil lowest (−161 and −89 °C). Formaldehyde (CH2O) is polar, so it adds dipole-dipole attraction and boils higher (−19 °C). Methanol and ethanol both carry an –OH group, so they hydrogen-bond — and they boil far higher (+65 and +78 °C). The measured points climb exactly with the strength order: dispersion < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding.

Where both molar mass AND force type matter: Methane vs. ethane shows dispersion alone — same force type, but ethane is larger (more electrons), so it boils ~70 degrees higher purely from stronger dispersion. Ethanol vs. methanol shows the same idea among the hydrogen-bonders: both hydrogen-bond, but the larger ethanol boils a bit higher. So within one force type, size (dispersion) breaks the tie; across force types, the stronger type wins outright.

Check yourself: did you write your word-prediction in (a) before sorting the numbers, and does your analysis name the force type for each molecule rather than just re-listing the temperatures?

All 8 problems attempted with your reasoning shown (which force, and why), not just final answers.
☐

☐

☐
You attempted each item before checking, and corrected any you missed.

You're starting the project you'll build across all three weeks of this module: an Intermolecular Forces & States Model — a molecular-scale exhibit that you'll narrate on camera at the end of the module. 🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED

▶  Your notes from Lessons 6.01–6.02 (the three intermolecular forces; the N/O/F rule for hydrogen bonding).

📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (your placed objects stay between visits all module)

A sticky note at your feet reads “Start here.” You won't have to guess what to do.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
These steps follow the way a scientist actually investigates: Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend. Don't skip the predict step — committing to a ranking before you build the models is the point.
1
Observe. At the bench, read the Whiteboard IFX and its three empty labeled zones. Recall the puzzle from Lesson 6.01: water boils at 100 °C, but methane — a molecule of similar size — boils at −161 °C. Leave open space along the bench to the right for the crystal lattice and dissolution station (Week 2) and property-explanation annotations (Week 3).
2
Question. On a sticky note, write the question you are investigating: “Why should water need so much more heat to boil than methane, when both are small molecules?” Place it on the bench beside the labeled zones.
3
Predict — before you build anything. On a second sticky note, commit a prediction: rank CH4, HCl, and H2O from lowest to highest boiling point, and name the strongest force you expect in each. Write the actual order down. This is your committed prediction — do not change it after you build the models.
4
Investigate. In the LDF zone, spawn two nonpolar molecules (for example, two CH4 or two Ne atoms) and place them near each other. Add a dashed-line connector and a sticky note: “London dispersion — weakest; present in all substances.”
5
Investigate. In the dipole-dipole zone, spawn two polar molecules (for example, two HCl). Mark the slightly positive (δ+) and slightly negative (δ−) ends, line up the + of one with the − of the other, and label: “Dipole-dipole — between permanent dipoles.”
6
Investigate. In the hydrogen-bond zone, spawn two water molecules (H2O). Draw the hydrogen bond from an H of one molecule to the O (lone pair) of the other, and label: “Hydrogen bond — strongest; H bonded to N, O, or F.”
7
Analyze. Step back and compare your three models. Rank them by strength of attraction and match each to the strength ladder (London dispersion < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding). Now check that ranking against the committed prediction from your Predict note — was your order right? Off anywhere? By how much?
8
Defend. Place a signed summary sticky note stating a claim with its evidence and reasoning: “Claim: among CH4, HCl, and H2O, water boils highest. Evidence: only water hydrogen-bonds (H on O); HCl is dipole-dipole; CH4 has only dispersion. Reasoning: stronger IMF → more energy to pull molecules apart → higher boiling point.” Sign your name.
9
Extend. On one last sticky note, predict a wrinkle: could a large nonpolar molecule with many electrons ever out-boil a small polar one — and which force would be doing that work? (Hint: dispersion forces add up.) You'll test ideas like this as the model grows in Weeks 2–3.
💾
Save & capture. Lock your three models and labels so they aren't bumped, save a snapshot named IMF_Wk1_YourName (your project's saved progress for next week), and take one in-headset screenshot showing all three labeled force models and your signed claim note. That screenshot is what you'll submit.

📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
1. Upload your in-headset screenshot showing the three labeled force models (LDF, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bond) and your “stronger IMF → higher boiling point” note to this Canvas assignment.
2. In the comment box, write a short CER reflection (2–4 sentences): a Claim about which of CH4, HCl, and H2O boils highest, the Evidence (the strongest force acting in each), and your Reasoning (why stronger intermolecular forces mean a higher boiling point). Add one sentence comparing the result to the ranking you committed in your Predict note. (This reflection is used when your work appears in the class gallery walk later this module.)
⏱️ TIME
About 35–45 minutes in the headset.

All three forces are modeled and labeled — LDF (two nonpolar molecules), dipole-dipole (two polar molecules), and a hydrogen bond (two water molecules).
☐
A boiling-point ranking of CH4, HCl, and H2O was committed on a sticky note before the models were built, then compared with the finished models.

Week 2 · Hands-On
Solubility Curves & Solid Types / Electrolytes
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: classifying solids by type and predicting their properties (6.04), and explaining dissolution, “like dissolves like,” and sorting electrolytes (6.05). You'll also practice reading a solubility curve — given as a small data table here — to decide whether a solution is unsaturated, saturated, or supersaturated, and to compare how solids and gases respond to temperature.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work — reasoning and data-reading, no calculator required for most items.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How does the way a substance is put together — the bonding in a solid, the polarity of a molecule, whether it breaks into ions — let you predict, before any experiment, how it will melt, dissolve, and conduct?
📋 HOW TO WORK THIS ASSIGNMENT
Work all four parts in your digital science notebook (no spreadsheet needed this week). Write a short answer or fill the requested value for each item. When you finish a part, open its answer key to check yourself — correct anything you missed, since the point is to learn the reasoning, not to be perfect on the first try.
📊 PART A · CLASSIFY THE SOLID & PREDICT PROPERTIES (6.04)

For each substance, name its solid type (ionic, molecular, covalent network, or metallic) and give the property described.

1. Iron — can be hammered into shape and conducts electricity as a solid. Name its solid type, and state why it bends instead of shattering.
2. Quartz (SiO2) — extremely hard, melts only at a very high temperature, does not conduct. Name its solid type.
3. Sugar (sucrose) — a soft solid that melts at a low temperature and does not conduct. Name its solid type and the kind of force holding its particles together.
4. Potassium iodide (KI) — high-melting, hard but brittle. Name its solid type, and predict whether it will conduct electricity (a) as a solid and (b) when dissolved in water.
▶  Check your thinking — Part A answer key
1. Metallic. Iron is a metal — cations in a sea of delocalized electrons. It bends instead of shattering because layers of cations can slide past one another while the electron sea keeps holding them together; nothing snaps.
2. Covalent network. Quartz is a continuous covalent web of silicon and oxygen atoms, so melting it means breaking real covalent bonds — hence very hard and very high-melting, and nonconducting.
3. Molecular solid, held together by intermolecular forces (for sucrose, including hydrogen bonding). Weak forces between separate molecules give a low melting point, softness, and no conduction.
4. Ionic. KI is a soluble ionic salt. (a) As a solid it does not conduct (ions are locked in the lattice). (b) When dissolved it conducts, because the freed K⁺ and I⁻ ions can move.
📊 PART B · READ THE SOLUBILITY CURVE (data provided)

The table below is a solubility curve written out as numbers: the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of water at each temperature. A point on the curve is exactly saturated; below the line is unsaturated (more can still dissolve); above the line is supersaturated (more is dissolved than equilibrium allows — unstable). Use it to answer the questions.

Solute 0 °C 20 °C 40 °C 60 °C 80 °C
KNO3 (g / 100 g water)133264110169
NaCl (g / 100 g water)3636373738
5. Which solute's solubility changes far more steeply as temperature rises — KNO3 or NaCl? What does that tell you about choosing a temperature to dissolve a lot of KNO3?
6. A beaker holds 60 g of KNO3 dissolved in 100 g of water at 40 °C. Using the table, is this solution unsaturated, saturated, or supersaturated? Explain.
7. You have 100 g of KNO3 dissolved in 100 g of water at 60 °C (still fully dissolved). You cool it slowly to 40 °C with no disturbance, and it all stays in solution. What kind of solution is it now, and roughly how many grams of KNO3 would crystallize out if a seed crystal were dropped in?
8. Gases vs solids: a sealed bottle of soda goes flat faster when left out warm, and a warm pond holds less dissolved oxygen than a cold one. Does gas solubility increase or decrease as temperature rises — and is that the same direction as KNO3 or the opposite?
✍️ REASON IN WORDS FIRST — THEN WRITE A SHORT DATA-ANALYSIS PARAGRAPH
9. Explain before you calculate. Before doing any arithmetic for question 7, write one or two sentences in plain words: what does it mean that the cooled solution is “supersaturated,” and how will you use the numbers at 60 °C and 40 °C to find how much KNO3 crystallizes out? Describe what the calculation will do and why — do not compute yet.
10. Data-analysis paragraph. In 3–4 sentences, describe the pattern in the solubility table: compare how KNO3 and NaCl each respond to rising temperature, then explain what that difference means for someone trying to purify a solid by dissolving it in hot water and cooling it — which of the two solids would this technique work well for, and why?
▶  Check your thinking — Part B answer key
5. KNO3 changes far more steeply (13 → 169 g across the range), while NaCl is nearly flat (36 → 38 g). To dissolve a lot of KNO3, use hot water — raising the temperature dramatically increases how much will dissolve. (Heating barely helps with NaCl.)
6. Unsaturated. At 40 °C the saturation limit is 64 g per 100 g water; 60 g is below the line, so more KNO3 could still dissolve.
7. Supersaturated. At 40 °C the limit is 64 g, but 100 g is still dissolved — more than equilibrium allows, an unstable state. A seed crystal would trigger crystallization of about 100 − 64 = 36 g of KNO3, leaving a saturated solution (~64 g dissolved).
8. Gas solubility decreases as temperature rises (warm soda goes flat; warm water holds less O2). This is the opposite direction from KNO3, whose solubility increases with temperature.
9. (reason-first, sample): “Supersaturated means the water is holding more KNO3 than it can normally hold at 40 °C, so it is unstable and the extra will drop out as crystals once something triggers it. To find how much, I’ll take the amount dissolved (what fit at 60 °C) and subtract the most that can stay dissolved at 40 °C — the difference must crystallize.” (The arithmetic in #7 then gives 100 − 64 = 36 g.) Any answer that states the subtraction in words before computing earns credit.
10. (data-analysis paragraph, sample): KNO3’s solubility climbs steeply with temperature (13 g at 0 °C up to 169 g at 80 °C), while NaCl barely moves (36–38 g across the whole range). Purifying by dissolving hot and then cooling (recrystallization) works well only when a lot of solid comes back out on cooling — so it works well for KNO3: dissolve a large amount in hot water, cool it, and most of the KNO3 crystallizes back as pure solid while impurities stay behind in solution. It would not work for NaCl, because cooling barely changes how much stays dissolved, so almost nothing would crystallize out.
📊 PART C · “LIKE DISSOLVES LIKE” PREDICTIONS (6.05)

Predict whether each pair will mix/dissolve well, and give the one-line reason. (Water and table salt are polar/ionic; oil and grease are nonpolar.)

9. Table salt (NaCl) in water. Will it dissolve well? Why?
10. Cooking oil in water. Will it dissolve well? Why?
11. Grease (nonpolar) in a nonpolar degreasing solvent. Will it dissolve well? Why?
▶  Check your thinking — Part C answer key
9. Yes. NaCl is ionic and water is polar — “like dissolves like.” Water's charged ends form strong ion–dipole attractions that pull the ions out of the lattice (hydration).
10. No. Oil is nonpolar and water is polar — not “like.” Water's hydrogen bonds cling to each other and exclude the nonpolar oil, so the two separate into layers.
11. Yes. Both grease and the solvent are nonpolar — “like dissolves like.” Comparable (London dispersion) attractions let the grease mix in. (This is why nonpolar solvents clean grease that water can't.)
📊 PART D · CLASSIFY THE ELECTROLYTE (6.05)

For each substance dissolved in water, classify it as a strong electrolyte, weak electrolyte, or nonelectrolyte, and say whether a bulb-and-battery tester would glow brightly, dimly, or not at all.

12. Hydrochloric acid (HCl), a strong acid.
13. Ethanol (a molecular alcohol).
14. Ammonia (NH3), a weak base.
15. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH), a soluble strong base.
16. Tie it together: two clear glasses both contain a dissolved solid and look identical, but one lights the bulb and the other doesn't. What single thing must be different about what happened when each solid dissolved?
▶  Check your thinking — Part D answer key
12. Strong electrolyte — HCl is a strong acid that ionizes essentially completely — bulb glows brightly.
13. Nonelectrolyte — ethanol dissolves as whole, neutral molecules and forms no ions — bulb does not glow.
14. Weak electrolyte — ammonia only partially ionizes — bulb glows dimly.
15. Strong electrolyte — NaOH is a soluble strong base that dissociates completely into Na⁺ and OH⁻ — bulb glows brightly.
16. One solid broke into ions when it dissolved (an electrolyte — free charges can carry a current, so the bulb lights), while the other dissolved as whole, neutral molecules (a nonelectrolyte — no free charges, so the bulb stays dark). Dissolving and conducting are two different questions.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Part A: all four solids classified by type with the requested property reasoning.
☐
Part B: solubility-curve items answered — saturated/unsaturated/supersaturated identified, the cooled-solution amount estimated, and the gas-vs-solid temperature trend stated.
☐
Items 9–10: the reasoning for the crystallization estimate is written in words before calculating, and a short data-analysis paragraph compares KNO3 and NaCl and draws a purification conclusion.
☐
Part C: three “like dissolves like” predictions with reasons; Part D: four electrolytes classified plus the tie-it-together answer.
☐
Each part checked against its answer key, with anything missed corrected.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
Part A — solid types
5 pts		 All four solids classified with sound property reasoning. Some items missing or unclassified. 5
Part B — solubility curve
5 pts		 Saturation states, the crystallization estimate, and the gas-vs-solid trend all answered from the data. Some curve items missing or misread. 5
Reasoning & data-analysis writing
3 pts · items 9–10		 The reason-in-words-first answer (#9) is written before calculating, and the data-analysis paragraph (#10) compares the two solutes and draws a purification conclusion. Reasoning written only after calculating, or the paragraph is missing/one-line. 3
Parts C & D — dissolving & electrolytes
5 pts		 Three like-dissolves-like predictions and four electrolyte classifications, plus the tie-it-together answer. Some predictions or classifications missing. 5
Self-check
2 pts		 Each part checked against its key and corrections noted. Some parts left unchecked. 2
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer keys let you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.

First, a crystal lattice: a small repeating grid of alternating positive and negative ions, like the inside of a grain of salt, labeled as an ionic solid with its giveaway properties. Then a dissolution station: a few water molecules crowding around the edge of that lattice and pulling ions off into solution — ion–dipole hydration caught in the act — with a small contrast jar showing a nonelectrolyte dissolving as whole molecules. Next week you'll add property-explanation annotations and then record the full walkthrough.
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your notes from Lessons 6.04–6.05 (the four solid types; ion–dipole hydration; strong electrolyte vs nonelectrolyte).
▶  Your IMF_Wk1_YourName snapshot from last week — you'll build right beside it.
▶  About 35–45 minutes in one sitting.
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (your placed objects stay between visits all module)
Session ID: see the pinned OptimaXR Sessions list in this module
Location: States & Solutions Lab
Spawn point: Lab Bench A
When you arrive: your three IMF models from Week 1 are still on the bench. To their right, a Whiteboard IFX shows this week's Step 1 beside an empty grid frame labeled Crystal Lattice and an empty tray labeled Dissolution Station. A sticky note reads “Start here.” You won't have to guess what to do.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
These steps follow the way a scientist actually investigates: Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend. Don't skip the predict step — committing a prediction before the water touches the lattice is the point.
1
Observe. Confirm your Week 1 IMF models are still on the bench and read the Whiteboard IFX. From the IFX object library, spawn spheres and build a crystal lattice — a small repeating grid of alternating positive and negative ions (an NaCl-style ionic lattice, e.g., a 3×3×3 block of alternating Na+ and Cl−), using two colors so the ions are easy to tell apart. Label it an ionic solid with a sticky note listing its giveaway properties: high melting point, hard but brittle, conducts only when molten or dissolved. Leave open space to the right for the Week 3 annotations.
2
Question. On a sticky note, write the question you are about to investigate: “When water meets this ionic lattice, what happens to its ions — and will the result carry an electric current?” Place it on the bench beside the lattice.
3
Predict — before you build the dissolution. On a second sticky note, commit a prediction: when water reaches the lattice, will the ions break free? Will the salt solution conduct? And will a jar of a molecular solute like sugar conduct? Write down what you expect and why. This note is your committed prediction — do not change it after you see what happens.
4
Investigate. Build the dissolution station: place a few water molecules at the lattice edge with their negative (oxygen) ends toward a positive ion and their positive (hydrogen) ends toward a negative ion. Pull one Na+ and one Cl− off the lattice and surround each with water — show them as hydrated, free ions drifting away.
5
Analyze. Label the freed ions Na+(aq) and Cl−(aq) and the attraction as ion–dipole (hydration). Then place a small contrast jar showing a few whole, neutral molecules dissolving without breaking apart, labeled nonelectrolyte (e.g., sugar). Compare the two: the salt released free ions, the sugar did not. Check both against your committed prediction from step 3 — were you right?
6
Defend. Place a signed sticky note stating a claim with its evidence and reasoning: “Claim: salt water is a strong electrolyte and sugar water is not. Evidence: the lattice released free Na+(aq) and Cl−(aq), while the sugar stayed as whole molecules. Reasoning: only free charges can carry a current, so only the salt solution conducts.” Sign your name.
7
Extend. On one last sticky note, predict what a weak electrolyte (such as vinegar / acetic acid) would look like at this scale — how would its picture differ from both the salt (fully ionized) and the sugar (no ions)? You'll build toward property-explanation annotations next week.
💾
Save & capture. Lock the lattice, the water molecules, and your notes so they aren't bumped, save a snapshot named IMF_Wk2_YourName (your project's saved progress for next week), and take one in-headset screenshot showing the labeled crystal lattice, the dissolution station (water pulling ions off, the hydrated Na+(aq)/Cl−(aq) labels, and the nonelectrolyte contrast jar), and your claim note. That screenshot is what you'll submit.
Need to stop partway? Because the Session is persistent, your placed and locked exhibits will be waiting when you return. Save the IMF_Wk2_YourName snapshot before you log out so nothing is lost.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
1. Upload your in-headset screenshot of the labeled crystal lattice, the dissolution station, and your claim note to this Canvas assignment.
2. In the comment box, write a short CER reflection (2–4 sentences): a Claim about which solution conducts, the Evidence you built (salt released free Na+(aq)/Cl−(aq); sugar stayed whole molecules), and your Reasoning (why free ions are what let a solution carry a current). Add one sentence comparing the result to the prediction you committed in step 3. (This reflection is used when your work appears in the class gallery walk later this module.)
⏱️ TIME
About 35–45 minutes in the headset.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA (COMPLETION-BASED)
☐
A crystal lattice of alternating positive/negative ions is built and labeled as an ionic solid with its properties.
☐
A dissolution station shows water molecules pulling ions off the lattice (ion–dipole hydration), with freed Na+(aq) and Cl−(aq) labeled.
☐
The strong electrolyte (ions → conducts) and a nonelectrolyte contrast jar (whole molecules → doesn't conduct) are both labeled.
☐
A prediction was committed on a sticky note before the dissolution was built, then compared with what happened; a signed claim note gives claim + evidence + reasoning.
☐
Screenshot uploaded and a short CER reflection (claim, evidence, reasoning) written. IMF_Wk2_YourName snapshot saved for next week.

Week 3 · Hands-On (Excel)
Colligative-Property Calculations
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: the two colligative equations — ΔTf = i · Kf · m and ΔTb = i · Kb · m (6.07) — and the van 't Hoff factor i (sugar 1, NaCl 2, CaCl₂ 3). Here you'll run them across several solutions in Excel, where the spreadsheet does the repeating arithmetic so you can watch how the freezing- and boiling-point shifts grow with molality and with the particle count.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work, and it rehearses the colligative reasoning your module property-argument writing assignment can draw on.
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
In Excel, you'll build a table that computes the freezing-point depression (ΔTf) and boiling-point elevation (ΔTb) for six water solutions that vary in both molality and van 't Hoff factor i. You'll then find each solution's new freezing point and boiling point, graph ΔTf versus molality, and answer a few questions about the pattern you see. The spreadsheet handles the repeated multiplication — your job is to set up the formulas correctly and read what the numbers reveal.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Two things change how far a freezing point drops — how concentrated the solution is, and how many particles each solute releases. Which one can you control by choosing a different salt, and what does the graph reveal about the other?
✏️ EXPLAIN YOUR REASONING FIRST — BEFORE YOU CALCULATE
Before you build a single formula, write two or three sentences in your notebook (or a text box in the sheet): looking only at the six solutions in the table, which one do you predict will have the lowest freezing point, and why? Reason in words from ΔTf = i · Kf · m — talk about both the molality and the van 't Hoff factor — before the spreadsheet does any arithmetic. You'll test your prediction against your computed numbers at the end.
▶  Check your reasoning (open only after you've committed a prediction)
The lowest freezing point should be Solution 4 (2.00 m NaCl). Its particle molality i · m = 2 × 2.00 = 4.0 is the highest in the table — higher even than Solution 6 (CaCl₂, i · m = 3 × 1.00 = 3.0), because the large molality outweighs CaCl₂'s larger i. So ΔTf is largest for Solution 4 (7.44 °C, freezing at −7.44 °C). If you predicted CaCl₂, that's a reasonable instinct — it shows exactly why you must compare i · m, not i alone.
🔢 CONSTANTS & REFERENCE YOU'LL NEED
Kf(water) = 1.86 °C/m  ·  Kb(water) = 0.512 °C/m
New freezing point = 0 °C − ΔTf  ·  New boiling point = 100 °C + ΔTb
van 't Hoff factor i: sugar/glucose = 1, NaCl = 2, CaCl₂ = 3.
📊 YOUR DATA · SIX WATER SOLUTIONS

Type this table into Excel exactly as shown. Each row is a different solution in water.

Solution Solute Molality m (mol/kg) van 't Hoff i
1Sugar0.501
2Glucose1.001
3NaCl1.002
4NaCl2.002
5CaCl₂0.503
6CaCl₂1.003
📝 WHAT TO DO IN EXCEL
1
Enter the six-row table with headers in row 1: Solution, Solute, Molality m, i. Put your two constants in cells off to the side, e.g. Kf = 1.86 and Kb = 0.512.
2
Add a ΔTf (°C) column: i × Kf × m, e.g. =D2*$G$1*C2 (point at your i, your Kf constant with $ locks, and your molality). Fill down all six rows.
3
Add a ΔTb (°C) column: i × Kb × m, e.g. =D2*$G$2*C2. Fill down all six rows.
4
Add a Freezing point (°C) column: =0-E2 (zero minus your ΔTf). Add a Boiling point (°C) column: =100+F2.
5
Graph ΔTf vs molality. Select your Molality column and your ΔTf column, insert a Scatter (XY) chart, and title it “Freezing-point depression vs molality.” Label the x-axis molality (mol/kg) and the y-axis ΔTf (°C).
6
In cells or a text box below the table, answer the three Analysis Questions below.
❓ ANALYSIS QUESTIONS (answer in your spreadsheet)
A. Compare Solution 3 (1.00 m NaCl) and Solution 6 (1.00 m CaCl₂). They have the same molality, yet different ΔTf values. Which one depresses the freezing point more, and which factor in ΔTf = i · Kf · m explains the difference?
B. Look at the two NaCl rows (Solutions 3 and 4). When you doubled the molality from 1.00 m to 2.00 m, what happened to ΔTf? What does that tell you about the shape of your ΔTf-vs-molality graph (for a fixed solute)?
C. Every freezing point you computed is below 0 °C and every boiling point is above 100 °C. In one or two sentences, explain in molecular terms why dissolving any of these solutes pushes the freezing point down and the boiling point up.
D. (Data-analysis write-up.) Write a short paragraph — three or four sentences — interpreting your ΔTf-vs-molality graph in words. Describe the shape of the line, say what its slope represents in the equation ΔTf = i · Kf · m, and explain how a line drawn for CaCl₂ would compare to the line for NaCl. Finally, state whether the numbers confirmed the prediction you wrote at the start.
▶  Check your work — answer key
Computed results (Kf = 1.86, Kb = 0.512):
• Sol 1 — sugar, 0.50 m, i = 1: ΔTf = 1 × 1.86 × 0.50 = 0.93 °C (FP −0.93 °C); ΔTb = 1 × 0.512 × 0.50 = 0.256 °C (BP 100.256 °C).
• Sol 2 — glucose, 1.00 m, i = 1: ΔTf = 1 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 1.86 °C (FP −1.86 °C); ΔTb = 1 × 0.512 × 1.00 = 0.512 °C (BP 100.512 °C).
• Sol 3 — NaCl, 1.00 m, i = 2: ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 3.72 °C (FP −3.72 °C); ΔTb = 2 × 0.512 × 1.00 = 1.024 °C (BP 101.024 °C).
• Sol 4 — NaCl, 2.00 m, i = 2: ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 2.00 = 7.44 °C (FP −7.44 °C); ΔTb = 2 × 0.512 × 2.00 = 2.048 °C (BP 102.048 °C).
• Sol 5 — CaCl₂, 0.50 m, i = 3: ΔTf = 3 × 1.86 × 0.50 = 2.79 °C (FP −2.79 °C); ΔTb = 3 × 0.512 × 0.50 = 0.768 °C (BP 100.768 °C).
• Sol 6 — CaCl₂, 1.00 m, i = 3: ΔTf = 3 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 5.58 °C (FP −5.58 °C); ΔTb = 3 × 0.512 × 1.00 = 1.536 °C (BP 101.536 °C).

A. CaCl₂ (Solution 6, ΔTf = 5.58 °C) depresses the freezing point more than NaCl (Solution 3, ΔTf = 3.72 °C), even though both are 1.00 m. The difference is the van 't Hoff factor i: CaCl₂ releases 3 particles per formula unit (i = 3) versus NaCl's 2 (i = 2), and colligative properties count particles. The ratio is exactly 3/2: 5.58 / 3.72 = 1.5.
B. Doubling the molality (1.00 m → 2.00 m) doubled ΔTf (3.72 °C → 7.44 °C). For a fixed solute, ΔTf is directly proportional to molality, so the graph of ΔTf vs molality is a straight line through the origin — its slope is i · Kf.
C. Dissolved particles get in the way of the solvent molecules organizing into a solid lattice, so the solution must be cooled below 0 °C before it can freeze (freezing-point depression). The same particles lower the solvent's vapor pressure, so the solution must be heated above 100 °C before its vapor pressure matches the surrounding air and it boils (boiling-point elevation).

D. The ΔTf-vs-molality graph is a straight line through the origin — for a fixed solute, ΔTf is directly proportional to molality. The line's slope is i · Kf: for NaCl the slope is 2 × 1.86 = 3.72 °C per unit molality, and a CaCl₂ line would be steeper (slope 3 × 1.86 = 5.58) because its larger van 't Hoff factor raises the slope. The computed numbers confirm the opening prediction: the lowest freezing point belongs to 2.00 m NaCl (ΔTf = 7.44 °C), because its particle molality i · m = 4.0 beats every other row.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Build this in Microsoft Excel from your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_ColligativeData_CHEM1H, save it to your Optima → Science OneDrive course folder, and submit through Canvas. New here? See the pinned “M365 Setup & File Organization Guide” page in this module.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: locking a constant with absolute references ($) and inserting a labeled scatter (XY) chart in Excel.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Data entered, with working ΔTf and ΔTb columns filled down all six solutions using formulas (not typed-in numbers).
☐
Freezing-point and boiling-point columns computed, and a labeled ΔTf-vs-molality scatter chart inserted.
☐
The opening prediction written before calculating, all four Analysis Questions answered (including the written graph interpretation, D), then checked against the answer key.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
ΔTf & ΔTb columns
8 pts		 ΔTf and ΔTb computed with formulas, filled down all six solutions. Some rows missing, or numbers typed by hand instead of formulas. 8
FP/BP & graph
6 pts		 Freezing- and boiling-point columns computed, and a labeled ΔTf-vs-molality scatter chart inserted. Columns or chart missing, or chart not labeled. 6
Prediction, analysis + self-check
6 pts		 Prediction written first; all four questions (incl. the written graph interpretation D) answered, then checked and corrected. Prediction missing, or some questions missing or not checked. 6
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer key lets you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M6 W3 Hands-On — Colligative-Property Calculations (Excel)
Upload your Excel file (.xlsx) through Canvas (OneDrive tab or file upload).
If a formula gives a result you don't trust, submit what you have with a note about where you got stuck — that's useful information, not a penalty.

🧘 PREFER NOT TO USE A HEADSET?
A full non-VR alternate — “Add Property-Explanation Annotations (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the exact same objectives and earns the same credit. Do one pathway, not both.
📚 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
This is the final build of your module-long Intermolecular Forces & States Model. Over the last two weeks you built molecular models of the three intermolecular forces (Week 1) and a crystal lattice with a dissolution station (Week 2). This week you connect the micro to the macro: you'll add property-explanation annotations — short labeled notes that tie each model to a real, observable property it causes. After this build, your model is complete and ready for the recorded walkthrough that is your module project. No new objects this week — the work is the explaining.
🔬 WORK LIKE AN INVESTIGATOR

▶  Your notes from Lessons 6.01–6.07 (IMFs → properties; lattice types → properties; colligative freezing-point depression ΔTf = i · Kf · m).

On your ionic lattice, add a note linking structure to property: e.g. “Strong ionic bonds in a rigid lattice → high melting point; brittle (shifting a layer brings like charges together and it shatters).”
4
At your dissolution station, add a colligative note: e.g. “Dissolved salt lowers water's freezing point: ΔTf = i · Kf · m. For 1.00 m NaCl, ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 3.72 °C, so it freezes at −3.72 °C — why salt melts ice on roads.”

Pick one of your model→property links and defend it: Claim — state the property; Evidence — the structural feature in your model (the hydrogen bonds, the ionic lattice, or the dissolved ions with ΔTf = i · Kf · m); Reasoning — why that structure produces that property.
