Module 6 Writing Assignment
Why Matter Behaves — A Scientific Argument
Word (.docx) · 100 pts · teacher-reviewed
📚 THE TASK
All module you have argued one idea from many angles: the properties we can see and measure are written into the forces between particles. Why does one liquid boil long before another? Why does ice float? Why does salt thrown on a winter road melt the ice? None of these are arbitrary — each follows from intermolecular forces or from what dissolved particles do to a solvent.
In this assignment you will write a scientific argument: make a claim about an observed property, then defend it with molecular-level evidence and clear reasoning. Choose one of the two prompts below.
PROMPT A · BOILING-POINT ORDERING
Three substances of similar molar mass — ethane (C2H6), formaldehyde (CH2O), and ethanol (C2H5OH) — have very different boiling points (−89 °C, −19 °C, and +78 °C). Argue why they line up in that order, from the intermolecular forces each one has.
PROMPT B · WHY ROAD SALT MELTS ICE
Cities scatter salt (NaCl, and sometimes CaCl2) on icy roads in winter. Argue why dissolved salt lowers the freezing point of water — and why CaCl2 works at even lower temperatures than NaCl — using colligative behavior. Support it with a freezing-point-depression calculation.
You'll write it in Microsoft Word, organized into the argument sections listed further down.
⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS
This argument is one of only two teacher-reviewed pieces in Module 6 (the other is your Intermolecular Forces & States Model VR project). Your teacher reads it personally and responds to your reasoning — so make it your careful best, and connect every claim to the molecular level.
🧮 YOUR TOOLKIT (USE THESE EXACT IDEAS & VALUES)
IMF strength (similar-size molecules): hydrogen bonding > dipole-dipole > London dispersion. Stronger forces → higher boiling/melting point.
Hydrogen bonding requires: H bonded to N, O, or F (so an –OH or –NH group enables it).
Freezing-point depression: ΔTf = i · Kf · m, with Kf(water) = 1.86 °C/m and the van’t Hoff factor i = particles per formula unit (NaCl → 2, CaCl2 → 3, sugar/glucose → 1). New freezing point = 0 °C − ΔTf.
Colligative properties depend on the number of dissolved particles, not their identity.
🧠 YOUR REASONING TOOLKIT (how to build the argument)
Use these steps in your own words — don't just copy the headings.
Step 1 — Identify the forces (Prompt A) or the particles (Prompt B).
A: for each molecule, name every intermolecular force it has (every molecule has London dispersion; polar ones add dipole-dipole; an –OH group adds hydrogen bonding). B: state how many particles each formula unit releases when it dissolves (NaCl → Na+ + Cl− = 2; CaCl2 → Ca2+ + 2 Cl− = 3).
Step 2 — Connect force/particles to the property.
A: stronger intermolecular forces take more energy to overcome, so they raise the boiling point. B: more dissolved particles lower the freezing point more (and raise the boiling point) — that's colligative behavior.
Step 3 — Put a number on it.
A: use the given boiling points to confirm your ordering matches the force strength. B: compute ΔTf for 1.00 m NaCl and for 1.00 m CaCl2 and report each solution's freezing point — show the math.
📝 STRUCTURE: WRITE THESE ARGUMENT SECTIONS
1
Claim. One or two clear sentences stating your answer (e.g., “Ethanol boils highest because it is the only one of the three that can hydrogen-bond,” or “Salt lowers water's freezing point because dissolved ions are a colligative effect, and CaCl2 works better because it releases more particles.”).
2
Molecular-level Evidence. Identify the intermolecular forces (A) or the dissolved particles (B) for each substance. A small labeled sketch or structure helps — show where the –OH is, or how each formula unit breaks into ions.
3
Reasoning. Tie the evidence to the property with the correct rule (stronger IMF → higher boiling point; more dissolved particles → lower freezing point). Include your calculation: confirm the boiling-point order against the given values (A), or compute ΔTf = i·Kf·m and the freezing point for each salt (B). Show every step with units.
4
Real-world link. Connect your argument to something observable: why a fuel like ethane is a gas at room temperature while ethanol is a pourable liquid (A), or why a city might switch from NaCl to CaCl2 on the coldest nights (B).
5
Address a counter-case. Name one reasonable objection to your claim and answer it with evidence — a real argument anticipates the other side. A: for example, “Doesn't the heaviest molecule always boil highest?” Here the three have similar molar masses, so it is the type of intermolecular force, not mass, that sets the order — formaldehyde is polar, yet ethanol still boils higher because hydrogen bonding outranks dipole-dipole. B: for example, “Wouldn't sugar melt ice just as well, since it dissolves too?” No — colligative effects depend on the number of dissolved particles, and one sugar molecule (i = 1) releases fewer particles than NaCl (i = 2) or CaCl2 (i = 3), so sugar depresses the freezing point far less.
6
Conclusion. Restate your claim in light of the evidence and your answer to the counter-case, and name the big idea: the macroscopic property you can measure is set by what happens between particles.
✎ LENGTH & STYLE
Aim for roughly 500–700 words across the five sections, plus your worked calculation (handwritten and photographed in, or typed). Use correct terminology — London dispersion, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding, colligative property, freezing-point depression, van’t Hoff factor, molality. Carry units through your math and keep a sensible number of significant figures. The chemistry and the reasoning are what's graded — not polished prose.
⚠️ A NOTE ON USING AI TOOLS
An AI tool will gladly rank boiling points or compute a freezing point for you — and it can quietly invent a force a molecule doesn't have, forget that London dispersion is in every molecule, or drop the van’t Hoff factor and still sound confident. If you consult one, treat it as a draft to check, never an answer to paste: re-identify the forces yourself from each structure, re-run ΔTf = i·Kf·m by hand, and make sure its reasoning matches the molecular evidence before you trust it. The instrument proposes; your argument verifies. That is exactly the skill this assignment is built to grow.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Write your argument in Microsoft Word from your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_PropertyArgument_CHEM1H, save it to your Optima → Science OneDrive course folder, and submit through Canvas. New here? See the pinned “M365 Setup & File Organization Guide” page in this module.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: structuring an argument with headings in Word and inserting a small labeled diagram or a photographed work page. If your teacher returns comments for revision, turn on Track Changes before revising.
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED (TEACHER RUBRIC — build natively as a Canvas Rubric)
Criterion Full marks Developing Pts
Claim A clear, specific, scientifically defensible claim that directly answers the chosen prompt. Claim vague, missing, or only restates the question. 12
Molecular-level evidence Correctly identifies the intermolecular forces in each molecule (A) or the dissolved particles per formula unit (B); structures/sketches accurate. Forces or particle counts partly wrong (e.g., London dispersion omitted; i miscounted). 25
Reasoning & calculation Links evidence to the property with the correct rule, and the calculation (boiling-point order confirmed, or ΔTf = i·Kf·m and freezing points) is correct with units and shown work. Reasoning asserted without the rule, or calculation wrong / missing / unshown. 28
Counter-case addressed Names a reasonable objection and answers it with molecular-level evidence (mass vs IMF type; particle count vs mere dissolving), strengthening the argument. No counter-case, or the objection is dismissed without evidence. 12
Real-world link Connects the argument to a genuine, correct observation in the everyday world. Link missing, generic, or scientifically off. 10
Conclusion & communication Conclusion ties back to the claim and names the big idea; correct terminology, clear organized argument form. Conclusion thin or just restates numbers; terms misused; disorganized. 13
Total: 100 pts
The molecular-level evidence and the reasoning/calculation carry the most weight, and answering a counter-case with evidence earns real credit — a correct ordering or freezing point with no molecular explanation earns little. Argue from the particles up.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M6 Scientific Argument — Why Matter Behaves
Submit your Word .docx through Canvas (OneDrive tab or file upload). If your teacher returns it with comments, revise with Track Changes on and resubmit as a _Revision1 file.

VR Project · 100 pts · teacher-reviewed · in-VR video recording
🧘 PREFER NOT TO USE A HEADSET?
A full non-VR alternate — “Intermolecular Forces & States Model — Narrated Walkthrough (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the same objectives and is graded on the same rubric. Do one pathway, not both.
📚 THE BIG PICTURE
Across this module you've built an Intermolecular Forces & States Model in OptimaXR, one week at a time, and used it to answer a single question: why does matter behave the way it does — why some things melt easily and others don't, why ice floats, why salt dissolves and oil won't, why road salt melts ice? Week 1 you built molecular-scale models of the three intermolecular forces — London dispersion, dipole-dipole, and a hydrogen bond between two water molecules; Week 2 you added a crystal lattice and a dissolution station showing water pulling ions off the lattice; Week 3 you added property-explanation annotations that link each model to something you can actually observe. Now you bring it all together.
Your task is to record a guided video walkthrough inside the headset — a short tour in which you narrate the chemistry of your model, connecting invisible forces between molecules to the visible, measurable properties of liquids, solids, and solutions. This recorded explanation, not a static screenshot, is what earns the grade. The model is the stage; your spoken reasoning is the performance.
⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS
This walkthrough is one of only two teacher-reviewed pieces in Module 6 (the other is your property-argument writing assignment). Your teacher will watch your recording and respond to your reasoning personally — so make it your best thinking, clearly explained.
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your finished build — the IMF_Final_YourName snapshot from the Week 3 build, including the Week 1 IMF models, the Week 2 lattice and dissolution station, and the Week 3 property annotations.
▶  A quiet space and about 30–40 minutes (planning, one or two recording takes, and submitting).
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (your finished build is waiting)
Session ID: see the pinned OptimaXR Sessions list in this module
Session name: States & Solutions Lab
Location: States & Solutions Lab
Spawn point: Lab Entrance
🎤 WHAT YOUR RECORDING MUST COVER (aim for 3–5 minutes)
1
Open at the entrance. Introduce your model and state the big question it answers: how do the invisible forces between molecules decide the visible properties we can see and measure — melting and boiling, dissolving, floating, freezing?
2
The three intermolecular forces (Week 1). Walk through your models of London dispersion (in all molecules; the only force in nonpolar ones), dipole-dipole (between polar molecules), and hydrogen bonding (your two water molecules — H bonded to O reaching for a neighbor's lone pair). Rank them by strength and say the key rule: stronger intermolecular forces mean a higher boiling and melting point.
3
Solids & the crystal lattice (Week 2). Show your lattice and name what kind of solid it is (ionic, like NaCl). Explain why that structure gives the properties it does — an ionic lattice is hard but brittle, has a high melting point, and conducts only when melted or dissolved (the ions must be free to move).
4
Dissolving & electrolytes (Week 2). At your dissolution station, show water molecules surrounding and pulling ions off the lattice (ion–dipole hydration). Explain “like dissolves like,” and why salt water conducts electricity (a strong electrolyte — full of free ions) while sugar water does not (a nonelectrolyte — whole molecules, no ions).
5
From model to measurable property (Week 3). Read your property annotations and tie at least two of them to numbers: why ice floats (hydrogen bonds hold an open, less-dense lattice), and a colligative example — dissolved particles lower the freezing point, which is why 1.00 m of salt (NaCl) lowers water's freezing point by about 3.72 °C (ΔTf = i·Kf·m = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00), so the road no longer ices at 0 °C.
6
Close by explaining the evidence — then name the limits. Tie each claim back to what your model actually shows: your IMF models are the evidence for the observed macroscopic properties — the open hydrogen-bonded lattice is why ice floats, the ionic lattice is why salt is brittle and high-melting, and the dissolved particles are why salt lowers the freezing point (ΔTf = i·Kf·m). Then state one honest limit — “like dissolves like” and colligative ideality are models that break down for real solutions. End on the through-line: the macroscopic properties we measure are written into the forces between molecules — read the forces and you can predict, and put numbers on, the behavior.
How to record: Use OptimaXR's video recording feature to capture your narrated tour from inside the headset (start the recording from the menu/tablet, walk and talk, then stop and save). If your setup can't capture in-headset audio, record your screen with narration instead. Aim for one clean take; a second take is fine.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
1. Upload your video recording (3–5 minutes) to this Canvas assignment as a media/file upload.
2. In the comment box, list the three weekly builds in one line each (Wk1 the three IMF models, Wk2 lattice + dissolution station, Wk3 property annotations) so your teacher can see the iteration behind the final build.
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED (TEACHER RUBRIC — build natively as a Canvas Rubric)
Criterion Full marks Developing Pts
Evidence-based scientific reasoning The walkthrough leads with evidence and reasoning: the three intermolecular forces and their strength order are used to explain the observed properties (why stronger IMFs raise the boiling and melting point); the crystal lattice and the dissolution station are used to justify why an ionic solid is brittle and why salt water conducts while sugar water does not; and the model→property links are argued from the molecular models to the macroscopic observations (an open hydrogen-bonded lattice → ice floats; dissolved particles → freezing-point depression, ΔTf = i·Kf·m). Every claim is tied back to the molecular evidence the model shows. States conclusions without evidence; names forces and properties without explaining why the structure produces the property. 35
Accurate chemistry The chemistry is correct — the three IMFs (London dispersion in all molecules, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding requiring H bonded to N, O, or F), the ionic crystal-lattice solid type and its properties, ion–dipole hydration and the strong-vs-nonelectrolyte distinction, and the colligative calculation (1.00 m NaCl → ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 3.72 °C) — and the demonstrated values are right. Contains chemistry errors; IMFs mislabeled or demonstrated values wrong. 25
Clear narration & model The narrated tour is organized and easy to follow, and the build (the three IMF models, the crystal lattice, the dissolution station, the property annotations) is recognizable and correct at a high-school level; audio and visuals are usable. Disorganized or hard to follow; models confused, missing, or don't show the chemistry; key parts inaudible. 20
Week-by-week iteration The build clearly shows all three stages (IMF models, lattice + dissolution station, property annotations), and the comment lists the three weekly builds. Only some stages present; little sign of building over time. 12
Uncertainty & limits reflection Names an honest limit — “like dissolves like” and colligative ideality are models that break down (real solutions deviate; a strong electrolyte's measured van’t Hoff factor runs slightly below the ideal whole number because of ion pairing) — showing the honesty of the quantitative. No acknowledgment of the model's limits or of real-solution deviations. 8
Total: 100 pts
The same five criteria are used for the non-VR alternate. A high-school-level model is expected — evidence-based scientific reasoning carries the most weight.

Week 1 · Hands-On
Entropy, Free Energy & the ΔG Calculation
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: the sign rules for ΔS (7.01), the Second-Law idea that the total entropy decides spontaneity (7.02), and a first look ahead at the single number that fuses energy and entropy — the Gibbs free energy, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Here you'll predict signs, read the spontaneity sign chart, and run the ΔG calculation by hand — including the unit trap that snares almost everyone.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work. Do it on paper or in your notebook — no spreadsheet needed this week.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Energy (ΔH) and entropy (ΔS) sometimes pull in the same direction and sometimes fight each other. How does a single number, ΔG, settle the argument — and when does temperature get the deciding vote?
🧰 YOUR TOOLBOX
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS  (T in kelvin) ·  ΔG < 0 spontaneous ·  ΔG > 0 nonspontaneous ·  ΔG = 0 at equilibrium.
Kelvin: T(K) = T(°C) + 273  (so 25 °C = 298 K).
⚠️ THE UNIT TRAP — READ THIS TWICE
ΔH is usually given in kJ, but ΔS is given in J/K. Before you subtract, you MUST put them in the same unit — convert ΔS from J/K to kJ/K by dividing by 1000 (e.g. 50 J/K = 0.050 kJ/K). Forgetting this makes your TΔS term 1000× too big and your answer nonsense. Convert first, subtract second.
📝 PART A · PREDICT THE SIGN OF ΔS (items 1–3)

For each process, state whether the entropy of the system increases (ΔS > 0) or decreases (ΔS < 0), and give a one-line reason.

1. Dry ice sublimes: CO2(s) → CO2(g).
2. Steam condenses on a mirror: H2O(g) → H2O(l).
3. 2 SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2 SO3(g).
📊 PART B · READ THE SPONTANEITY SIGN CHART (items 4–5)

Use the chart below: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS decides spontaneity. For each case, say whether it is spontaneous at all temperatures, no temperatures, only low T, or only high T.

ΔH ΔS Spontaneous when…
− (exothermic)+ (increase)at ALL temperatures
+ (endothermic)− (decrease)at NO temperatures
− (exothermic)− (decrease)only at LOW T
+ (endothermic)+ (increase)only at HIGH T
4. A reaction has ΔH = −120 kJ and ΔS = +150 J/K. Spontaneous at all, none, low, or high T?
5. A reaction has ΔH = +85 kJ and ΔS = −40 J/K. Spontaneous at all, none, low, or high T?
🧮 PART C · COMPUTE ΔG AND DECIDE (items 6–8)

Use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Convert ΔS to kJ/K first. Show TΔS, then ΔG, then state spontaneous or not.

6. ΔH = −100 kJ, ΔS = +50 J/K, T = 298 K. Find TΔS and ΔG. Spontaneous?
7. ΔH = +30 kJ, ΔS = +90 J/K, T = 500 K. Find TΔS and ΔG. Spontaneous? (Watch the units!)
8. ΔH = +30 kJ, ΔS = +90 J/K, T = 200 K. Find TΔS and ΔG. Spontaneous? Compare your answer to item 7 — what role did temperature play?
💡 WORKED EXAMPLE (the method for item 6)
ΔH = −100 kJ, ΔS = +50 J/K, T = 298 K.
Step 1 — fix the units: ΔS = 50 J/K = 0.050 kJ/K.
Step 2 — TΔS: 298 K × 0.050 kJ/K = 14.9 kJ.
Step 3 — ΔG: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −100 − 14.9 = −114.9 kJ.
Verdict: ΔG < 0, so the reaction is spontaneous. (Both ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, so the sign chart already promised “spontaneous at all T” — the calculation confirms it.)
✍️ PART D · EXPLAIN YOUR REASONING IN WORDS (item 9)

Numbers alone aren't understanding. Put the chemistry into a sentence or two of your own words — do this before you open the model answer.

9. Items 7 and 8 are the same reaction (ΔH = +30 kJ, ΔS = +90 J/K) at two different temperatures, yet one is spontaneous and the other is not. In 2–3 sentences, explain why temperature changed the verdict — referring to how the TΔS term competes with ΔH in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. (Write your explanation first; then check it below.)
▶  Model answer — open only after you've written yours
Because ΔH is positive (endothermic), energy alone opposes the reaction; only the entropy term can make ΔG negative. Since ΔS is positive, the TΔS term grows as temperature rises — at 500 K, TΔS = 45 kJ is large enough to overcome the +30 kJ ΔH, so ΔG is negative and the reaction is spontaneous; at 200 K, TΔS is only 18 kJ, too small to overcome ΔH, so ΔG is positive and it is not. Temperature is the deciding vote whenever ΔH and ΔS push in opposite directions (here, both positive) — a higher T lets entropy win.
🤖 AI IS AN INSTRUMENT, NOT AN ORACLE
If you ask an AI tool to compute a ΔG, it will often forget to convert ΔS from J/K to kJ/K — returning an answer about 1000 times too large, or even the wrong sign. Treat any AI result as a claim to verify, not an answer: redo the J→kJ conversion and the subtraction by hand, and confirm the sign matches the sign chart. Reasoning from the evidence is the skill; the calculator is just an instrument.
🔑 CHECK YOUR WORK
▶  Answer key — open after you've tried all eight
Part A — sign of ΔS:
1. ΔS > 0 (increase). Solid → gas frees particles into a huge volume; sublimation is a big jump in disorder.
2. ΔS < 0 (decrease). Gas → liquid pulls free-flying molecules into a tight liquid — fewer arrangements.
3. ΔS < 0 (decrease). 3 moles of gas (2 SO2 + 1 O2) become 2 moles of gas (2 SO3) — fewer gas moles.

Part B — sign chart:
4. ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0 → spontaneous at ALL temperatures (both factors favor it).
5. ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0 → spontaneous at NO temperatures (both factors oppose it).

Part C — ΔG calculations (convert ΔS to kJ/K first!):
6. ΔS = 0.050 kJ/K; TΔS = 298 × 0.050 = 14.9 kJ; ΔG = −100 − 14.9 = −114.9 kJ → spontaneous (ΔG < 0).
7. ΔS = 0.090 kJ/K; TΔS = 500 × 0.090 = 45 kJ; ΔG = +30 − 45 = −15 kJ → spontaneous (ΔG < 0). The big TΔS term overpowered the positive ΔH.
8. ΔS = 0.090 kJ/K; TΔS = 200 × 0.090 = 18 kJ; ΔG = +30 − 18 = +12 kJ → not spontaneous (ΔG > 0). Same reaction as item 7, but the lower temperature shrank TΔS so it could no longer overcome ΔH. This is the “ΔH+, ΔS+ → spontaneous only at HIGH T” case — temperature cast the deciding vote.

Unit-trap check: if any answer came out in the thousands (like −14,900 kJ for item 6), you forgot to convert ΔS from J/K to kJ/K. Divide ΔS by 1000 and redo.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Items 1–3: ΔS sign stated with a one-line reason (phase change or gas-mole count) for each.
☐
Items 4–5: spontaneity classified correctly from the sign chart (all / none / low / high T).
☐
Items 6–8: ΔS converted to kJ/K, TΔS and ΔG shown with units, and a spontaneous / not verdict given.
☐
Item 9: a 2–3 sentence explanation, in your own words, of why temperature changed the verdict — written before checking the model answer.
☐
All work checked against the answer key, with the unit trap confirmed handled.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
ΔS signs (items 1–3)
5 pts		 All three signs given with a correct one-line reason each. Some signs missing or reasons absent. 5
Sign chart (items 4–5)
4 pts		 Both cases classified correctly (all / none / low / high T). One case missing or misclassified. 4
ΔG calculations (items 6–8)
7 pts		 All three computed with units converted, TΔS and ΔG shown, verdict stated. Some steps missing, or the J→kJ conversion skipped. 7
Reasoning in words (item 9)
2 pts		 A clear 2–3 sentence explanation of the temperature effect, written before checking the model answer. Explanation vague, missing, or only restates the numbers. 2
Self-check
2 pts		 Work compared to the answer key and corrections noted. Not checked. 2
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer key lets you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.

Work the eight items in your notebook or on paper, then upload a clear photo or scan (or type your answers directly into the Canvas text box).

4
Investigate. Pick up the process cards (for example: ice melting, steam condensing, salt dissolving, 2 NO2(g) → N2O4(g), a hot drink cooling to room temperature, rust un-rusting back into iron). Drop each into the correct entropy bin (ΔS > 0 or ΔS < 0) and then the correct spontaneity bin, adding a short reason note to each (e.g. “gas formed,” “dissolving,” “temperature up,” “more gas moles.”) Reminder: rust un-rusting and a cool drink reheating itself are nonspontaneous; the rest run on their own.
5
Analyze. Compare your sort to your Prediction note. Which card, if any, surprised you? Flag the one that lowers the system's entropy or absorbs heat yet is still spontaneous — that's the case only the total-entropy rule can explain.

Week 2 · Hands-On
Equilibrium Constant (K) & Reaction Quotient (Q) Problems
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: writing the equilibrium constant K = [products]/[reactants] (each species raised to its coefficient, pure solids and liquids omitted, from 7.04), computing K from equilibrium concentrations, interpreting a large or small K, and comparing the reaction quotient Q to K to predict which way a reaction shifts.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work — the same reasoning your VR demo and your Le Châtelier writing assignment will draw on.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
A single number, K, captures how far a reaction goes before it balances — and a second number, Q, tells you which way a mixture must still move to get there. How do you build each one from a balanced equation, and how do you read what they mean?
🔢 REFERENCE YOU'LL NEED
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD:  K = [C]c[D]d ÷ ([A]a[B]b) — products over reactants, each to its coefficient.
Omit pure solids (s) and pure liquids (l). Include gases (g) and aqueous species (aq) only.
Q has the same form as K but uses current concentrations.   Q < K → shift right;   Q > K → shift left;   Q = K → at equilibrium.
Large K (» 1) → products favored.   Small K (« 1) → reactants favored.
🤖 AI IS AN INSTRUMENT, NOT AN ORACLE
If you ask an AI tool to write a K expression or compare Q to K, treat its answer as a draft to verify, not a final answer. AI chatbots routinely forget to drop pure solids and liquids, mix up which side goes on top, or flip the Q-vs-K conclusion. Check every expression against the two rules yourself, and re-do at least one calculation by hand. The skill being graded is your reasoning, not a copied output.
✏️ THE PROBLEMS (work all nine in your notebook)
Part A — Write the K expression (products/reactants to coefficients; omit pure solids & liquids).
1. 2 NO(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2 NO2(g)
2. N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g)
3. CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g)  (watch the solids!)

Part B — Compute K from equilibrium concentrations.
4. For H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g), at equilibrium [H2] = 0.20 M, [I2] = 0.20 M, [HI] = 1.60 M. Compute Kc.
5. For N2O4(g) ⇌ 2 NO2(g), at equilibrium [N2O4] = 0.40 M and [NO2] = 0.20 M. Compute Kc.

Part C — Compare Q to K to predict the shift. (Same reaction as #4, Kc = 64.)
6. A flask holds [H2] = 1.0 M, [I2] = 1.0 M, [HI] = 1.0 M. Compute Q and predict the shift direction.
7. A flask holds [H2] = 0.10 M, [I2] = 0.10 M, [HI] = 2.0 M. Compute Q and predict the shift direction.

Part D — Interpret the size of K.
8. Reaction X has K = 3 × 108; reaction Y has K = 4 × 10−7. For each, state whether the equilibrium mixture is mostly products or mostly reactants, and which reaction goes “more nearly to completion.”

Part E — Explain your thinking (written reasoning).
9. In 2–3 complete sentences, explain this claim in your own words: “A large K tells you a reaction favors products, but it does not tell you the reaction is fast.” Then add one sentence connecting your answer to the idea of dynamic equilibrium (equal rates, constant — but not zero — concentrations). Write your response before opening the model answer below.
✅ CHECK YOUR WORK
▶  Answer key — reveal after you've tried all eight
Part A — K expressions
1. K = [NO2]2 ÷ ([NO]2[O2]). The coefficient 2 on NO and on NO2 become exponents.
2. K = [NH3]2 ÷ ([N2][H2]3). The 2 and the 3 become exponents.
3. K = [CO2]. Both CaCO3 and CaO are pure solids, so they are omitted — only the gas remains.

Part B — Compute K
4. Kc = [HI]2 ÷ ([H2][I2]) = (1.60)2 ÷ (0.20 × 0.20) = 2.56 ÷ 0.040 = 64. (K » 1, so products are favored.)
5. Kc = [NO2]2 ÷ [N2O4] = (0.20)2 ÷ (0.40) = 0.040 ÷ 0.40 = 0.10. (K < 1, so reactant N2O4 is favored.)

Part C — Q vs K (Kc = 64)
6. Q = (1.0)2 ÷ (1.0 × 1.0) = 1.0. Since Q (1.0) < K (64), the reaction shifts forward (right) — it makes more HI until Q rises to 64.
7. Q = (2.0)2 ÷ (0.10 × 0.10) = 4.0 ÷ 0.010 = 400. Since Q (400) > K (64), the reaction shifts reverse (left) — it remakes H2 and I2 until Q falls to 64.

Part D — Size of K
8. Reaction X (K = 3 × 108, » 1) is mostly products at equilibrium — it goes far to the right and most nearly to completion. Reaction Y (K = 4 × 10−7, « 1) is mostly reactants — very little product forms. X goes more nearly to completion.
💬 CHECK YOUR REASONING (PROBLEM 9)
Write your own 2–3 sentences first — then reveal this to compare. Your wording will differ; look for the same ideas.
▶  Model answer — reveal after you've written your own
A large K describes how far a reaction goes — the equilibrium position sits far toward products, so at equilibrium the mixture is mostly product. But K says nothing about how fast the reaction gets there: speed is a matter of kinetics (activation energy, catalysts, temperature), which is a separate question from the equilibrium position. A reaction can have an enormous K yet be so slow it appears not to react at all without a catalyst. This connects to dynamic equilibrium because K is fixed once the forward and reverse rates become equal; at that point the concentrations hold steady — constant, but not zero and not necessarily equal — even though molecules keep converting in both directions.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All three K expressions written with correct exponents, and pure solids/liquids correctly omitted (problem 3).
☐
Both K calculations (problems 4–5) shown with the setup, not just a final number.
☐
Both Q calculations (problems 6–7) computed and a correct shift direction stated for each.
☐
Problem 8 interpreted (mostly products vs. reactants), then all nine checked against the answer keys.
☐

ICE-Table Calculations & Le Châtelier Shifts
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: Le Châtelier's principle (7.05) — predicting the direction an equilibrium shifts under a concentration, pressure, or temperature stress — and the ICE-table method (7.06) for computing K or an unknown equilibrium concentration. This set puts both to work: you'll predict shifts and run the numbers.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work, and the Le Châtelier reasoning here is exactly what your module CER writing assignment will draw on.
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Work the seven problems and the reasoning question (Problem 8) below in your notebook (no spreadsheet needed this week). Show your ICE tables and the arithmetic for the calculations, and write out your reasoning for Problem 8 in full sentences — the thinking is the point. When you finish, open the answer keys to check yourself and correct anything you missed.
🔢 REMINDERS YOU'LL NEED
• Le Châtelier: a stressed equilibrium shifts to partially counteract the stress. Add → shift away; remove → shift toward. Higher pressure → toward fewer gas moles. For temperature, treat heat as a reactant (endothermic) or product (exothermic). A catalyst does not shift the position.
• ICE table: Initial / Change / Equilibrium; the Change row uses the balanced coefficients (reactants −, products +).
• K expression: K = [products]coeffs / [reactants]coeffs.
📝 THE PROBLEMS (work all seven, plus the reasoning question, in your notebook)
Part A — Predict the Le Châtelier shift (left, right, or no shift):

1. For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), which way does the equilibrium shift if you (a) add more O2, and (b) remove SO3 as it forms?

2. For N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g) (1 mol gas ⇌ 2 mol gas), which way does the equilibrium shift if you (a) increase the pressure by shrinking the container, and (b) add a catalyst?

3. The reaction CO(g) + 2H2(g) ⇌ CH3OH(g) is exothermic. Which way does it shift if you (a) raise the temperature, and (b) lower the temperature?

Part B — Set up an ICE table and solve:

4. For H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), a flask starts with 0.80 M H2 and 0.80 M I2 (no HI). At equilibrium [HI] = 1.20 M. Build the ICE table, find x, and report the equilibrium [H2] and [I2].

5. Using your results from Problem 4, calculate Kc = [HI]² / ([H2][I2]).

6. For N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g), a flask starts with 1.00 M N2O4 and no NO2. At equilibrium [NO2] = 0.40 M. Build the ICE table (Change: −x for N2O4, +2x for NO2), find x, and report the equilibrium [N2O4]. Then compute Kc = [NO2]² / [N2O4].

7. For the reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) with Kc = 4.0, a flask starts with 1.00 M A and no B. Let x be the amount of A that reacts. Set up the ICE table, write Kc = x / (1.00 − x), and solve for x to find the equilibrium [A] and [B].

Part C — Explain your reasoning (write 2–3 sentences):

8. A classmate says, “If we add an iron catalyst to the reaction in Problem 6, we'll get more NO2 at equilibrium.” In your own words, explain whether they are right, and why — connect your answer to what a catalyst does to the forward and reverse reactions. Then check yourself against the model response below.
▶  Check your work — answer key
Part A — shifts:
1. (a) Adding O2 (a reactant) → shifts right. (b) Removing SO3 (a product) → shifts right to replace it.
2. (a) Increasing pressure → shifts toward fewer gas moles: 1 mol (left) vs. 2 mol (right), so shifts left (toward N2O4). (b) A catalyst → no shift (it only speeds the approach to equilibrium).
3. The reaction is exothermic, so heat is a product. (a) Raising T adds a product → shifts left. (b) Lowering T removes a product → shifts right (toward methanol).

Part B — calculations:
4. Change: −x, −x, +2x. [HI] = 2x = 1.20 → x = 0.60. [H2] = 0.80 − 0.60 = 0.20 M; [I2] = 0.20 M.
5. Kc = (1.20)² / (0.20 × 0.20) = 1.44 / 0.04 = 36.
6. Change: −x, +2x. [NO2] = 2x = 0.40 → x = 0.20. [N2O4] = 1.00 − 0.20 = 0.80 M. Kc = (0.40)² / 0.80 = 0.16 / 0.80 = 0.20.
7. ICE: A = 1.00 − x, B = x. Kc = x / (1.00 − x) = 4.0 → x = 4.0(1.00 − x) = 4.0 − 4.0x → 5.0x = 4.0 → x = 0.80. So [A] = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 M and [B] = 0.80 M. (Check: 0.80 / 0.20 = 4.0 ✓.)
▶  Check your reasoning — model response to Problem 8
The classmate is wrong. A catalyst speeds up the forward and the reverse reactions by the same amount, so the system reaches equilibrium faster but arrives at the exact same balance point — the same equilibrium concentrations and the same value of Kc. Because it does not favor one direction over the other, a catalyst never changes how much product forms; it only changes how soon you get there. To actually increase NO2 at equilibrium you would need a real stress, such as raising the temperature (this reaction is endothermic) or lowering the pressure. Your wording can differ — look for these ideas: (1) catalyst speeds both directions equally, (2) equilibrium position / K is unchanged, (3) only the rate of reaching equilibrium changes.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All three Part A shift predictions are answered with a direction (left / right / no shift) and a brief reason.
☐
Each Part B problem shows a labeled ICE table, the value of x, and the requested concentrations or K value.
☐
Problem 8 is answered in 2–3 sentences explaining why a catalyst does or does not change the amount of product at equilibrium.
☐
Work and reasoning checked against the answer keys and corrections noted where needed.

Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
Part A shifts
6 pts		 All three problems answered with direction and reason. Some parts missing or no reason given. 6
Part B ICE & K work
8 pts		 All four problems show an ICE table, x, and the requested results with work. Some problems missing tables/work or answers only. 8
Reasoning & self-check
6 pts		 Problem 8 reasoning written in full sentences; all work compared to the answer keys and corrected. Not checked, or corrections not shown. 6
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer key lets you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.

Le Châtelier Shift Narration
Assignment · 20 pts · ~35–45 min
✔️ THIS IS THE ALTERNATE
This pathway earns the same credit and meets the same objectives as the OptimaXR version. Complete this OR the VR assignment — not both.
📚 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
You'll continue your Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station — a set of diagrams built up across the module — using a PowerPoint deck or a hand-drawn poster. This is Build 3 of 5. You'll work like a scientist: observe a balanced reaction, commit a prediction for how it will react before you diagram, then build a stress panel showing how the equilibrium shifts to partially counteract three stresses — an added reactant, a pressure change, and a temperature change — each with the shift direction labeled, plus a note that a catalyst does not shift the equilibrium. You'll finish by defending your work with a short Claim–Evidence–Reasoning (CER) slide or panel. In Weeks 4–5 you'll add a pH & indicator diagram and a titration setup, then record a short narrated walkthrough.
🎨 CHOOSE ONE FORMAT
Option A — Digital (PowerPoint)
Add new slides to the deck you started in Weeks 1–2: a Prediction slide (your committed guesses first), then one slide each for the three stresses (added reactant, pressure, temperature), each showing the shift direction, a slide noting a catalyst causes no shift, and a closing CER slide (claim, evidence, reasoning).
Option B — Hands-on (poster)
Add a stress panel to your poster: jot your committed predictions first, draw the three stresses with shift arrows and labels, add the “catalyst = no shift” note and a short CER panel (claim, evidence, reasoning), and photograph the updated poster into one document.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
The steps follow a scientist's arc: Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend. You commit a prediction before you diagram, then hold your work up against it.
1
OBSERVE. Pick a reversible reaction to use as your demo (for example, N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, or the N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 demo). Note whether it is exothermic or endothermic, and count the gas moles on each side. Leave room — you'll add more in Weeks 4–5.
2
QUESTION & PREDICT — commit first. Before you diagram anything, ask: if I disturb this balanced system, which way will it move? On your deck (or in a corner of the poster) write a committed prediction for all three stresses now — added reactant, pressure increase, and temperature rise — one arrow each (left / right / no shift). Commit before you investigate; you'll check yourself against these later.
3
INVESTIGATE · Added reactant: draw the reaction with extra reactant added and an arrow showing the shift toward products. Label: “Add reactant → shifts right (consumes the added reactant).”
4
INVESTIGATE · Pressure: show the container squeezed smaller (higher pressure) and an arrow shifting toward the side with fewer moles of gas. Label: “Increase pressure → shifts toward fewer gas moles.”
5
INVESTIGATE · Temperature: write heat on the correct side (product if exothermic, reactant if endothermic), then draw an arrow for the shift when temperature rises. Label: “Heat is a reactant (endo) or product (exo) — treat it like a substance.”
6
ANALYZE. Set each shift beside your committed prediction from Step 2. Where they match, mark a check; where they differ, correct it and add one line naming what you missed (temperature and pressure trip people up most). Then add a summary note: “A catalyst speeds both directions equally — it does NOT shift the equilibrium.” Sign your name.
7
DEFEND — make a CER slide (or poster panel). Add a short Claim–Evidence–Reasoning: Claim — a system at equilibrium counteracts a stress; Evidence — your three labeled shifts; Reasoning — tie it to the particles: a stress changes how often forward vs reverse events happen until the rates rebalance at a new equilibrium. (You'll speak this same CER aloud in the final Week-5 recording.)
8
EXTEND & SAVE. Save your updated file (deck or photo document). Keep it — you'll add the pH & indicator diagram and the titration setup in Weeks 4–5, then record a short narrated walkthrough.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Build Option A in Microsoft PowerPoint from your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_LeChatelierShift_CHEM1H, save it to your Optima → Science OneDrive course folder, and submit through Canvas. New here? See the pinned “M365 Setup & File Organization Guide” page in this module.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: using shapes, arrows & text boxes to diagram a process and its responses on slides.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
1. Upload your file (PowerPoint .pptx, or a document/PDF of your poster photos) — including your prediction, the three labeled shifts, the catalyst note, and your CER — to this Canvas assignment.
2. In the comment box, write a one-sentence caption: name the three stresses and state which way the equilibrium shifts for each.
3. Also in the comment box, add your CER reflection (2–3 sentences): Claim — what a stressed equilibrium does; Evidence — the shifts you diagrammed; Reasoning — why it happens, in terms of forward vs reverse rates.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA (COMPLETION-BASED)
☐
All three stress shifts are diagrammed and labeled with a direction — added reactant (right), pressure increase (toward fewer gas moles), and temperature (using heat as reactant/product).
☐
The temperature shift correctly places heat as a product (exothermic) or reactant (endothermic) based on the reaction chosen.
☐
A committed prediction for all three stresses was written before diagramming, and checked against the finished shifts.
☐
A signed summary note states that a catalyst does not shift the equilibrium.
☐
A CER slide or panel states a claim, cites the three shifts as evidence, and reasons from forward/reverse rates.
☐
File uploaded, named correctly, and a one-sentence caption plus CER reflection written.

Week 4 · Hands-On
pH & pOH Problem Set
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: proton transfer and conjugate pairs (7.07), the pH/pOH conversions and the pH + pOH = 14 rule (7.08), and strong-vs-weak strength with Ka (7.09). Here you'll do the calculations by hand — the real fluency every later acid-base problem depends on.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work. Show your steps, then check yourself against the key.
🔢 FORMULAS & REFERENCE YOU'LL NEED
pH = −log[H3O+]  ·  pOH = −log[OH−]  ·  [H3O+] = 10−pH
pH + pOH = 14.00 (at 25 °C)  ·  Kw = [H3O+][OH−] = 1.0 × 10−14 (25 °C)
Neutral pH = 7  ·  acidic < 7  ·  basic > 7.   Round pH/pOH answers to two decimal places.
📝 DIRECTIONS
Work all eight items in your science notebook (or a document), showing your setup and steps — not just final answers. Use the pH/pOH calculator on Lesson 7.08 to check your arithmetic if you like, but the work must be your own. When you're done, open the answer key and correct anything you missed in a different color.
🧪 THE PROBLEMS (8 ITEMS)
1. A solution has [H3O+] = 1.0 × 10−4 M. Find its pH, and state whether it is acidic, basic, or neutral.
2. A solution has [H3O+] = 1.0 × 10−11 M. Find its pH, and classify it.
3. A solution has a pH of 2.00. Find its [H3O+] (use [H3O+] = 10−pH).
4. A solution has a pH of 8.00. Find its pOH and its [OH−].
5. A cleaning solution has [OH−] = 1.0 × 10−3 M. Find its pOH, then its pH, and classify it.
6. Classify each as acidic, basic, or neutral: (a) pH 6.50, (b) pH 7.00, (c) pH 12.30, (d) pH 4.00.
7. For the reaction HF + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + F−, name both conjugate acid-base pairs and identify which species is the Brønsted-Lowry acid.
8. Three acids have Ka values of 1 × 10−2, 1.8 × 10−5, and 4 × 10−10. Rank them from strongest to weakest acid, and explain in one sentence how Ka tells you.
▶  Check your work — answer key
1. pH = −log(1.0 × 10−4) = 4.00. Below 7, so acidic.
2. pH = −log(1.0 × 10−11) = 11.00. Above 7, so basic.
3. [H3O+] = 10−2.00 = 1.0 × 10−2 M (0.010 M).
4. pOH = 14.00 − 8.00 = 6.00; [OH−] = 10−6.00 = 1.0 × 10−6 M.
5. pOH = −log(1.0 × 10−3) = 3.00; pH = 14.00 − 3.00 = 11.00. Above 7, so basic.
6. (a) pH 6.50 → acidic; (b) pH 7.00 → neutral; (c) pH 12.30 → basic; (d) pH 4.00 → acidic.
7. HF is the Brønsted-Lowry acid (it donates a proton); its conjugate base is F− (the HF / F− pair). H2O is the base; its conjugate acid is H3O+ (the H2O / H3O+ pair). Each pair differs by exactly one H+.
8. Strongest → weakest: 1 × 10−2 > 1.8 × 10−5 > 4 × 10−10. A larger Ka means the ionization lies further toward products — more protons donated — so it marks the stronger acid.
✍️ EXPLAIN YOUR REASONING (SELF-CHECK)
Before you check the key, write two or three sentences in your own words answering the question below. This is part of your self-check — there is no separate point value; it is folded into the “self-check & corrections” credit already in the rubric.
Two solutions are each 0.10 M — one is HCl, the other is acetic acid. Which has the lower pH, and why? Explain in terms of how completely each acid ionizes, not just “it's stronger.”
▶  Reveal a model answer
HCl has the lower pH. Both solutions are equally concentrated (0.10 M), so the difference is not how much acid is dissolved. HCl is a strong acid: it ionizes essentially completely, so nearly all of it releases H3O+, giving [H3O+] ≈ 0.10 M and pH ≈ 1.0. Acetic acid is weak: it ionizes only partially (Ka ≈ 1.8 × 10−5), so only a small fraction of its molecules donate a proton, leaving a much lower [H3O+] and a higher pH (about 2.9). The gap comes entirely from how completely each ionizes — strength, not concentration.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All eight items attempted with setup and steps shown, not just final answers.
☐
pH/pOH answers rounded to two decimals; classifications (acidic/basic/neutral) stated where asked.
☐
The “Explain your reasoning” written response completed (2–3 sentences) and compared to the model answer.
☐
Work checked against the answer key, with any corrections made in a different color.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
pH / pOH / concentration conversions (items 1–5)
10 pts		 All five worked with steps shown and answers rounded correctly. Some items missing, or only final answers with no steps. 10
Classify, conjugate pairs & Ka ranking (items 6–8)
6 pts		 Classifications, both conjugate pairs, and the Ka ranking with reasoning all complete. Some parts missing or reasoning not given. 6
Self-check, reasoning & corrections
4 pts		 Work checked against the key, the “explain your reasoning” response written, and corrections shown. Not checked, or no corrections made. 4
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer key lets you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Upload a clear photo or scan of your worked notebook pages (or a typed document) through Canvas.
If a problem gives a result you don't trust, submit what you have with a note about where you got stuck — that's useful information, not a penalty.

VR Assignment · 20 pts · one headset session (~35–45 min)

A full non-VR alternate — “pH & Indicator Station (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the exact same objectives and earns the same credit. Do one pathway, not both.
📚 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
This is Build 4 of 5 of your module-long Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station — the same persistent lab you've been growing since Week 1 (entropy sort → reversible-reaction demo → Le Châtelier stress panel). This week you add a pH & Indicator Station: a labeled pH scale from 0 to 14, with strong and weak acids and bases placed where they belong, plus indicator color swatches. You'll mark the neutral point at 7 and annotate the two relationships that govern the scale: pH = −log[H3O+] and pH + pOH = 14. Next week (Build 5) you'll add a titration setup and record the full walkthrough video for your project.
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your notes from Lessons 7.07–7.09 (proton transfer; pH/pOH; strong vs. weak acids and bases).
▶  Your earlier Builds 1–3, which stay in place in the same persistent Session.
▶  About 35–45 minutes in one sitting.
👀 OBSERVE → QUESTION → PREDICT · DO THIS BEFORE YOU BUILD
Observe. From this week's lessons: HCl and acetic acid are both acids, yet at the same concentration HCl drives pH far lower. Question. Where should a strong acid, a weak acid, and a strong base each land on a 0–14 pH scale — and why do a strong and a weak acid at equal concentration sit at different pH?
Predict first — commit before you build. In your notebook (or the Canvas comment box) write one sentence predicting: will a strong acid or a weak acid of the same concentration sit lower on the pH scale, and what does a lower pH say about [H3O+]? Lock this prediction in now — do not revise it later. You'll test it against the station you build.
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (your placed objects stay between visits all module)
Session ID: see the pinned OptimaXR Sessions list in this module
Location: Equilibrium & Acids Lab
Spawn point: Lab Bench A
When you arrive: your Builds 1–3 are where you left them. A Whiteboard IFX by the open bench space shows this week's Step 1 and a blank pH 0–14 rail with empty labeled slots for acids, bases, and indicators. A sticky note reads “Build 4: pH & Indicator Station.” You won't have to guess what to do.
📝 INVESTIGATE · BUILD IT, IN ORDER
1
In the open bench space (to the right of your Le Châtelier panel), spawn a long horizontal pH rail and mark it 0 to 14. Mark the midpoint 7 with a sticky note: “7 = neutral; below 7 acidic; above 7 basic (25 °C).” Leave space at the far end — the Week-5 titration setup goes there.
2
Place at least one strong acid (e.g., HCl) low on the scale and label it “strong — ionizes ~100%.” Place one weak acid (e.g., acetic acid) higher up, closer to the middle, labeled “weak — ionizes partially (Ka ≈ 1.8 × 10−5).”
3
Place at least one strong base (e.g., NaOH) high on the scale, labeled “strong base — dissociates completely.”
4
Add indicator color swatches along the rail to show the scale changing color across the range (for instance a swatch that is one color in the acidic region and another in the basic region). Label one swatch with an indicator name you know, such as “phenolphthalein: colorless in acid, pink in base.”
5
Add a relationships panel beside the rail with two equations: “pH = −log[H3O+]” and “pH + pOH = 14 (25 °C); Kw = 1.0 × 10−14.” Sign your name on it.
6
Lock your new station so it isn't bumped, then take a snapshot and save it as EqAcid_Wk4_YourName. This snapshot is your project's saved progress for the final recording week.
7
Take one screenshot inside the headset that clearly shows your labeled pH scale, the placed strong/weak acids and base, indicator swatches, and the relationships panel. That screenshot is what you'll submit.
Need to stop partway? Because the Session is persistent, your placed and locked builds will be waiting when you return. Save the EqAcid_Wk4_YourName snapshot before you log out so nothing is lost.
🔬 ANALYZE → DEFEND → EXTEND
Analyze. Stand back and look at your finished scale. Did the strong acid land lower than the weak acid? Compare where each landed against the prediction you committed to before building — and note whether your prediction held.
Defend — write a short CER reflection (3–4 sentences; you'll submit this with your work):
• Claim: which acid on your scale is more acidic, and was your committed prediction right?
• Evidence: the pH positions and labels on your station, and what a lower pH means about [H3O+].
• Reasoning: tie it to strong vs. weak — explain why complete vs. partial ionization, not concentration, produces the gap.
Extend. Carbonic acid forms when CO2 dissolves in seawater — a weak acid slowly lowering ocean pH. Where would it sit on your scale, and would you expect it to produce a large or a small pH change? (Next week, Build 5, you'll add a titration setup and record your full walkthrough.)
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
1. Upload your in-headset screenshot showing the labeled pH scale (with neutral 7 marked), the strong acid, weak acid, and strong base placed and labeled, indicator swatches, and the relationships panel.
2. Your committed prediction (the one sentence you wrote before building) and your CER reflection (3–4 sentences: Claim, Evidence, Reasoning) — typed in the comment box or included in your notebook photo.
3. A one-sentence caption: state what a lower pH means about [H3O+] and name one strong and one weak acid you placed. (Your caption will be used when your work appears in the class gallery walk later this module.)
⏱️ TIME
About 35–45 minutes in the headset.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA (COMPLETION-BASED)
☐
A labeled 0–14 pH scale with the neutral point at 7 marked, and the acidic/basic sides identified.
☐
At least one strong acid, one weak acid, and one strong base placed and correctly labeled (complete vs. partial ionization).
☐
Indicator color swatches added, and a signed relationships panel with pH = −log[H3O+] and pH + pOH = 14.
☐
A committed prediction written before building, and a CER reflection (Claim / Evidence / Reasoning) submitted afterward.
☐
Screenshot uploaded and one-sentence caption written. EqAcid_Wk4_YourName snapshot saved for the final recording week.

Titration-Curve Analysis
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: the titration and its equivalence point (7.12) and the equation MaVa = MbVb for a 1:1 strong–strong titration. Here you take a real set of (volume, pH) readings, plot the titration curve in Excel, read the equivalence-point volume off the steep region, and use it to compute an unknown acid concentration — exactly what a chemist does at the bench.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work, and it rehearses the titration reasoning you'll narrate in your Week-5 VR Titration Station recording.
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
A student titrated 25.0 mL of hydrochloric acid (HCl) of unknown concentration with 0.100 M sodium hydroxide (NaOH), recording the pH after each addition. In Excel, you'll enter their data, plot pH versus volume of NaOH added as a Scatter (XY) chart, identify the equivalence-point volume from the steep vertical region of the curve, and then use MaVa = MbVb to compute the unknown HCl concentration. The spreadsheet draws the curve; your job is to read it correctly and finish the calculation.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
The pH barely budges for the first 25 mL, then leaps several units over a single milliliter. How does that sudden steep jump tell you exactly how much acid was in the flask — and therefore how concentrated it was?
🔢 WHAT YOU'RE GIVEN
Volume of HCl titrated: Va = 25.0 mL = 0.0250 L
Concentration of NaOH titrant: Mb = 0.100 M
Reaction is 1:1 (HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O), so at equivalence MaVa = MbVb.
📊 YOUR DATA · pH AS NaOH IS ADDED

Type this two-column table into Excel exactly as shown. Each row is one buret reading during the titration.

Volume of NaOH added (mL) Measured pH
0.00.92
5.01.08
10.01.24
15.01.43
20.01.65
25.02.00
28.02.42
29.02.73
30.07.00
31.011.25
32.011.55
35.011.92
40.012.19
📝 WHAT TO DO IN EXCEL
1
Enter the two-column table with headers in row 1: Volume NaOH (mL) and pH. Put your givens off to the side, e.g. Va = 25.0 mL and Mb = 0.100.
2
Plot the titration curve. Select both columns, insert a Scatter (XY) chart (use the “Scatter with Smooth Lines and Markers” style), and title it “Titration Curve: HCl with 0.100 M NaOH.” Label the x-axis Volume NaOH added (mL) and the y-axis pH.
3
Find the equivalence-point volume. Locate the steep, nearly vertical jump on your curve. The equivalence point is at its midpoint — the volume where pH passes through 7. In a cell labeled V_eq, type that volume (in mL).
4
Compute moles of NaOH at equivalence in a labeled cell: =Mb*(V_eq/1000) (divide mL by 1000 to get liters). Because the reaction is 1:1, this equals the moles of HCl.
5
Compute the HCl concentration in a labeled cell: =mol_HCl/(Va/1000) — moles of HCl divided by the acid's volume in liters. This is Ma.
6
In cells or a text box below the table, answer the three Analysis Questions below.
❓ ANALYSIS QUESTIONS (answer in your spreadsheet)
A. From your curve, what is the equivalence-point volume (in mL), and how did the shape of the curve tell you where it is?
B. Show your MaVa = MbVb work and report the HCl concentration to three significant figures.
C. This was a strong acid titrated with a strong base, and the equivalence-point pH is 7.00. In one or two sentences, explain (using Lesson 7.10) why the salt formed (NaCl) leaves the solution neutral — and what would have been different if the acid had been weak instead.
🧠 REASON IT THROUGH (WRITE 2–3 SENTENCES, THEN SELF-CHECK)
D. Suppose you had titrated the same 25.0 mL of this HCl with 0.200 M NaOH — twice as concentrated — instead of 0.100 M. Would the equivalence-point volume be larger, smaller, or unchanged? Explain your reasoning in terms of moles, then predict the new volume. Write your answer in the spreadsheet before opening the model answer below.
▶  Check your reasoning — model answer for D
Smaller — about 15.0 mL. The amount of HCl in the flask has not changed, so you still need the same number of moles of NaOH to reach the equivalence point: 0.00300 mol. But now each milliliter of titrant carries twice as much NaOH, so it takes only half the volume to deliver those moles. Check: Vb = mol / Mb = 0.00300 mol / 0.200 mol/L = 0.0150 L = 15.0 mL. The equivalence point is set by moles, not volume — a more concentrated titrant simply reaches it sooner. (Notice the computed HCl concentration would still come out to 0.120 M, exactly as before.)
▶  Check your work — answer key
Equivalence-point volume: V_eq = 30.0 mL of NaOH. It is the midpoint of the steep vertical jump (pH leaps from about 2.7 at 29.0 mL to about 11.3 at 31.0 mL), passing through pH 7.00 at 30.0 mL.

Moles of NaOH at equivalence: 0.100 mol/L × 0.0300 L = 0.00300 mol = moles of HCl (1:1 reaction).

HCl concentration: Ma = mol HCl / Va = 0.00300 mol / 0.0250 L = 0.120 M.
Check with MaVa = MbVb: Ma = (0.100 × 30.0) / 25.0 = 3.00 / 25.0 = 0.120 M. ✓

A. 30.0 mL. The curve is nearly flat (gentle) until about 28 mL, then jumps almost vertically over roughly one milliliter; the equivalence point is the middle of that jump, where pH = 7.
B. Ma = (MbVb)/Va = (0.100 M × 30.0 mL)/(25.0 mL) = 0.120 M HCl.
C. NaCl comes from the strong acid HCl and the strong base NaOH, so both Na+ and Cl− are spectator ions that don't react with water — the solution stays neutral (pH 7) at equivalence. If the acid had been weak, the salt's anion would be the conjugate base of a weak acid and would hydrolyze, so the equivalence-point pH would be above 7 (basic) and the steep region would center higher.

☐

☐

Module 7 Writing Assignment
Equilibrium Under Pressure — A Le Châtelier CER
Word (.docx) · 100 pts · teacher-reviewed
📚 THE TASK
A reaction at equilibrium is not finished — it is balanced. Push on it, and it pushes back. Le Châtelier's principle says a system at equilibrium responds to a stress by shifting to partially counteract it. That single idea reaches far past the lab bench: it governs the chemistry of the ocean as it absorbs our carbon dioxide, and it decides how the world feeds itself through the synthesis of fertilizer.
In this assignment you will write a CER — a Claim, Evidence, and Reasoning argument — about a real equilibrium system under stress. Make a claim about how the equilibrium responds, defend it with the equilibrium chemistry and Le Châtelier's principle, reason carefully from cause to effect, and connect it to the stakes for people and the planet. Choose one of the two prompts below.
PROMPT A · OCEAN ACIDIFICATION
Rising atmospheric CO2 dissolves into seawater, feeding the equilibrium CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−. Predict and justify how adding more CO2 shifts this system, what happens to ocean pH, and why that threatens shell-building organisms (corals, oysters, plankton).
PROMPT B · THE HABER-BOSCH PROCESS
Ammonia for fertilizer is made by N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. Predict and justify how to maximize the yield of NH3 using pressure and temperature, explain the real-world compromise industry makes, and connect it to the societal stakes of feeding the world.
You'll write it in Microsoft Word, organized into the CER sections listed further down.
⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS
This CER is one of only two teacher-reviewed pieces in Module 7 (the other is your Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station VR project). Your teacher reads it personally and responds to your reasoning — so make it your careful best, and justify every shift from the chemistry, not from a guess. This is exactly Quarter 4's question in action: how does chemistry shape our world?
🧮 YOUR TOOLKIT (USE THESE EXACT IDEAS & VALUES)
Le Châtelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts to partially counteract a stress. Add a reactant → shift right (toward products); add a product → shift left; remove a product → shift right.
Pressure: increasing pressure (decreasing volume) shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas.
Temperature: treat heat as a reactant (endothermic) or a product (exothermic). For an exothermic reaction (heat is a product), lowering temperature shifts right.
pH: pH = −log[H+]; more H+ means a lower pH (more acidic).
Prompt A facts: adding CO2 drives CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3− to the right, raising [H+] and lowering ocean pH; the extra H+ also ties up carbonate (CO32−) that organisms need to build CaCO3 shells.
Prompt B facts: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 goes from 4 mol of gas to 2 mol of gas, so high pressure favors NH3; ΔH = −92 kJ/mol (exothermic), so low temperature favors NH3 — but low temperature is too slow, so industry compromises (~400–450 °C, ~150–300 atm, iron catalyst). Fritz Haber received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Carl Bosch scaled it to industry.
🧠 YOUR REASONING TOOLKIT (how to build the argument)
Use these steps in your own words — don't just copy the headings.
Step 1 — Name the equilibrium and the stress.
A: write the carbonate equilibrium and identify the stress (we keep adding CO2, a reactant). B: write the Haber equilibrium with its ΔH, and identify the levers you can change (pressure, temperature).
Step 2 — Apply Le Châtelier to predict the shift.
A: adding a reactant (CO2) shifts the system right — toward more H+. B: high pressure shifts toward the fewer-moles side (2 mol NH3), and because the reaction is exothermic, lower temperature shifts right too.
Step 3 — Trace it to the real outcome.
A: more H+ means a lower pH, and the extra H+ consumes the carbonate that shell-builders need — so reefs and shellfish suffer. B: name the temperature/rate compromise and why cheap, abundant ammonia changed the world's food supply.
📝 STRUCTURE: WRITE THESE CER SECTIONS
1
Claim. One or two clear sentences stating how the equilibrium responds and what it means (e.g., “Adding CO2 shifts the carbonate equilibrium right, lowering ocean pH and threatening shell-builders,” or “NH3 yield is maximized at high pressure and low temperature, though industry must compromise on temperature for speed.”).
2
Evidence (the equilibrium). Write the balanced equilibrium and lay out the relevant facts: which species are reactants and products, how many moles of gas are on each side (B), the sign of ΔH (B), and what stress is being applied. State the Le Châtelier rule(s) you will use.
3
Reasoning (Le Châtelier). This is the heart of the CER. Walk step by step from the stress to the predicted shift to the consequence, citing the correct rule each time: add a reactant → shift right; raise pressure → shift toward fewer gas moles; lower T (exothermic) → shift right. For A, connect the rightward shift to rising [H+] and a falling pH; for B, justify both the pressure and the temperature choice.
4
Societal cost–benefit (Responsibility). Do not just mention the stakes — weigh them. Name a genuine benefit and a genuine cost, then take a reasoned, evidence-based position on what we should do about it. For A: the benefit of the ocean absorbing our CO2 set against the cost to reefs, fisheries, and the people who depend on them. For B: how cheap ammonia underwrites the food supply of billions set against its energy use and environmental costs. State the trade-off explicitly and decide from the evidence, not from preference (Honesty & Responsibility threads).
5
Conclusion. Restate your claim in light of the evidence and reasoning, and name the big idea: a system at equilibrium answers a stress in a direction we can predict — and that prediction shapes the ocean, the food supply, and the world we live in.
✎ LENGTH & STYLE
Aim for roughly 500–700 words across the five CER sections. Write the balanced equilibrium clearly (typed or handwritten and photographed in). Use correct terminology — equilibrium, Le Châtelier's principle, shift, reactant/product, moles of gas, exothermic, pH, [H+]. The chemistry and the reasoning are what's graded — not polished prose. Justify each shift with a rule, not a hunch.
⚠️ A NOTE ON USING AI TOOLS
An AI tool will happily tell you which way an equilibrium shifts — and it can get it backwards: confidently shifting toward more gas moles under pressure, flipping the temperature rule for an exothermic reaction, or claiming a lower [H+] gives a lower pH. If you consult one, treat it as a draft to check, never an answer to paste: re-derive each shift yourself by applying Le Châtelier's principle to the balanced equilibrium, and re-reason the pH direction by hand. The instrument proposes; your reasoning against the equilibrium verifies. That is exactly the AI-literacy skill this assignment is built to grow.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Write your CER in Microsoft Word from your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_LeChatelierCER_CHEM1H, save it to your Optima → Science OneDrive course folder, and submit through Canvas. New here? See the pinned “M365 Setup & File Organization Guide” page in this module.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: structuring a CER with headings in Word and inserting a balanced equilibrium equation (typed with subscripts/superscripts, or a photographed work page). If your teacher returns comments for revision, turn on Track Changes before revising.
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED (TEACHER RUBRIC — build natively as a Canvas Rubric)
Criterion Full marks Developing Pts
Claim A clear, specific, scientifically defensible claim that directly answers the chosen prompt (the direction of the shift and what it means). Claim vague, missing, or only restates the question. 15
Equilibrium evidence Correct balanced equilibrium; relevant facts laid out (species, gas-mole counts and/or sign of ΔH, the stress applied) and the right Le Châtelier rule(s) named. Equation wrong/missing; facts incomplete or rules not identified. 25
Le Châtelier reasoning Steps logically from stress → predicted shift → consequence, citing the correct rule each time; pH direction (A) or both pressure & temperature choices (B) justified correctly. Shift asserted without a rule, reasoning gaps, or a reversed prediction (e.g., wrong pH or temperature direction). 30
Societal cost–benefit (Responsibility) Weighs a genuine benefit against a genuine cost (shell-builders & ocean health; or the food supply against its energy/environmental costs) and takes a reasoned, evidence-based position — the Responsibility thread in action. Only one side named, generic, or scientifically off; no trade-off actually weighed. 15
Conclusion & communication Conclusion ties back to the claim and names the big idea; correct terminology, clear organized CER form. Conclusion thin or just restates; terms misused; disorganized. 15
Total: 100 pts
The equilibrium evidence and the Le Châtelier reasoning carry the most weight — a correct prediction with no chemistry behind it earns little. Reason from the equilibrium up.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Submit your Word .docx through Canvas (OneDrive tab or file upload). If your teacher returns it with comments, revise with Track Changes on and resubmit as a _Revision1 file.

🧘 PREFER NOT TO USE A HEADSET?
A full non-VR alternate — “Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station — Narrated Walkthrough (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the same objectives and is graded on the same rubric. Do one pathway, not both.
📚 THE BIG PICTURE
Across this module you've built an Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station in OptimaXR, one week at a time, to answer a single running question: how do chemists predict and control change — which way a process goes on its own, how a balanced reaction responds when pushed, and how acidic or basic a solution is? Week 1 you built an entropy & spontaneity sort; Week 2 a reversible-reaction equilibrium demo; Week 3 a Le Châtelier shift panel; Week 4 a pH & indicator station; Week 5 a titration station. Now you bring it all together.
Your task is to record a guided video walkthrough inside the headset — a short tour in which you narrate the chemistry of your station, from spontaneity and entropy through equilibrium, Le Châtelier shifts, the pH scale, and a titration to its equivalence point. This recorded explanation, not a static screenshot, is what earns the grade. The station is the stage; your spoken reasoning is the performance.
⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS
This walkthrough is one of only two teacher-reviewed pieces in Module 7 (the other is your Le Châtelier CER writing assignment). Your teacher will watch your recording and respond to your reasoning personally — so make it your best thinking, clearly explained.
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your finished build — the EqAcid_Final_YourName snapshot from the Week 5 build, including the Week 1 entropy/spontaneity sort, the Week 2 equilibrium demo, the Week 3 Le Châtelier shift panel, the Week 4 pH/indicator station, and the Week 5 titration station.
▶  A quiet space and about 30–40 minutes (planning, one or two recording takes, and submitting).
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (your finished build is waiting)
Session ID: see the pinned OptimaXR Sessions list in this module
Session name: Equilibrium & Acids Lab
Location: Equilibrium & Acids Lab
Spawn point: Lab Entrance
🎤 WHAT YOUR RECORDING MUST COVER (aim for 3–5 minutes)
1
Open at the entrance. Introduce your station and state the big question it answers: how do chemists predict which way a process goes, how a balanced reaction answers a push, and how acidic or basic a solution is?
2
Spontaneity & entropy (Week 1). Walk your entropy/spontaneity sort. Explain that a spontaneous process needs no continuous outside push, that entropy measures the dispersal of energy and matter (it rises solid → liquid → gas, on dissolving, and when more gas moles form), and state the two key rules: for a spontaneous process ΔSuniv > 0, and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (ΔG < 0 means spontaneous).
3
Dynamic equilibrium & K (Week 2). At your reversible-reaction demo, show both arrows and explain that at dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant — the reaction has not stopped. Define K = [products] / [reactants] (each raised to its coefficient), and note that a large K means products are favored.
4
Le Châtelier shifts (Week 3). Use your shift panel to narrate how the system answers a stress: add a reactant → shift right; raise the pressure → shift toward fewer gas moles; change the temperature → shift per the heat term. Use the Haber example: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol — high pressure (4 mol → 2 mol gas) and low temperature both favor NH3.
5
The pH scale & acid strength (Week 4). At your pH/indicator station, walk the 0–14 scale: pH = −log[H3O+], neutral = 7, acidic < 7, basic > 7, and pH + pOH = 14. Place a strong acid (ionizes ~100%, e.g., HCl) and a weak acid (partially ionizes, e.g., acetic acid) on the scale and explain the difference, using your indicator color swatches.
6
Titration to the equivalence point (Week 5). At your titration station (buret, flask, indicator), show what happens as base is added to an acid, mark the equivalence point (moles of base = moles of acid), and put a number on it: for a monoprotic strong–strong titration, MaVa = MbVb — e.g., 25.0 mL of HCl neutralized by 30.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH gives 0.00300 mol acid, so the HCl is 0.120 M.
7
Close with the evidence, then the through-line. Before you sign off, state the evidence behind your three biggest claims: why the change you showed is spontaneous (ΔSuniv > 0, or ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0), what in your demo shows the system has reached equilibrium (forward and reverse rates equal, concentrations constant), and how you determined the pH (from [H3O+] on the 0–14 scale). Then connect the whole station into one idea: chemistry is not just about what happens, but about predicting and controlling it — whether a change goes on its own, which way a balanced reaction will move when pushed, and how strong an acid or base really is.
How to record: Use OptimaXR's video recording feature to capture your narrated tour from inside the headset (start the recording from the menu/tablet, walk and talk, then stop and save). If your setup can't capture in-headset audio, record your screen with narration instead. Aim for one clean take; a second take is fine.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
1. Upload your video recording (3–5 minutes) to this Canvas assignment as a media/file upload.
2. In the comment box, list the five weekly builds in one line each (Wk1 entropy/spontaneity sort, Wk2 equilibrium demo, Wk3 Le Châtelier shift panel, Wk4 pH/indicator station, Wk5 titration station) so your teacher can see the iteration behind the final build.
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED (TEACHER RUBRIC — build natively as a Canvas Rubric)
Criterion Full marks Developing Pts
Evidence-based scientific reasoning Every conclusion is backed by the evidence in the station. The student explains why the process is spontaneous (ΔSuniv > 0; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS), what shows the reaction is at dynamic equilibrium (equal forward/reverse rates, constant concentrations, K), how each Le Châtelier shift follows from the stress, and how pH is determined from [H3O+] on the 0–14 scale. Reasoning moves observation → evidence → explanation, not assertion. States conclusions without the supporting evidence, or the evidence given does not justify the claim; mostly naming, not explaining why. 35
Accurate chemistry The chemistry is correct throughout — spontaneity/entropy rules, the K expression and its meaning, the Le Châtelier shift directions (with the Haber example), strong vs weak acids on the pH scale, and the titration to equivalence (MaVa = MbVb) are all stated accurately. Contains chemistry errors — e.g., a reversed shift, a misread pH, or a wrong spontaneity rule. 25
Clear narration & model The recorded tour is organized and easy to follow, and the five-station build is recognizable and correct at a high-school level (equilibrium demo shows both directions; shift panel shows the right directions; the pH scale runs 0–14 with strong/weak placed sensibly; the titration marks a real equivalence point). Audio/visuals are usable. Disorganized or hard to follow; stations confused, missing, or do not show the chemistry; key parts unclear or inaudible. 20
Week-by-week iteration The build clearly shows all five stages (entropy sort, equilibrium demo, shift panel, pH station, titration station), and the comment lists the five weekly builds. Only some stages present; little sign of building over time. 12
Uncertainty/limits & real-world reflection Notes at least one limit of the model or a source of uncertainty (e.g., the model simplifies real equilibrium; an equivalence point read from an indicator is approximate) and connects the chemistry to a real-world or societal stake (e.g., ocean acidification, the Haber process and the food supply, or buffering in blood/oceans). No mention of the model's limits or uncertainty, and no real-world/societal connection. 8
Total: 100 pts
The same five criteria are used for the non-VR alternate. A high-school-level model is expected — evidence-based reasoning and accuracy of the explanation carry the most weight.
