Week 1 · Hands-On
Redox Balancing — Numbers, Agents & Half-Reactions
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: the oxidation-number rules and the OIL RIG definitions (8.01), the oxidizing-agent / reducing-agent vocabulary, and the half-reaction method for balancing redox in acidic solution. Here you'll assign oxidation numbers, name what is oxidized and reduced (and which is each agent), and balance simple half-reactions step by step — checking both atoms and charge by hand.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work. Do it on paper or in your notebook — no spreadsheet needed this week.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Electrons can't appear or disappear — whatever one substance loses, another gains. How do oxidation numbers let you track that transfer, and how do you balance an equation so that the electrons, the atoms, and the charge all account perfectly?
🧰 YOUR TOOLBOX
OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (number up), Reduction Is Gain (number down). ·  Oxidized species = reducing agent; reduced species = oxidizing agent.
Oxidation-number rules: free element = 0 · monatomic ion = its charge · Group 1 = +1, Group 2 = +2 · F = −1 · O usually −2 · H usually +1 · sum = overall charge.
Half-reaction method (acidic): balance atoms → balance O with H2O → balance H with H+ → balance charge with e−.
⚠️ THE HABIT THAT CATCHES ERRORS — READ THIS TWICE
It is easy to reverse the agents: the species that is oxidized is the reducing agent, and the species that is reduced is the oxidizing agent — each is named for what it does to its partner. And a half-reaction is not finished until the charge matches on both sides, not just the atoms. Always close by adding up the charge on each side — if they don't match, your electrons are wrong.
📝 PART A · ASSIGN OXIDATION NUMBERS (items 1–3)

Give the oxidation number of the bold element in each, and name the rule(s) you used.

1. Sulfur in SO2  (O is −2; molecule is neutral).
2. Nitrogen in the nitrate ion NO3−  (O is −2; ion charge is −1).
3. Chromium in the dichromate ion Cr2O72−  (O is −2; ion charge is −2).
📊 PART B · OXIDIZED / REDUCED & THE AGENTS (items 4–5)

For each reaction, state which element is oxidized and which is reduced (track the oxidation numbers), then name the oxidizing agent and the reducing agent.

4. Mg(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
5. 2 Al(s) + 3 Cu2+(aq) → 2 Al3+(aq) + 3 Cu(s)
🧮 PART C · BALANCE HALF-REACTIONS IN ACIDIC SOLUTION (items 6–8)

Balance each half-reaction in acidic solution. Balance atoms first, then O with H2O, then H with H+, then charge with e−. Show each step, and finish by stating whether the half is oxidation or reduction. Check the charge on both sides.

6. Fe2+ → Fe3+  (the simplest case — no O or H to balance).
7. Cr2O72− → Cr3+  (balance Cr, then O with H2O, then H with H+, then charge with e−).
8. Using your answers to items 6 and 7, combine the two halves into one balanced overall equation (the dichromate–iron(II) reaction). (Multiply to equalize the electrons first.)
💡 WORKED EXAMPLE (the method, on a different half-reaction)
Balance MnO4− → Mn2+ in acidic solution.
Step 1 — balance atoms other than O, H: Mn is already 1 : 1. ✓
Step 2 — balance O with H2O: 4 O on the left, so add 4 H2O on the right: MnO4− → Mn2+ + 4 H2O.
Step 3 — balance H with H+: 8 H on the right (from 4 H2O), so add 8 H+ on the left: MnO4− + 8 H+ → Mn2+ + 4 H2O.
Step 4 — balance charge with e−: left charge = −1 + 8 = +7; right charge = +2. Add 5 e− to the left to bring it to +2: MnO4− + 8 H+ + 5 e− → Mn2+ + 4 H2O.
Type: electrons are gained, so this is a reduction half (Mn: +7 → +2). Charge check: left +2, right +2. ✓
✍️ PART D · EXPLAIN YOUR REASONING (SELF-CHECK)

In two or three sentences, answer in your own words — this is the reasoning behind the whole set: Why must every oxidation be matched by a reduction, and how does the charge check on a balanced half-reaction prove your electron count is right? Write your answer before you open the model response below.

▶  Model answer — open after you've written yours
Electrons cannot be created or destroyed, so any electrons one substance loses (oxidation) must be gained by another (reduction) in the same reaction — that is why the two halves always occur together, and why the electrons must cancel exactly when you add the halves. The charge check is the proof: because charge is conserved, a correctly balanced half-reaction has equal total charge on both sides. If the two sides do not match, you added the wrong number of electrons — the size of the mismatch is the size of the error. Matching charge (together with matching atoms) is what tells you the electron bookkeeping is correct.
🤖 AI IS AN INSTRUMENT, NOT AN ORACLE
If you ask an AI tool to do these, it will often mislabel the oxidizing agent (calling the oxidized species the “oxidizing” agent — it's reversed) or miscount the electrons in a half-reaction so the charge doesn't balance. Treat any AI answer as a claim to verify, not the answer: re-apply OIL RIG by hand (the oxidized species is the reducing agent), and add up the charge on both sides — if they don't match, the electron count is wrong. Reasoning from the rules and the charge balance is the skill; the tool is just an instrument.
🔑 CHECK YOUR WORK
▶  Answer key — open after you've tried all eight
Part A — oxidation numbers:
1. S in SO2 = +4. Two O give 2(−2) = −4; for the neutral molecule, S + (−4) = 0, so S = +4.
2. N in NO3− = +5. Three O give −6; for an ion of charge −1, N + (−6) = −1, so N = +5.
3. Cr in Cr2O72− = +6. Seven O give −14; for charge −2, 2Cr + (−14) = −2, so 2Cr = +12, Cr = +6 each.

Part B — oxidized / reduced & agents:
4. Mg: 0 → +2 (oxidized → Mg is the reducing agent). H: +1 → 0 in H2 (reduced → HCl / H+ is the oxidizing agent). Chlorine stays −1 throughout (spectator). (Hand-check the H: it goes from +1 in HCl to 0 in H2 gas.)
5. Al: 0 → +3 (oxidized → Al is the reducing agent). Cu: +2 → 0 (reduced → Cu2+ is the oxidizing agent).

Part C — half-reactions in acid:
6. Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e−. (Atoms balance; charge: left +2, right +3 + (−1) = +2. ✓) Electrons are lost → oxidation half.
7. Cr2O72− + 14 H+ + 6 e− → 2 Cr3+ + 7 H2O.
  • Balance Cr: 2 Cr3+ on the right.
  • Balance O: 7 O on the left → 7 H2O on the right.
  • Balance H: 14 H on the right → 14 H+ on the left.
  • Balance charge: left = −2 + 14 = +12; right = 2(+3) = +6; add 6 e− to the left → +12 − 6 = +6. ✓ Electrons are gained → reduction half (Cr: +6 → +3).
8. The Fe half loses 1 e−; the dichromate half gains 6 e−. Multiply the Fe half by 6, then add and cancel the 6 electrons:
  Cr2O72− + 14 H+ + 6 Fe2+ → 2 Cr3+ + 6 Fe3+ + 7 H2O.
  Charge check: left = −2 + 14 + 6(+2) = −2 + 14 + 12 = +24; right = 2(+3) + 6(+3) + 0 = 6 + 18 = +24. ✓

Agent-direction check: if you wrote that an oxidized species (like Mg or Al) was the “oxidizing” agent, flip it — the oxidized species is always the reducing agent. Charge check: if any half-reaction's two sides don't have equal total charge, your electron count is off — recount and redo.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Items 1–3: each oxidation number given with the rule(s) used to find it.
☐
Items 4–5: oxidized and reduced elements identified, and the oxidizing & reducing agents named in the correct direction.
☐
Items 6–8: half-reactions balanced for atoms and charge, electrons shown, each labeled oxidation or reduction, and the overall equation combined correctly.
☐
All work checked against the answer key, with the agent direction and the charge balance confirmed.
☐
Part D: the written-reasoning explanation completed in your own words, then compared to the model answer.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
Oxidation numbers (items 1–3)
6 pts		 All three numbers correct with the rule(s) shown. Some numbers missing or rules absent. 6
Oxidized/reduced & agents (items 4–5)
4 pts		 Both reactions: oxidized/reduced correct and agents named in the right direction. Agents reversed or one reaction missing. 4
Balanced half-reactions (items 6–8)
8 pts		 All balanced for atoms and charge, electrons shown, overall equation combined. Some steps missing, or charge not checked. 8
Self-check & reasoning (Part D)
2 pts		 Work compared to the answer key, corrections noted, and the Part D reasoning written in your own words. Not checked, or Part D reasoning missing. 2
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer key lets you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M8 W1 Hands-On — Redox Balancing (Numbers, Agents & Half-Reactions)
Work the eight items in your notebook or on paper, then upload a clear photo or scan (or type your answers directly into the Canvas text box).
If a half-reaction's charge won't balance no matter what you try, submit what you have with a note about where you got stuck — that's useful information, not a penalty.

VR Assignment · 20 pts · one headset session (~35–45 min)
🧘 PREFER NOT TO USE A HEADSET?
A full non-VR alternate — “Galvanic Cell Foundation (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the exact same objectives and earns the same credit. Do one pathway, not both.
📚 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
You're starting the project you'll build across all four weeks of this module: the Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build — a working model you'll narrate on camera at the end of the module. This week you build the foundation: a galvanic (voltaic) cell. You'll set up two electrodes in two half-cells (beakers), join them with a salt bridge and an external wire, and mark which way the electrons flow. You'll label the anode (oxidation, −) and cathode (reduction, +), and draw the electron flow anode → cathode through the wire. One anchor sticky note — “Galvanic cell: a spontaneous redox reaction makes electricity; electrons flow anode → cathode” — will sit at the heart of the build all module. In later weeks you'll add a cell-potential panel (Week 2), real cells & electrolysis (Week 3), and a reaction-rate & catalysis demo (Week 4) — and finally record the full walkthrough.
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your notes from Lessons 8.01–8.02 (oxidation/reduction and OIL RIG; anode = oxidation/−, cathode = reduction/+; electrons flow anode → cathode; the salt bridge carries ions).
▶  About 35–45 minutes in one sitting.
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (your placed objects stay between visits all module)
Session ID: see the pinned OptimaXR Sessions list in this module — join Electrochem & Rates Lab
Location: Electrochem & Rates Lab
Spawn point: Lab Bench A
When you arrive: a Whiteboard IFX facing the bench shows this week's Step 1 and the anchor rule “a spontaneous redox reaction makes electricity; electrons flow anode → cathode.” Two empty beakers, a set of electrode strips, a salt-bridge tube, and a length of wire are laid out on the tray, with labels you can pick up. A sticky note at your feet reads “Start here.” You won't have to guess what to do.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
This build follows an investigation arc: Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend. Don't skip the prediction — commit to it before you build.
1
OBSERVE. At the bench, read the Whiteboard IFX and the anchor rule, and recall from Lesson 8.01 that when zinc and copper(II) touch directly in one beaker the reaction is spontaneous but its energy escapes uselessly as heat — no current. Claim: The zinc electrode is the anode and the copper electrode is the cathode; electrons flow through the wire from the zinc anode to the copper cathode. Week 2 · Hands-On
Cell Potentials & ΔG° = −nFE°
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: reading a standard reduction-potential table (8.03), identifying cathode and anode, computing E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, judging spontaneity from its sign, and linking voltage to free energy with ΔG° = −nFE° (8.04). Here you'll do all of it by hand — including the double-negative subtraction and the sign-and-unit trap that snare almost everyone.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work. Do it on paper or in your notebook — no spreadsheet needed this week.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Given only a table of standard reduction potentials, how do you predict a cell's voltage, decide whether it will run on its own, and convert that voltage into the free energy the reaction can deliver?
🧰 YOUR TOOLBOX
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode  (both from the table; cathode = the higher E°).
E°cell > 0 → spontaneous (galvanic) ·  E°cell < 0 → not spontaneous as written.
ΔG° = −nFE°  with F = 96,485 C/mol and n = moles of electrons transferred ·  (V × C = J).
Reduction half-reaction E° (V)
Ag+ + e− → Ag+0.80
Cu2+ + 2 e− → Cu+0.34
2 H+ + 2 e− → H20.00
Zn2+ + 2 e− → Zn−0.76
⚠️ THE TRAP — READ THIS TWICE
Two slips to avoid. (1) The double negative. When the anode's E° is negative, subtracting it ADDS: E°cell = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = 0.34 + 0.76 = +1.10 V, never −0.42 V. (2) The ΔG° sign and units. The formula has a minus sign — ΔG° = −nFE° — and with F ≈ 96,485 the raw answer is in joules. Divide by 1000 for kJ. A real cell gives a few hundred kJ, not a few hundred thousand.
📝 PART A · IDENTIFY CATHODE/ANODE AND COMPUTE E°cell (items 1–3)

For each cell, (a) name which half-reaction is the cathode and which is the anode, (b) compute E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode showing the subtraction, and (c) state whether the cell is spontaneous (galvanic).

1. A cell made from Cu2+/Cu and Ag+/Ag.
2. A cell made from Zn2+/Zn and Ag+/Ag.
3. A cell made from Zn2+/Zn and Cu2+/Cu (the Daniell cell).
📊 PART B · SPONTANEITY CHECK (items 4–5)

For each value of E°cell, state whether the cell is spontaneous (galvanic) or not spontaneous as written, and in one line say what that sign also tells you about ΔG° (positive or negative).

4. A cell has E°cell = +0.46 V.
5. A cell has E°cell = −0.34 V.
💡 WORKED EXAMPLE (the method for Parts A–B)
Cell: Zn2+/Zn (−0.76 V) paired with Cu2+/Cu (+0.34 V).
Step 1 — pick the cathode (higher E°): Cu2+/Cu at +0.34 V > Zn at −0.76 V, so copper is the cathode, zinc is the anode.
Step 2 — subtract, table values as written: E°cell = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = 0.34 + 0.76 = +1.10 V.
Step 3 — verdict: positive → spontaneous (galvanic), and so ΔG° < 0. Notice the double negative made the subtraction an addition.
🧮 PART C · FREE ENERGY FROM VOLTAGE (item 6)

Use ΔG° = −nFE° with F = 96,485 C/mol. Show the substitution, give the answer in joules, then convert to kJ and state spontaneous or not.

6. The Daniell (Zn–Cu) cell transfers n = 2 electrons and has E°cell = +1.10 V (from item 3). Compute ΔG° in joules, convert to kJ, and state whether the reaction is spontaneous. (Keep the minus sign and watch J vs. kJ!)
✍️ PART D · EXPLAIN YOUR REASONING (item 7 · self-check)

Numbers are only half the work — put the idea into words. In 2–3 sentences, explain to a classmate why a positive E°cell and a negative ΔG° are two ways of saying the exact same thing about a reaction. Refer to the minus sign in ΔG° = −nFE° and to what “spontaneous” means. Write your answer in your notebook first, then open the model answer to compare.

7. Why must a cell with a positive E°cell also have a negative ΔG°? Answer in 2–3 sentences using the equation.
▶  Model answer — open after you've written yours
In ΔG° = −nFE°, the quantities n (moles of electrons) and F (the Faraday constant) are always positive, so the leading minus sign forces ΔG° to take the opposite sign of E°cell. A positive E°cell therefore always produces a negative ΔG° — and a negative ΔG° is exactly the thermodynamic definition of a spontaneous reaction, the same verdict the positive voltage already announced. So “the cell pushes electrons on its own” (positive voltage) and “the reaction releases free energy” (negative ΔG°) are one fact in two languages, welded together by that minus sign.
🤖 AI IS AN INSTRUMENT, NOT AN ORACLE
Ask an AI tool to find a cell potential and it will often flip the E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode subtraction (putting the wrong half-reaction at the cathode, or mishandling the −0.76 V double negative) and report the wrong sign. Ask it for a ΔG° and it commonly drops the minus sign in ΔG° = −nFE° or leaves the answer in joules. Treat any AI result as a claim to verify, not an answer: confirm the higher-E° half-reaction is the cathode, redo the subtraction by hand, and check that a positive E°cell gives a negative ΔG°. Reasoning from the evidence is the skill; the calculator is just an instrument.
🔑 CHECK YOUR WORK
▶  Answer key — open after you've tried all six calculation items (item 7 has its own model answer above)
Part A — cathode/anode & E°cell:
1. Cu–Ag: Ag+/Ag is the cathode (higher E°, +0.80 V); Cu2+/Cu is the anode (+0.34 V). E°cell = (+0.80) − (+0.34) = +0.46 V → spontaneous (galvanic).
2. Zn–Ag: Ag+/Ag is the cathode (+0.80 V); Zn2+/Zn is the anode (−0.76 V). E°cell = (+0.80) − (−0.76) = 0.80 + 0.76 = +1.56 V → spontaneous (galvanic). (Double negative → addition.)
3. Zn–Cu: Cu2+/Cu is the cathode (+0.34 V); Zn2+/Zn is the anode (−0.76 V). E°cell = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = 0.34 + 0.76 = +1.10 V → spontaneous (galvanic).

Part B — spontaneity check:
4. E°cell = +0.46 V → spontaneous (galvanic); positive E°cell means ΔG° < 0.
5. E°cell = −0.34 V → not spontaneous as written (the reverse reaction is the spontaneous one); negative E°cell means ΔG° > 0.

Part C — ΔG° = −nFE° (keep the minus sign; convert J → kJ):
6. ΔG° = −(2)(96,485 C/mol)(1.10 V) = −212,267 J. Convert: −212,267 J × (1 kJ / 1000 J) ≈ −212 kJ → spontaneous (ΔG° < 0), exactly as the positive +1.10 V promised.

Trap check: if any E°cell came out negative for a cell you expected to work, you likely put the lower-E° half-reaction at the cathode, or mishandled the −0.76 V double negative. And if your ΔG° came out positive or in the hundred-thousands of kJ, you dropped the minus sign or forgot to divide joules by 1000.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Items 1–3: cathode and anode named, E°cell subtraction shown, and a spontaneous/not verdict given for each cell.
☐
Items 4–5: spontaneity classified from the sign, with the matching sign of ΔG° stated.
☐
Item 6: ΔG° computed with the minus sign kept, answer shown in both J and kJ, and a spontaneous/not verdict given.
☐
Item 7: a 2–3 sentence written explanation of why a positive E°cell means a negative ΔG°, compared against the model answer.
☐
All work checked against the answer key, with the double-negative and sign-and-unit traps confirmed handled.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
Cathode/anode & E°cell (items 1–3)
9 pts		 All three cells: cathode/anode named, subtraction shown, verdict given. Some electrodes mislabeled or subtraction not shown. 9
Spontaneity & ΔG° sign (items 4–5)
4 pts		 Both classified correctly with the matching ΔG° sign. One case missing or the ΔG° sign absent. 4
ΔG° = −nFE° (item 6)
5 pts		 Substitution shown, minus sign kept, J and kJ both given, verdict stated. Sign dropped or kJ conversion skipped. 5
Self-check & written reasoning (item 7)
2 pts		 Item 7 explanation written and calculations compared to the answer key, with corrections noted. Reasoning skipped or work not checked. 2
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer key lets you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M8 W2 Hands-On — Cell Potentials & ΔG° = −nFE°
Work the six items in your notebook or on paper, then upload a clear photo or scan (or type your answers directly into the Canvas text box).
If a calculation gives a result you don't trust, submit what you have with a note about where you got stuck — that's useful information, not a penalty.

VR Assignment · 20 pts · one headset session (~35–45 min)
🧘 PREFER NOT TO USE A HEADSET?
A full non-VR alternate — “Cell Potential Panel (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the exact same objectives and earns the same credit. Do one pathway, not both.
📚 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
This is Build 2 of 4 of the project you began last week: the Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build — the exhibit you'll narrate on camera at the end of the module. You return to the same persistent bench, where last week's galvanic cell (anode −, cathode +, salt bridge, electrons flowing anode → cathode) is still waiting. This week you add a Cell Potential Panel: a voltmeter that reads the cell's E°cell (about +1.10 V for the Zn–Cu cell), and a standard-reduction-potential ranking strip that orders several half-reactions from most-positive at the top (the strongest oxidizer, which becomes the cathode) down to the most-negative. You'll label the rule E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode and sign a sticky note carrying the module's through-line. In the weeks ahead you'll add real cells & electrolysis (Week 3) and a rate & catalysis demo (Week 4) — then record the full walkthrough.
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your notes from Lessons 8.03–8.04 (the reduction-potential table; E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; ΔG° = −nFE°).

▶  About 35–45 minutes in one sitting.
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)

2
Question. Stand at the cell and pose the week's question, out loud or on a sticky note: Which metal is the cathode, and exactly how many volts should the meter read? You'll answer it by prediction first, then by measurement.
3
Predict (commit first). Before you spawn the voltmeter, commit a prediction on a sticky note: name which half-reaction is the cathode (the higher E°) and the value of E°cell you expect from E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. Commit to a number before you measure — that is the whole point of the panel.

Investigate. Now spawn a voltmeter and connect it across your Zn–Cu cell; set its display to read E°cell = +1.10 V. Analyze. Place the rule label E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode over the panel and use the 3D pen to draw arrows from the Cu tile (cathode) and the Zn tile (anode) to the voltmeter, showing where +1.10 V comes from. Defend. Place and sign a sticky note with the module's through-line: “E°cell > 0 → spontaneous → ΔG° = −nFE° < 0.” In your own words, add one line arguing why a positive voltage and a negative free-energy change say the same thing.
7

Week 3 · Hands-On
Cells, Electrodes & Faraday's Law
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: batteries as packaged galvanic cells — primary vs. secondary (8.05); corrosion as unwanted oxidation (8.06); and electrolysis — the galvanic-vs-electrolytic contrast and Faraday's law: Q = I·t, mol e− = Q/F, then the half-reaction's electron ratio to mass (8.07). Here you'll classify cells, identify electrodes, and run a plating calculation by hand — watching the two traps that snare almost everyone.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work. Do it on paper or in your notebook — no spreadsheet needed this week.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
A galvanic cell makes electricity; an electrolytic cell spends it. Some batteries recharge and some don't. And a measured current deposits an exact mass of metal. How do you read each device correctly — and count the electrons to predict what it makes?
🧰 YOUR TOOLBOX
Galvanic = spontaneous (E°cell > 0), makes electricity ·  Electrolytic = driven (E°cell < 0), uses electricity.
Primary = single-use ·  Secondary = rechargeable.  In both cell types: anode = oxidation, cathode = reduction.
Faraday's law: Q = I · t (amps × seconds = coulombs) → mol e− = Q ÷ F, F = 96,485 C/mol → mol metal (use half-reaction) → mass.
⚠️ THE TWO TRAPS — READ THIS TWICE
Trap 1 — seconds. Time MUST be in seconds before you compute Q. Minutes × 60, hours × 3600. Leaving time in minutes makes Q (and your answer) far too small.
Trap 2 — electrons per atom. Read the half-reaction. Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu needs two electrons per atom, so you DIVIDE moles of electrons by 2. Ag+ + e− → Ag needs only one — no dividing. Forgetting this gives an answer that's off by a whole factor.
📝 PART A · CLASSIFY THE CELLS (items 1–3)

For each device, state whether it is galvanic or electrolytic, and (where it applies) primary or secondary. Give a one-line reason.

1. An alkaline AA battery powering a flashlight.
2. A cell splitting water into H2 and O2 using a plugged-in power supply.
3. The lithium-ion battery in a phone that is recharged each night.
📊 PART B · IDENTIFY THE ELECTRODES (items 4–5)

Remember: in every cell, the anode is where oxidation happens and the cathode is where reduction happens. Only the terminal sign changes between cell types.

4. In an alkaline battery, zinc is oxidized and manganese dioxide (MnO2) is reduced. Which is the anode and which is the cathode?
5. In an electrolytic cell, name which electrode is the anode and which is the cathode by their reactions, and state the sign (+ or −) of each. (Hint: the signs are opposite to a galvanic cell.)
🧮 PART C · FARADAY'S LAW (items 6–8)

Use Q = I·t, then mol e− = Q ÷ 96,485, then the half-reaction. Put time in seconds first, and divide by the electrons per atom. Show Q, mol e−, mol metal, and mass.

6. A current of 2.00 A flows for 1.00 hour through a copper(II) solution. Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu (Cu = 63.55 g/mol). Find the mass of copper deposited. (This is the worked example — follow the method.)
7. A current of 1.50 A flows for 20.0 minutes through a silver solution. Ag+ + e− → Ag (Ag = 107.87 g/mol). Find the mass of silver deposited. (Watch Trap 1 — and note silver needs only one electron.)
8. A current of 3.00 A flows for 30.0 minutes through a copper(II) solution. Find the mass of copper deposited, then compare to item 6 — what changed, and why is the mass different?
💡 WORKED EXAMPLE (the method for item 6)
2.00 A for 1.00 hour, Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu, Cu = 63.55 g/mol.
Step 1 — time in seconds: 1.00 h = 3600 s.
Step 2 — charge Q = I·t: 2.00 A × 3600 s = 7200 C.
Step 3 — moles of electrons: 7200 ÷ 96,485 = 0.0746 mol e−.
Step 4 — moles of Cu: 2 e− per Cu, so 0.0746 ÷ 2 = 0.0373 mol Cu.
Step 5 — mass: 0.0373 × 63.55 ≈ 2.37 g Cu.
Answer: about 2.37 g of copper.
✍️ PART D · EXPLAIN YOUR REASONING (item 9 — self-check)

Write 3–4 sentences in your notebook, then open the model answer to compare. There is no single “right” wording — check that your reasoning uses evidence, not preference.

9. A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell can keep making electricity indefinitely, while an ordinary battery eventually dies. (a) Explain why, in terms of where each device gets its reactants. (b) Then name one real trade-off — cost, materials, or environmental impact — that a decision-maker should weigh before choosing a fuel cell over a battery for a given job.
▶  Model answer — open after you've written yours
(a) A battery carries its reactants sealed inside, so once they are consumed the reaction stops and the battery is dead. A fuel cell is fed a continuous flow of reactants (hydrogen and oxygen) from outside, so it keeps producing electricity — with water as its only product — for as long as the fuel keeps arriving. The difference is the source of the reactants, not the underlying galvanic chemistry.

(b) Any one well-reasoned trade-off, backed by evidence rather than preference, earns full credit — for example: cost (fuel cells and their catalysts can be expensive to build); materials (producing and storing hydrogen fuel, and the catalysts a fuel cell needs, require resources that must be sourced responsibly); or environmental impact (a fuel cell is only truly “clean” if the hydrogen is made cleanly — hydrogen produced from fossil fuels carries a carbon cost, so the whole life cycle must be weighed against the benefit). The point is that “best” depends on the job and the evidence.
🤖 AI IS AN INSTRUMENT, NOT AN ORACLE
If you ask an AI tool to do a Faraday's-law problem, it commonly leaves the time in minutes or hours instead of converting to seconds, or forgets to divide by the electrons per atom (the “÷ 2” for Cu2+). Treat any AI result as a claim to verify, not an answer: redo Q = I·t with time in seconds, divide by 96,485, then divide by the electrons in the half-reaction — and sanity-check that a small current over a few minutes plates a fraction of a gram, not kilograms. Reasoning through the chain yourself is the skill; the calculator is just an instrument.
🔑 CHECK YOUR WORK
▶  Answer key — open after you've tried all eight
Part A — classify the cells:
1. Galvanic (it produces electricity from a spontaneous reaction) and primary (single-use — an alkaline cell isn't rechargeable).
2. Electrolytic — it needs an external power supply to drive a non-spontaneous reaction (splitting water has E°cell < 0). Primary/secondary doesn't apply (it's not a battery).
3. Galvanic while discharging (it powers the phone) and secondary (rechargeable — the charger reverses the reaction).

Part B — identify the electrodes:
4. Zinc is the anode (it is oxidized); MnO2 is the cathode (it is reduced). Anode = oxidation, cathode = reduction — always.
5. In an electrolytic cell the anode is still where oxidation happens and the cathode still where reduction happens — but the signs are anode = + (positive) and cathode = − (negative), opposite a galvanic cell, because the external power source forces the polarity.

Part C — Faraday's law:
6. Q = 2.00 × 3600 = 7200 C; mol e− = 7200 ÷ 96,485 = 0.0746; mol Cu = 0.0746 ÷ 2 = 0.0373; mass = 0.0373 × 63.55 = 2.37 g Cu.
7. 20.0 min = 1200 s; Q = 1.50 × 1200 = 1800 C; mol e− = 1800 ÷ 96,485 = 0.01866; silver needs only 1 e− per atom, so mol Ag = 0.01866; mass = 0.01866 × 107.87 = 2.01 g Ag. (No “÷ by electrons” step beyond ÷ 1.)
8. 30.0 min = 1800 s; Q = 3.00 × 1800 = 5400 C; mol e− = 5400 ÷ 96,485 = 0.05597; mol Cu = 0.05597 ÷ 2 = 0.02799; mass = 0.02799 × 63.55 = 1.78 g Cu. Compared to item 6 (2.37 g): the charge passed here is smaller (5400 C vs. 7200 C) even though the current is larger, because the time is shorter — less total charge means less copper. Faraday's law depends on the charge Q = I·t, not on current alone.

Trap check: if an answer came out tiny (item 7 near 0.03 g) you may have left the time in minutes — convert to seconds and redo. If a copper answer came out about double (item 6 near 4.7 g) you forgot to divide by 2 for Cu2+.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Items 1–3: each device classified (galvanic/electrolytic, and primary/secondary where it applies) with a one-line reason.
☐
Items 4–5: anode and cathode named by their reactions, and the electrolytic-cell signs (anode +, cathode −) stated correctly.
☐
Items 6–8: time converted to seconds, Q and mol e− shown, divided by the right number of electrons, and a final mass with units.
☐
Item 9: a 3–4 sentence written explanation (why a fuel cell doesn't run down, plus one evidence-based trade-off), compared against the model answer.
☐
All work checked against the answer key, with both traps confirmed handled.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
Classify cells (items 1–3)
6 pts		 All three classified correctly with a one-line reason each. Some classifications missing or reasons absent. 6
Identify electrodes (items 4–5)
4 pts		 Anode/cathode named by reaction and electrolytic signs correct. One part missing or a sign reversed. 4
Faraday's law (items 6–8)
8 pts		 All three computed with time in seconds, Q and mol e− shown, correct electron ratio, mass with units. Some steps missing, or a trap (seconds / electron ratio) skipped. 8
Self-check + written reasoning (item 9)
2 pts		 Items 1–8 compared to the answer key with corrections noted, and item 9 reasoning written and checked against the model answer. Not checked, or item 9 reasoning missing. 2
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer key lets you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M8 W3 Hands-On — Cells, Electrodes & Faraday's Law
Work the eight items in your notebook or on paper, then upload a clear photo or scan (or type your answers directly into the Canvas text box).
If a calculation gives a result you don't trust, submit what you have with a note about where you got stuck — that's useful information, not a penalty.

VR Assignment · 20 pts · one headset session (~35–45 min)
🧘 PREFER NOT TO USE A HEADSET?
A full non-VR alternate — “Real Cells & Electrolysis Panel (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the exact same objectives and earns the same credit. Do one pathway, not both.
📚 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
This is Build 3 of 4 of the project you began two weeks ago: the Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build — the exhibit you'll narrate on camera at the end of the module. You return to the same persistent bench, where your Week-1 galvanic cell and Week-2 cell-potential panel are still waiting. This week you add a Real Cells & Electrolysis Panel beside them: at least one battery labeled primary vs. secondary (an alkaline cell and a lithium-ion cell), an H2–O2 fuel cell (continuous reactant flow → electricity + water), a small corrosion / sacrificial-anode demo (an iron piece protected by a more-active metal like Mg or Zn), and an electrolytic cell driven by an external power source — plus a sticky note contrasting galvanic and electrolytic. This is the sorting from Lessons 8.05–8.07, made big enough to point at and narrate. Next week (Build 4) you'll add a rate & catalysis demo, then record the full walkthrough.
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your Week-1 galvanic cell and Week-2 cell-potential panel still in place at Lab Bench A.
▶  Your notes from Lessons 8.05–8.07 (primary vs. secondary, the fuel-cell reaction, the sacrificial anode, and the galvanic-vs-electrolytic contrast).
▶  About 35–45 minutes in one sitting.
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (your placed objects stay between visits all module)
Session ID: see the pinned OptimaXR Sessions list in this module (the Electrochem & Rates Lab session)
Location: Electrochem & Rates Lab
Spawn point: Lab Bench A
When you arrive: your Week-1 galvanic cell and Week-2 cell-potential panel are waiting at Lab Bench A. A new Whiteboard IFX shows this week's Step 1 and four empty slots labeled Battery, Fuel Cell, Corrosion, and Electrolytic Cell. A sticky note at your feet reads “Galvanic makes it; electrolytic uses it.”
🔭 HOW THIS BUILD WORKS · THE INVESTIGATION ARC
You'll move through the same arc a scientist uses: Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend. Commit a prediction first (below), build the panel to test it (the numbered steps), then analyze and defend what you found in a short written reflection at the end.
🔍 STEP 0 · OBSERVE → QUESTION → PREDICT (COMMIT BEFORE YOU BUILD)
Observe. Your Week-1 galvanic cell drives electrons through a wire all on its own — a spontaneous reaction making electricity.
Question. The four devices you're about to build — a battery, an H2–O2 fuel cell, a corrosion / sacrificial-anode demo, and an electrolytic cell — are all electrochemistry. But which ones make electricity from a spontaneous reaction (galvanic), and which one spends electricity to force a non-spontaneous reaction (electrolytic)?
Predict — commit first. Before you spawn anything, spawn a sticky note and write a one-line prediction: for each of the four devices, mark it galvanic or electrolytic, and predict which single one is the electrolytic cell. Sign the note. You'll test this prediction as you build — do not change it until the Analyze step.
📝 INVESTIGATE · WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Return to your Week-1/Week-2 build and confirm it's intact — the galvanic cell (anode −, cathode +, salt bridge) and the cell-potential panel. Spawn a new Real Cells & Electrolysis Panel beside it with four slots. Leave bench space to the right for the Week-4 rate & catalysis demo.
2
Battery slot: spawn at least one battery — build or label an alkaline cell (mark it primary — single-use) and a lithium-ion cell (mark it secondary — rechargeable). Sticky note: “Primary = single-use; secondary = rechargeable (reaction can be reversed).”
3
Fuel-cell slot: build an H2–O2 fuel cell with arrows showing reactants flowing in and water flowing out. Sticky note: “2H2 + O2 → 2H2O — continuous fuel → electricity, water the only product.”
4
Corrosion slot: place an iron piece with a block of a more-active metal (magnesium or zinc) attached. Add an arrow showing the active metal corroding. Sticky note: “Sacrificial anode — the more-active metal is oxidized instead of the iron.”
5
Electrolytic-cell slot: build a cell driven by an external power source (a battery/power-supply prop wired in). Mark the anode (+) and cathode (−) — note the signs are flipped from your galvanic cell, but oxidation is still at the anode. Sticky note: “Electrolytic: outside power drives a non-spontaneous reaction (E°cell < 0).”
6
Add one summary sticky note contrasting the two cell families: “Galvanic = spontaneous, E°cell > 0, MAKES electricity. Electrolytic = driven, E°cell < 0, USES electricity.” Sign your name on it.
7
Lock your panel and labels so they aren't bumped, then take a snapshot and save it as ElectroRate_Wk3_YourName. This snapshot is your project's saved progress for next week.
8
Take one screenshot inside the headset that clearly shows all four labeled cells (battery, fuel cell, corrosion, electrolytic) and your galvanic-vs-electrolytic summary note. That screenshot is what you'll submit.
Need to stop partway? Because the Session is persistent, your placed and locked work — including Weeks 1–2 — will be waiting when you return. Save the ElectroRate_Wk3_YourName snapshot before you log out so nothing is lost.
🧠 ANALYZE → DEFEND → EXTEND · CER REFLECTION
Analyze. Go back to the prediction you committed in Step 0. Which of the four devices turned out to be galvanic, and which single one is electrolytic? Did your prediction hold, or did building it change your mind?
Defend your answer in a short CER written in the comment box (2–4 sentences):
• Claim — which of your four cells is the electrolytic one (and which are galvanic)?
• Evidence — what did you build or label that shows it (e.g., an external power source, the sign of the terminals, spontaneous vs. driven)?
• Reasoning — connect the evidence to the rule: galvanic cells make electricity from a spontaneous reaction (E°cell > 0); an electrolytic cell spends outside electricity to drive a non-spontaneous one (E°cell < 0).
Extend. Leave bench room to the right: next week (Build 4) you'll add a rate & catalysis demo, then record the full narrated walkthrough that ties all four builds together.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
1. Upload your in-headset screenshot showing the four labeled cells (battery primary/secondary, H2–O2 fuel cell, corrosion / sacrificial anode, electrolytic cell) and your galvanic-vs-electrolytic note to this Canvas assignment.
2. In the comment box, write a one-sentence caption: name the four cells and state, in your own words, the difference between a galvanic and an electrolytic cell. (Your caption will be used when your work appears in the class gallery walk later this module.)
3. Add your CER reflection (Claim–Evidence–Reasoning from the Analyze step above): state whether your Step-0 prediction held and defend which cell is electrolytic, with evidence and reasoning.
⏱️ TIME
About 35–45 minutes in the headset.

☐

☐

Week 4 · Hands-On (Excel)
Rate-Law Determination from Initial-Rate Data
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: the rate law rate = k[A]m[B]n (8.09) and the method of initial rates — comparing trials where one concentration changes at a time to find each reactant's order. Here you take a real set of initial-rate data into Excel, determine the orders from the data, write the rate law, and compute the rate constant k — exactly the reasoning a chemist uses at the bench.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work, and it puts the central kinetics rule into practice: orders come from experiment, never from the coefficients.
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
A chemist studied the reaction A + B → products by running four trials, each time changing one starting concentration while holding the other fixed, and measured the initial rate of each. In Excel, you'll enter the data table, then compare trials to find the order in A and the order in B, write the rate law, and use one trial to compute the rate constant k by formula. Excel does the arithmetic; the chemistry — reasoning out the orders from how the rate responds — is your job.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When you double one reactant's concentration, the rate sometimes doubles and sometimes quadruples. How does watching which of those happens — trial by trial — let you read the reaction's hidden orders straight out of the data?
📊 YOUR DATA · FOUR INITIAL-RATE TRIALS FOR A + B → PRODUCTS

Type this table into Excel exactly as shown. Each row is one experiment with different starting concentrations.

Trial [A] (M) [B] (M) Initial rate (M/s)
10.100.100.0050
20.200.100.0100
30.100.200.0200
40.200.200.0400
Note the design: trials 1&2 change only [A]; trials 1&3 change only [B]. Trial 4 changes both and is your independent check.
🧮 HOW THE METHOD WORKS (A SHORT REMINDER)
To find an order, compare two trials in which only that reactant changes, and see how the rate responds: rate ×2 → first order; rate ×4 → second order; rate unchanged (×1) → zero order. (That's 2 raised to the order: 21=2, 22=4, 20=1.) Once you have the orders, plug one trial's numbers into rate = k[A]m[B]n and solve for k.
🤖 AI AS AN INSTRUMENT · VERIFY, DON'T TRUST
If you ask an AI assistant for the rate law, it will very often hand back the coefficients of the equation as the orders — here it might guess “first order in A, first order in B” just because the equation reads A + B. That is the exact mistake this assignment trains you to avoid. The orders are hiding in the data, not the equation. Determine each order yourself by comparing the trials, and confirm your rate constant k comes out the same from more than one trial. Use AI to check your arithmetic if you like — but the orders must come from the experiment, verified by hand.
📝 WHAT TO DO IN EXCEL
1
Enter the four-row table with headers in row 1: Trial, [A] (M), [B] (M), Initial rate (M/s).
2
Find the order in A. Compare trials 1 and 2 (where [B] is fixed). In a cell, compute the rate ratio with a formula like =rate2/rate1. Decide from the ratio (×2, ×4, or ×1) whether A is first, second, or zero order, and type the order in a labeled cell m.
3
Find the order in B. Compare trials 1 and 3 (where [A] is fixed) with =rate3/rate1. Decide the order in B and type it in a labeled cell n.
4
Write the rate law in a text cell using your m and n: rate = k[A]m[B]n. Also compute the overall order in a cell: =m+n.
5
Compute k from Trial 1 in a labeled cell, using your orders. With m and n in place, a formula like =rate1/((A1)^m*(B1)^n) gives the rate constant. Then repeat with Trial 4 to confirm you get the same k.
6
In cells or a text box below the table, answer the three Analysis Questions below.
❓ ANALYSIS QUESTIONS (answer in your spreadsheet)
A. What is the order in A and the order in B? For each, name the two trials you compared and the rate ratio that told you the order.
B. Write the full rate law and state the overall order. Then show your computation of k from Trial 1, including its units.
C. A classmate says “the equation is A + B, so it must be first order in each.” Using your data, explain in one or two sentences why you cannot get the orders from the equation — and what the data actually show.
D. Justify the order in B directly from the data table. In two or three sentences, name the two trials you compared, state exactly what [B] did and what the rate did, and explain why that factor points to the order you assigned — as if you were defending it to a skeptical lab partner.
▶  Check your work — answer key
Order in A (trials 1 & 2, [B] fixed): [A] doubles (0.10 → 0.20) and the rate doubles (0.0050 → 0.0100), ratio = 2. Rate ×2 → first order in A (m = 1).

Order in B (trials 1 & 3, [A] fixed): [B] doubles (0.10 → 0.20) and the rate quadruples (0.0050 → 0.0200), ratio = 4. Rate ×4 → second order in B (n = 2).

Rate law: rate = k[A][B]2 — overall order = 1 + 2 = 3 (third order).

Rate constant from Trial 1: 0.0050 = k(0.10)(0.10)2 = k(0.10)(0.010) = k(0.0010), so k = 0.0050 / 0.0010 = 5.0 M−2·s−1.
Check with Trial 4: k = 0.0400 / [(0.20)(0.20)2] = 0.0400 / [(0.20)(0.040)] = 0.0400 / 0.0080 = 5.0 M−2·s−1. ✓ Same k — the rate law is consistent.

A. Order in A = 1 (trials 1&2, ratio 2); order in B = 2 (trials 1&3, ratio 4).
B. rate = k[A][B]2; overall order 3; k = 5.0 M−2·s−1 (units chosen so rate comes out in M/s for a third-order reaction).
C. The orders come from experiment, not the equation. The data show the reaction is second order in B (doubling [B] quadrupled the rate), which the coefficients could never have told us. Reading orders off the equation would have given the wrong rate law.
D. Model answer: Comparing Trials 1 and 3 (where [A] is held fixed at 0.10 M), [B] doubles from 0.10 M to 0.20 M and the initial rate quadruples from 0.0050 M/s to 0.0200 M/s — a rate ratio of 4. Because doubling a concentration multiplies the rate by 2 raised to that reactant's order, and 2² = 4, the reaction must be second order in B (n = 2). Holding [A] constant is what makes this fair: the ×4 response can only be due to the change in [B].
📁 M365 REMINDER
Build this in Microsoft Excel from your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_RateLaw_CHEM1H, save it to your Optima → Science OneDrive course folder, and submit through Canvas. New here? See the pinned “M365 Setup & File Organization Guide” page in this module.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: building rate ratios with cell references and using exponent formulas (the ^ operator) to chain a calculation to a final value in Excel.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The four-trial data table is entered, and the rate ratios for A and B are computed by formula.
☐
The order in A (1) and order in B (2) are identified from the data, the rate law rate = k[A][B]2 is written, and the overall order (3) is stated.
☐
k is computed by formula and confirmed from a second trial (k = 5.0 M−2·s−1), and all three Analysis Questions are answered, then checked against the answer key.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
Data & rate ratios
8 pts		 All four trials entered and the rate ratios for A and B computed by formula. Some data missing, or ratios typed by hand instead of by formula. 8
Orders, rate law & k
6 pts		 Orders identified from the data, rate law written, and k computed by formula and confirmed. Rate law or k missing, or orders read off the coefficients. 6
Analysis + self-check
6 pts		 All three questions answered, then checked and corrected. Some questions missing or not checked. 6
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer key lets you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M8 W4 Hands-On — Rate-Law Determination (Excel)
Upload your Excel file (.xlsx) through Canvas (OneDrive tab or file upload).
If a formula gives a result you don't trust, submit what you have with a note about where you got stuck — that's useful information, not a penalty.

VR Assignment · 20 pts · one headset session (~40–50 min)
🧘 PREFER NOT TO USE A HEADSET?
A full non-VR alternate — “Reaction-Rate & Catalysis Demo (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the exact same objectives and earns the same credit. Do one pathway, not both.
🎥 THIS IS THE FINAL BUILD — RECORD THE WALKTHROUGH
This week completes your four-week project. After you finish the Reaction-Rate & Catalysis Demo, you will record the full walkthrough video of your whole Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build. That recording is submitted to the separate, graded Module VR Project assignment — this weekly assignment still just asks for a completion screenshot + caption. Plan time to do both this week.
📚 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
You're adding the fourth and final station to your module-long Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build: a Reaction-Rate & Catalysis Demo, set beside your three electrochemistry stations. You'll build an energy-profile diagram showing the activation-energy barrier Ea for a reaction, with a second curve showing a lower Ea when a catalyst is present; a factors-affecting-rate panel (concentration, temperature, surface area, catalyst); and a small collision-theory demo showing that particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation. Then you'll record a narrated walkthrough of the entire build — the galvanic cell (Wk1), the cell-potential panel (Wk2), the real-cells & electrolysis panel (Wk3), and this rate/catalysis demo (Wk4) — explaining the chemistry as you go.
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your notes from Lessons 8.08–8.10 (reaction rate & the five factors; rate laws & collision theory; activation energy Ea; mechanisms & catalysts).
▶  Your three earlier builds, already saved in the persistent Session.
▶  About 40–50 minutes in one sitting (building + recording).
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (all three earlier builds are waiting for you)
Session: “Electrochem & Rates Lab” — see the pinned OptimaXR Sessions list in this module
Spawn point: Lab Bench A (build) · Lab Entrance (for the final recording walk-through)
When you arrive: your three earlier stations are along the bench. A Whiteboard IFX above the last open space shows this week's Step 1 and the kinetics vocabulary — activation energy (Ea), catalyst, collision theory, rate factors — beside an empty labeled zone marked Reaction-Rate & Catalysis Demo. A sticky note reads “Build 4 of 4 here, then record from the entrance.”
🔬 HOW THIS INVESTIGATION FLOWS
Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend. You'll notice a phenomenon, commit a prediction before you build, build your demo to test it, then analyze what you made, defend it with a short Claim–Evidence–Reasoning, and extend it to the wider world. Work the stages in order — the prediction comes first, on purpose.
👀 OBSERVE & QUESTION
Observe: a glow stick fades faster in warm water than in ice water, and a car's catalytic converter needs a costly platinum-group surface to do its job. Question: what actually controls how fast a reaction runs — and how can a catalyst speed one up without being used up or changing how much product forms? Your build this week is the answer, made visible.
✅ PREDICT FIRST — COMMIT BEFORE YOU BUILD
Before you build anything, write a committed prediction in your notebook (or a starting sticky note): “Adding a catalyst will change ______ about the reaction, but will NOT change ______.” Decide now whether a catalyst changes how fast the reaction goes, how much product forms, or both — and jot why. You'll hold your finished energy-profile diagram up against this prediction in the Analyze step. Committing first is the point; do not peek ahead.
📝 INVESTIGATE · WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
In the Reaction-Rate & Catalysis Demo zone, build an energy-profile diagram (use the 3D pen or spawn a curve): reactants on the left, products on the right, and a hill between them whose height is the activation energy Ea. Label the peak.
2
Draw a second curve over the first with a lower hill, labeled “catalyzed path — lower Ea.” Add a sticky note: “A catalyst lowers Ea and speeds the reaction without being used up; it doesn't change ΔG or the products.”
3
Spawn a factors-affecting-rate panel with four labeled tiles — concentration, temperature, surface area, catalyst — each with a one-line note on how it speeds the reaction (more/harder collisions, or a lower barrier).
4
Build a small collision-theory demo: two particles meeting, with notes showing that a reaction needs enough energy (at least Ea) and the correct orientation. Add the through-line sticky note: “Thermodynamics gives direction; kinetics gives speed.” Sign it.
5
Lock the demo and its labels, then take a snapshot saved as ElectroRate_Final_YourName. This is your finished project's saved state.
6
Record the walkthrough video. Move to the Lab Entrance spawn point and start an in-headset recording. Walk past all four stations in order, narrating the chemistry of each: the galvanic cell, cell potential, real cells & electrolysis, and this rate & catalysis demo. Aim for about 3–5 minutes.
7
Take one screenshot inside the headset that clearly shows your finished Reaction-Rate & Catalysis Demo with the labeled Ea and catalyzed-path curves. That screenshot is what you submit here; the recorded video goes to the separate Module VR Project assignment.
Need to stop partway? Because the Session is persistent, your placed and locked stations will be waiting when you return. Save the ElectroRate_Final_YourName snapshot before you log out so nothing is lost.
🔍 ANALYZE · READ YOUR OWN MODEL
Stand back and look at your finished energy-profile diagram. The two curves start at the same reactants and end at the same products — only the height of the hill differs. Ask yourself: does the catalyzed (lower) curve end at a different product energy, or the same one? Now hold that against the prediction you committed before building. Did the model confirm your prediction or correct it? Note in a sentence what your diagram shows about which quantity a catalyst changes (the speed) and which it leaves alone (ΔG, the equilibrium, and the products).
💬 DEFEND · A SHORT CLAIM–EVIDENCE–REASONING
In 3–4 sentences (in your notebook, and folded into your recorded narration), answer the demo's driving question: “Why can a catalyst make a slow reaction race without being used up or changing how much product forms?” Structure it as Claim → Evidence → Reasoning, pointing to your own energy-profile diagram as the evidence.
▶  Write yours first, then check a model CER
Claim: A catalyst speeds the reaction up by lowering the activation energy — it does not change the reaction's direction or how much product forms.
Evidence: My energy-profile diagram shows two paths between the same reactants and products; the catalyzed path has a lower hill (lower Ea) than the uncatalyzed one, and both curves end at the same product energy.
Reasoning: By collision theory, a lower Ea means a larger fraction of collisions carry enough energy to react, so the rate rises. Because the catalyst is regenerated and lowers the barrier for the forward and reverse directions equally, ΔG, the equilibrium position, and the products stay the same — only the speed changes.
🔮 EXTEND · BEYOND THE BENCH
Connect your demo back to the opening question. The same lowered barrier you drew is what lets a catalytic converter clean exhaust and what enzymes do inside your cells. In your recording, add one sentence naming a real catalyst and the reaction it speeds — and consider the frontier: scientists are working on cheaper, earth-abundant catalysts and engineered enzymes to do this work with less energy and waste.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT (TO THIS WEEKLY ASSIGNMENT)
1. Upload your in-headset screenshot showing your finished Reaction-Rate & Catalysis Demo with its labeled Ea and lower catalyzed-path curve.
2. In the comment box, write a one-sentence caption: state what a catalyst does to Ea and what it does not change.
3. Add your committed prediction and your 3–4 sentence CER (self-checked against the model above) — a couple of lines in the comment box or your notebook. This stays self-check; it is scored for completion, not correctness.
Remember: your recorded walkthrough video is submitted separately to the graded Module VR Project assignment — not here.
⏱️ TIME
About 40–50 minutes in the headset (building the demo plus recording the walkthrough).
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA (COMPLETION-BASED)
☐
An energy-profile diagram is built with the activation energy Ea marked, plus a second lower curve labeled as the catalyzed path.
☐
A factors-affecting-rate panel (concentration, temperature, surface area, catalyst) and a collision-theory demo (enough energy AND correct orientation) are placed and labeled, with the through-line sticky note signed.
☐
A narrated walkthrough video of all four stations is recorded (for the separate Module VR Project).
☐
A prediction was committed before building, and a short Claim–Evidence–Reasoning is written and self-checked against the model.
☐
Screenshot uploaded and one-sentence caption written here. ElectroRate_Final_YourName snapshot saved.

Module 8 Writing Assignment
Powering the Future — A Battery Argument
Word (.docx) · 100 pts · teacher-reviewed
📚 THE TASK
Every battery is a galvanic cell — a spontaneous redox reaction packaged to push electrons through a circuit. But no single chemistry is best for everything: a phone, a car, and a power grid each demand different things. In this assignment you will argue which battery (or cell) chemistry best fits a stated use case, defending your choice with the electrochemistry — cell potential, the redox couple, rechargeability, energy density — and then weighing the real costs and benefits with the honesty the question deserves.
This is a scientific argument: a claim, defended with evidence and reasoning, and accountable to the trade-offs. Choose one use case below, then choose a cell chemistry to advocate for it.
USE CASE A · ELECTRIC VEHICLE
A car needs high energy density (lots of energy per kilogram), rechargeability, a long cycle life, and reasonably fast charging. Weight matters a great deal.
USE CASE B · GRID / HOME SOLAR STORAGE
A storage bank needs low cost, a long cycle life, safety, and large capacity. It sits still, so weight matters far less.
USE CASE C · SIMPLE DISPOSABLE DEVICE
A TV remote or wall clock needs a cheap, reliable, shelf-stable cell with low energy demand. Recharging isn't needed.
You'll write it in Microsoft Word, organized into the argument sections listed further down.
⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS
This argument is one of only two teacher-reviewed pieces in Module 8 (the other is your Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build VR project). Your teacher reads it personally and responds to your reasoning — so make it your careful best, and justify your claim from the electrochemistry, not from a guess. This is exactly Quarter 4's question in action: how does chemistry shape our world? — and its virtue, Responsibility: chemistry's power comes with real costs.
🧮 YOUR TOOLKIT (USE THESE EXACT IDEAS & VALUES)
A battery is a galvanic cell: a spontaneous redox reaction drives electrons from the anode (oxidation) to the cathode (reduction) through the circuit. A positive E°cell drives the voltage; E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, and E°cell > 0 means spontaneous (ΔG° = −nFE° < 0).
Primary vs secondary: a primary cell is single-use (the redox reaction isn't practically reversible); a secondary cell is rechargeable (an outside current drives the reaction backward — electrolysis — to restore the reactants).
Energy density ≠ voltage: voltage (volts) is the “push” per electron; energy density is how much energy is stored per kilogram (or liter). A cell can have a modest voltage but high energy density, or vice versa — don't confuse them.
Alkaline cell (primary): Zn anode / MnO2 cathode, about 1.5 V; cheap, shelf-stable, not rechargeable.
Lead-acid (secondary): about 2 V per cell; six cells ≈ 12 V (car battery); cheap and reliable but heavy (low energy density).
Lithium-ion (secondary): high voltage and high energy density, many recharge cycles — the standard for phones and EVs; uses lithium, cobalt, and nickel.
Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell: not a fixed-charge battery but a cell fed continuous reactants: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O; the only product is water.
🧠 YOUR REASONING TOOLKIT (how to build the argument)
Use these steps in your own words — don't just copy the headings.
Step 1 — Pin down the use case and what it demands.
Name the use case (A, B, or C) and list the two or three properties that matter most for it (e.g., for the EV: high energy density and rechargeability; for the grid: low cost and long cycle life).
Step 2 — Pick a chemistry and tie its electrochemistry to those demands.
Choose lithium-ion, lead-acid, alkaline, or an H2–O2 fuel cell. Explain it as a galvanic cell (the redox couple, that it's spontaneous, why it's primary or secondary) and connect that chemistry to what the use case needs.
Step 3 — Weigh the costs honestly, then decide.
No chemistry is free of trade-offs: materials sourcing (e.g., lithium and cobalt mining), lifespan, recyclability, safety, and environmental cost. Acknowledge the strongest objection to your choice, then explain why your chemistry is still the best fit — reasoning from evidence, not preference.
📝 STRUCTURE: WRITE THESE SECTIONS
1
Claim. One or two clear sentences naming your use case and the chemistry you say is best for it (e.g., “For an electric vehicle, a lithium-ion battery is the best chemistry,” or “For grid storage, lead-acid is the more responsible choice.”).
2
Electrochemical evidence. Lay out the chemistry of your cell: that it's a galvanic cell running a spontaneous redox reaction (name the redox couple or the half-reactions if you can), its approximate voltage, whether it's primary or secondary (and what that means for recharging), and its energy density. Use the toolkit values — and keep voltage and energy density distinct.
3
Reasoning. This is the heart of the argument. Connect the evidence to the claim step by step: this use case needs X; my chemistry provides X because of its electrochemistry; therefore it fits. Compare against at least one rival chemistry and explain why yours wins for this case (e.g., why high energy density makes lithium-ion right for an EV but is wasted on a wall clock).
4
Cost / benefit & responsibility. Weigh the real-world costs and benefits across all three dimensions — materials (sourcing and recyclability), economics (cost to make and to run), and environment & safety (impact and hazards) — alongside lifespan. Name the strongest objection to your choice and answer it. Reason from evidence, not preference (Honesty thread).
5
Conclusion. Restate your claim in light of the evidence and the trade-offs, and name the big idea: a battery is chemistry put to work, and choosing one well means matching the redox chemistry to the job — and owning its costs.
✎ LENGTH & STYLE
Aim for roughly 500–700 words across the five sections. Use correct terminology — galvanic cell, oxidation/reduction, anode/cathode, cell potential (E°cell), primary/secondary cell, energy density. The chemistry and the reasoning are what's graded — not polished prose. Justify your claim with the electrochemistry, not a hunch, and keep voltage and energy density separate.
⚠️ A NOTE ON USING AI TOOLS
An AI tool will happily recommend a battery — and it can get the chemistry wrong: overstating a cell's specs, inventing a voltage or an energy-density figure, or confusing energy density with voltage as if they were the same number. If you consult one, treat it as a draft to check, never an answer to paste: verify every electrochemical claim against this assignment's toolkit values and the redox reasoning, and re-derive that E°cell > 0 means a spontaneous (galvanic) cell yourself. The instrument proposes; your reasoning against the electrochemistry verifies. That is exactly the AI-literacy skill this assignment is built to grow.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Write your argument in Microsoft Word from your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_BatteryArgument_CHEM1H, save it to your Optima → Science OneDrive course folder, and submit through Canvas. New here? See the pinned “M365 Setup & File Organization Guide” page in this module.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: structuring an evidence-based argument with headings in Word and, if you compare options, inserting a simple comparison table. If your teacher returns comments for revision, turn on Track Changes before revising.
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED (TEACHER RUBRIC — build natively as a Canvas Rubric)
Criterion Full marks Developing Pts
Claim A clear, specific, defensible claim that names the use case and the chemistry chosen for it. Claim vague, missing, or only restates the prompt. 15
Electrochemical evidence Correct, relevant electrochemistry: the cell as a spontaneous galvanic cell (redox couple/half-reactions), approximate voltage, primary vs secondary, and energy density — with voltage and energy density kept distinct and the toolkit values used accurately. Chemistry thin, incomplete, or wrong (e.g., voltage/energy-density confused, invented specs). 25
Reasoning Steps logically from the use case's demands → the cell's electrochemistry → the fit, and compares against at least one rival chemistry, explaining why this one wins for this case. Claim asserted without connecting it to the chemistry; no comparison; reasoning gaps. 30
Cost/benefit & responsibility Weighs genuine trade-offs (sourcing, lifespan, recyclability, safety, environment), names the strongest objection and answers it, reasoning from evidence not preference. Trade-offs missing, generic, or one-sided; no counterargument considered. 15
Conclusion & communication Conclusion ties back to the claim and names the big idea; correct terminology, clear organized argument. Conclusion thin or just restates; terms misused; disorganized. 15
Total: 100 pts
The electrochemical evidence and the reasoning carry the most weight — a confident recommendation with no electrochemistry behind it earns little. Reason from the cell up.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M8 Argument — Powering the Future (Battery Argument)
Submit your Word .docx through Canvas (OneDrive tab or file upload). If your teacher returns it with comments, revise with Track Changes on and resubmit as a _Revision1 file.

A full non-VR alternate — “Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build — Narrated Walkthrough (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the same objectives and is graded on the same rubric. Do one pathway, not both.
📚 THE BIG PICTURE
Across this module you've built an Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build in OptimaXR, one week at a time, to answer a single running question: how do chemists turn chemistry into electricity, predict whether a cell will run on its own, and control how fast a reaction goes? Week 1 you built a galvanic cell foundation; Week 2 a cell-potential panel; Week 3 a real cells & electrolysis panel; Week 4 a reaction-rate & catalysis demo. Now you bring it all together.
Your task is to record a guided video walkthrough inside the headset — a short tour in which you narrate the chemistry of your build, from spontaneous redox in a galvanic cell, through cell potential and free energy, to electrolysis, and on to what makes a reaction fast or slow. This recorded explanation, not a static screenshot, is what earns the grade. The build is the stage; your spoken reasoning is the performance.
⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS
This walkthrough is one of only two teacher-reviewed pieces in Module 8 (the other is your Battery Argument writing assignment). Your teacher will watch your recording and respond to your reasoning personally — so make it your best thinking, clearly explained.
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your finished build — the ElectroRate_Final_YourName snapshot from the Week 4 build, including the Week 1 galvanic cell, the Week 2 cell-potential panel, the Week 3 real-cells & electrolysis panel, and the Week 4 rate & catalysis demo.
▶  A quiet space and about 30–40 minutes (planning, one or two recording takes, and submitting).
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (your finished build is waiting)
Session ID: see the pinned OptimaXR Sessions list in this module
Session name: Electrochem & Rates Lab
Location: Electrochem & Rates Lab
Spawn point: Lab Entrance
🎤 WHAT YOUR RECORDING MUST COVER (aim for 3–5 minutes)
1
Open at the entrance. Introduce your build and state the big question it answers: how do chemists turn chemistry into electricity, predict whether a cell will run, and control how fast a reaction goes?
2
Galvanic cell & redox (Week 1). Walk your galvanic cell. Explain that a galvanic cell runs a spontaneous redox reaction to make electricity, that oxidation is loss of electrons at the anode (the negative terminal) and reduction is gain of electrons at the cathode (the positive terminal), and that electrons flow anode → cathode through the external wire while the salt bridge keeps each half-cell neutral. Use the Daniell cell: Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu.
3
Cell potential, free energy & equilibrium (Week 2). At your cell-potential panel, read the voltmeter (Zn–Cu ≈ +1.10 V) and explain E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. State the through-line: a positive E°cell means a spontaneous (galvanic) cell, and ΔG° = −nFE°cell — so E°cell > 0 gives ΔG° < 0 and K > 1 (products favored).
4
Real cells, corrosion & electrolysis (Week 3). Use your real-cells & electrolysis panel to contrast a primary (single-use) cell with a secondary (rechargeable) cell, point out an H2–O2 fuel cell, show the corrosion / sacrificial-anode demo, and then explain the key reversal: an electrolytic cell uses outside power to drive a non-spontaneous reaction (E°cell < 0). Galvanic makes electricity; electrolytic uses it.
5
Rates & catalysis (Week 4). At your reaction-rate & catalysis demo, walk the energy-profile diagram: a reaction needs an activation energy Ea to proceed, and a catalyst lowers Ea by offering an alternate pathway without being used up. Name the factors that raise rate (concentration, temperature, surface area, catalyst, nature of reactants) and state collision theory: collisions must have enough energy and the right orientation.
6
Close with the evidence — this is required. Before your final through-line, justify the chemistry with the evidence: explain why the galvanic cell is spontaneous (E°cell > 0, so ΔG° = −nFE°cell < 0), how an electrolytic cell differs (it must be driven by outside power, E°cell < 0), and how a catalyst speeds a reaction (it lowers Ea by an alternate pathway without being used up). Then land the through-line: thermodynamics tells us the direction — whether a cell runs on its own — while kinetics tells us the speed; together they let chemists both predict and control chemical change.
How to record: Use OptimaXR's video recording feature to capture your narrated tour from inside the headset (start the recording from the menu/tablet, walk and talk, then stop and save). If your setup can't capture in-headset audio, record your screen with narration instead. Aim for one clean take; a second take is fine.

1. Upload your video recording (3–5 minutes) to this Canvas assignment as a media/file upload.
2. In the comment box, list the four weekly builds in one line each (Wk1 galvanic cell foundation, Wk2 cell-potential panel, Wk3 real cells & electrolysis panel, Wk4 reaction-rate & catalysis demo) so your teacher can see the iteration behind the final build.

Criterion Full marks Developing Pts
Evidence-based scientific reasoning (redox / E°cell / rate evidence) Explains the evidence behind the chemistry, not just the labels: why the galvanic cell is spontaneous (E°cell > 0, so ΔG° = −nFE°cell < 0), why electrons flow anode → cathode, what E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode shows, why an electrolytic cell must be driven (E°cell < 0), and how a catalyst speeds a reaction by lowering Ea. Every claim is grounded in the redox, cell-potential, and rate evidence in the build. States conclusions without the evidence behind them, or the reasoning has gaps or errors. 35
Accurate chemistry The chemistry is correct throughout — anode oxidation / cathode reduction, electron direction, the Zn–Cu cell at ≈ +1.10 V, galvanic vs electrolytic, Ea and catalysis — with no significant errors. Contains chemistry errors (reversed electron flow or signs, electrolysis called spontaneous, or a catalyst said to be consumed or to change ΔG, K, or the products). 25
Clear narration & model The narrated tour is organized and easy to follow, and the model/build is recognizable and correct at a high-school level (two half-cells with salt bridge and electron direction, a cell-potential panel, spontaneous-vs-driven cells, and an energy profile with a lower catalyzed curve); audio and visuals are usable. No reflection on the model's limits or on any real-world / societal connection. 8
Total: 100 pts
The same five criteria and points apply to both the VR and non-VR pathways — same objectives, same rubric. A high-school-level model is expected; evidence-based scientific reasoning carries the most weight.

Week 1 · Hands-On
Balancing Nuclear Equations
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: nuclide notation and the band of stability (9.01), and the conservation of mass number (A) and atomic number (Z) across the decay types — alpha, beta-minus, positron emission, and gamma (9.02).
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work. Two parts: a set of nuclear equations you balance, and a few short reasoning items on decay type, the band of stability, and penetrating power.
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
A nuclear equation balances on just two running totals: the mass number A and the atomic number Z. In Part A you'll fill the missing particle or daughter nuclide in six equations, using those two rules. In Part B you'll reason in words: classify a decay from how A and Z changed, predict a decay from the band of stability, and rank radiation. Work each item before you open the matching ▶ Check your thinking box — the honest attempt is where the learning happens.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When a nucleus decays, how do I use the conservation of A and Z to find exactly what it becomes — and what it gives off?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
In the Canvas text-entry box for this assignment, number your responses to match Part A (1–6) and Part B (1–3).
2
Part A: Write the missing particle or nuclide in full notation (mass number, then atomic number, then symbol), and show the A and Z arithmetic. Then open its check box and compare.
3
Part B: Answer in one or two sentences each, then check.
⚠️ AI AS AN INSTRUMENT · VERIFY THE BALANCE YOURSELF
An AI tool can produce a daughter nuclide that looks right but quietly breaks a conservation rule — off by one on Z, or naming the wrong element for that Z. Do the A and Z arithmetic by hand, then confirm the element symbol against a periodic table. Conservation of A and Z is the primary evidence; the AI is just a second opinion you check, never the authority.
🧪 PART A · BALANCE THE EQUATION (6 problems)

Fill the blank (?) so that the total mass numbers (A) match and the total atomic numbers (Z) match. Use a periodic table to name the element from its Z.

A1.   226 88Ra → ? + 42He   (alpha decay)
A2.   3215P → 3216S + ?   (beta-minus decay)
A3.   2211Na → ? +  0+1e   (positron emission)
A4.   6027Co* → 6027Co + ?   (gamma emission; the * marks an energized nucleus)
A5.   ? → 222 86Rn + 42He   (find the parent of this alpha decay)
A6.   234 90Th → 234 91Pa + ?   (which particle, and what decay type is this?)
▶  Check your thinking — Part A answer key
A1. Alpha removes A = 4, Z = 2. Daughter A = 226 − 4 = 222; Z = 88 − 2 = 86 → 222 86Rn (radon). Check: 226 = 222 + 4; 88 = 86 + 2.

A2. A unchanged (32 = 32), and Z rose 15 → 16, so a beta particle was emitted:  0−1e. Check: 32 = 32 + 0; 15 = 16 + (−1).

A3. Positron emission: A unchanged, Z − 1. Daughter A = 22; Z = 11 − 1 = 10 → 2210Ne (neon). Check: 22 = 22 + 0; 11 = 10 + 1.

A4. Same nuclide before and after, so the emission carries no A and no Z: a gamma ray, 00γ. Check: 60 = 60 + 0; 27 = 27 + 0.

A5. Work backward: parent A = 222 + 4 = 226; parent Z = 86 + 2 = 88 → 226 88Ra (radium). Check: 226 = 222 + 4; 88 = 86 + 2.

A6. A unchanged (234 = 234), Z rose 90 → 91, so a beta particle,  0−1e, was emitted — this is beta-minus decay. Check: 234 = 234 + 0; 90 = 91 + (−1).
🔢 PART B · REASON IT OUT (explain in words)

Short answers — one or two sentences each.

B1. (Classify from the change.) A nucleus decays and its daughter has the same mass number A but an atomic number Z that is one higher. Which decay type was it, and what happened inside the nucleus at the particle level?
B2. (Band-of-stability prediction.) A certain nuclide sits above the band of stability — it has too many neutrons relative to its protons. Which decay type would you predict, and why does that move it toward the band?
B3. (Rank the radiation.) Rank alpha, beta, and gamma radiation from least to most penetrating, and name a material that stops each. In one sentence, why can an alpha source be relatively harmless outside the body but dangerous if inhaled?
▶  Check your thinking — Part B worked answers
B1. Beta-minus (β−) decay. A neutron converted into a proton, ejecting a fast electron ( 0−1e). The nucleon count is unchanged (so A is the same), but there is now one more proton (so Z rises by 1).

B2. Beta-minus (β−) decay. Having too many neutrons, the nucleus turns one neutron into a proton; this lowers the neutron count and raises the proton count, improving the neutron-to-proton balance and shifting the nuclide down toward the band of stability.

B3. Least to most penetrating: alpha < beta < gamma. Alpha is stopped by paper, skin, or clothing; beta by a few millimeters of aluminum or plastic; gamma needs thick lead or concrete. An alpha source is relatively harmless outside because skin or clothing stops it, but if inhaled or swallowed it deposits its strong ionizing damage directly inside tissue.
🧠 STRETCH YOUR REASONING · SELF-CHECK (not scored)

This one connects both lessons. Write two or three sentences before you open the model answer — this item isn't graded, but the thinking is exactly what the exam will ask for.

C1. A nuclide sits above the band of stability (too many neutrons). Explain, in your own words, why beta-minus decay is the natural “fix” for it — using both the band of stability (9.01) and the two conservation rules (9.02). Why does this decay leave A unchanged while raising Z by 1?
▶  Check your thinking — model answer
A nucleus above the band has too many neutrons relative to its protons, so to move toward the band it needs to trade a neutron for a proton. Beta-minus decay does exactly that: a neutron converts into a proton and ejects a fast electron ( 0−1e). By the conservation rules, one nucleon simply changed identity — a neutron became a proton — so the total nucleon count (A) is unchanged, while the proton count (Z) rises by 1 and the atom becomes the next element up. Lowering the neutron count and raising the proton count improves the neutron-to-proton ratio, shifting the nuclide down toward the band of stability. Both ideas agree: the band tells us which way the nucleus must move, and the conservation rules tell us exactly what it emits to get there.
