Half-Life & Decay Calculations
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: radioactive decay as first-order kinetics, the constant half-life, the fraction-remaining pattern (1/2)n, carbon-14 dating (t½ ≈ 5730 yr), and the iron-peak energy story behind fission and fusion.
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work. Two parts: a set of half-life problems you reason through by hand, and an Excel decay table + line graph that lets you see the exponential curve.
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Half-life math rests on one move done carefully: count the half-lives first (n = elapsed time ÷ t½), then apply (1/2)n. In Part A you'll work five problems — mass and fraction remaining, finding elapsed time from a fraction, and a carbon-14 dating age. In Part B you'll build a decay table in Excel and graph it, watching the exponential shape appear. Work each Part A item before you open the matching ▶ Check your thinking box.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How much of a radioactive sample is left after a given time — and how can the amount remaining tell me how old something is?
⚠️ AI AS AN INSTRUMENT — VERIFY BEFORE YOU TRUST
If you ask an AI tool to do these half-life problems, watch it carefully. AI commonly miscounts half-lives (subtracting halves linearly instead of dividing time by t½) or mixes up the time units (days vs. years), then states a confident, wrong answer. Treat its result as an instrument reading, not the truth: re-derive n = time ÷ t½ and (1/2)n by hand and confirm the numbers yourself.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Part A: Work all five problems on paper or in your notebook. Show your work: state n, then (1/2)n, then the answer with units. Check each against its answer key.
2
Part B: Build the decay table and line graph in Excel (see the M365 reminder below). Save the file with the required name.
3
Submit: upload your Excel file and type your Part A answers into the Canvas text-entry box (or include them on a sheet in the workbook).
🧮 PART A · HALF-LIFE PROBLEMS (show your work)

For each: find n = elapsed time ÷ t½, then use fraction = (1/2)n and mass = initial × (1/2)n.

A1. A sample begins with 240 g of a nuclide with a half-life of 6 hours (like technetium-99m). How much remains after 24 hours?
A2. Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction of an iodine-131 sample remains after 40 days?
A3. Cobalt-60 has a half-life of about 5.27 years. A medical source has decayed to 1/8 of its original amount. About how many years have passed?
A4. A wooden artifact is found to contain 1/4 of the carbon-14 that a living tree of the same size would have. Using t½ ≈ 5730 years, about how old is the artifact?
A5. A bone is dated to about 17,190 years old. Using carbon-14 (t½ ≈ 5730 yr), how many half-lives is that, and what fraction of the original carbon-14 remains?
▶  Check your thinking — Part A worked answers
A1. n = 24 h ÷ 6 h = 4 half-lives. Fraction = (1/2)4 = 1/16. Mass = 240 g × 1/16 = 15 g. (Halve four times: 240 → 120 → 60 → 30 → 15.)

A2. n = 40 days ÷ 8 days = 5 half-lives. Fraction = (1/2)5 = 1/32 (≈ 0.03125, about 3.1%).

A3. 1/8 = (1/2)3, so 3 half-lives have passed. Time = 3 × 5.27 yr ≈ 15.8 years.

A4. 1/4 = (1/2)2, so 2 half-lives have passed. Age = 2 × 5730 yr ≈ 11,460 years.

A5. n = 17,190 yr ÷ 5730 yr = 3 half-lives. Fraction remaining = (1/2)3 = 1/8 (≈ 12.5%).
📊 PART B · BUILD A DECAY TABLE & GRAPH IN EXCEL

A table of numbers becomes a story when you graph it. Start a sample at 100 g and watch it decay over six half-lives.

1
Make three columns: Time (half-lives) with rows 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Amount remaining (g); and Percent remaining (%).
2
Fill the amount column using a formula. Start with =100 at n = 0, then in each next row use a formula that halves the row above (for example, =B2/2). For percent, use =B2/100*100 or simply the amount ÷ starting amount.
3
Select the Time and Amount columns and insert a line chart (or scatter-with-lines). Title it “Radioactive Decay” and label the axes (x = half-lives, y = amount in grams).
4
In a cell below the chart, write one sentence: describe the shape of the curve and why it never reaches zero.
▶  Check your thinking — Part B expected table & curve
Your table should read:
n = 0 → 100 g (100%)
n = 1 → 50 g (50%)
n = 2 → 25 g (25%)
n = 3 → 12.5 g (12.5%)
n = 4 → 6.25 g (6.25%)
n = 5 → 3.125 g (3.125%)
n = 6 → 1.5625 g (1.5625%)

The curve drops steeply at first, then flattens as it approaches — but never touches — the x-axis. This is exponential decay: each step removes half of what remains, so the amount keeps getting smaller without ever reaching exactly zero. (A correct one-sentence note captures this idea.)
✎️ PART C · REASON IT OUT (WRITTEN SELF-CHECK)

Answer both prompts in 2–3 sentences each (in your notebook or the Canvas text box), in your own words — then open the model answer and compare. This is part of your honest self-check: no extra points, just a chance to be sure the ideas are solid, not only the arithmetic.

C1. In the (1/2)n model, explain why a radioactive sample never reaches exactly zero, even after many half-lives.
C2. Two students have the same nuclide but different amounts — one starts with 10 g, the other with 500 g. Will their samples share the same half-life? Explain why or why not.
▶  Check your thinking — Part C model answer
C1. Each half-life removes half of what currently remains, not a fixed amount, so you keep halving a smaller and smaller number. Halving never lands on exactly zero — it just shrinks without limit. (A real sample is a finite number of atoms and does eventually run out, but the (1/2)n model treats the amount as continuous and approaches zero without touching it.)

C2. Yes — both share the same half-life. Half-life is a fixed property of the nuclide and does not depend on how much you start with (or on temperature or chemical form). The 500 g sample undergoes more decays per second because it has more nuclei, but each sample still loses half of itself in the same span of time.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Build Part B in Microsoft Excel from your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_HalfLifeDecay_CHEM1H, save it to your Optima → Science OneDrive course folder, and submit through Canvas. New here? See the pinned “M365 Setup & File Organization Guide” page in this module.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: building a data table and inserting a line chart in Excel.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA

All 5 Part A problems show work (n, fraction, answer) with correct units.
☐
The Excel decay table covers half-lives 0–6 with amount and percent remaining.
☐
A titled, axis-labeled line graph and a one-sentence note on the exponential shape.
☐
Both Part C reasoning prompts answered in your own words before opening the model answer.
☐

Total: 20 pts

Radioisotope Application Analysis
Assignment · 20 pts · Completion + self-check
📖 WHAT THIS BUILDS ON
From this week's lessons: choosing a radioisotope by matching its half-life and radiation type to the job (9.05), and the biological effects of radiation — dose units (gray vs. sievert), internal vs. external hazard, and evidence-based cost–benefit reasoning (9.06).
This is your week's “doing chemistry” work. Two parts: choosing and justifying isotopes for real jobs, then reasoning about dose and safety. No spreadsheet this week — this is reasoning on paper.
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
A nuclear chemist's real skill isn't memorizing isotopes — it's reasoning from properties to the right choice. In Part A you'll pick a suitable isotope (or radiation type) for five jobs and justify each from half-life, radiation type, and how it interacts with the body or material. In Part B you'll reason about dose and safety: identify gray vs. sievert, explain an internal-vs-external hazard, and weigh a cost–benefit decision. Work each item before you open the matching ▶ Check your thinking box.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How do I choose the right radioisotope for a job — and how do I weigh its benefits against its risks with evidence?
⚠️ AI AS A SCIENTIFIC INSTRUMENT · VERIFY THE NUMBER
If you use an AI tool to check an isotope or a dose figure here, be careful: AI will state a half-life, a sievert value, or a “safe limit” confidently and sometimes wrongly — and it commonly confuses gray with sievert. Treat any AI answer as a starting point to verify against primary evidence (a reliable reference, your lesson notes, your own unit reasoning). AI proposes; your reasoning verifies.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
In the Canvas text-entry box for this assignment, number your responses to match Part A (1–5) and Part B (1–4).
2
Part A: Name a suitable isotope or radiation type, then justify it in one or two sentences from half-life + radiation type + how it interacts. Then open the check box.
3
Part B: Write a clear reasoned answer for each, then check it. There's room for more than one defensible response — the reasoning is what counts.
☣️ PART A · CHOOSE & JUSTIFY THE ISOTOPE (5 jobs)

For each job, name a suitable isotope or radiation type and justify it from half-life + radiation type + how it interacts with the body/material. (You may use the isotopes from Lesson 9.05.)

#The job
1Treat an overactive thyroid gland.
2Aim a radiation beam at a tumor from outside the body (and the same kind of source to sterilize equipment for years).
3Date a wooden artifact from an ancient settlement (a few thousand years old).
4Detect smoke in a small sealed household device.
5Continuously gauge the thickness of sheet metal moving along a production line.
▶  Check your thinking — Part A answer key
1. Iodine-131 (half-life ~8 days; β/γ) — the thyroid naturally concentrates iodine, so swallowed radioactive iodine self-targets the gland and delivers its dose right where it's needed, sparing the rest of the body.

2. Cobalt-60 (half-life ~5.3 years; γ) — gamma penetrates deeply enough to reach a tumor from outside (or to kill bacteria through packaging), and the multi-year half-life makes it a steady, long-lasting source. A ~6-hour isotope would be gone too fast.

3. Carbon-14 (half-life ~5730 years; β) — the clock length matches the age range (it works up to ~50,000 years), and wood was once living, so it took up carbon-14 while alive. A billion-year isotope like U-238 would barely have changed and couldn't resolve a few-thousand-year age.

4. Americium-241 (an α source) — alpha ionizes the air inside the chamber to allow a current, but it can't penetrate the sealed plastic housing, so it does its job without escaping the device. The weak penetration is the feature.

5. A penetrating source (e.g., a beta or gamma emitter), such as a long-lived industrial isotope — the radiation must pass through the metal so a detector on the far side reads how much gets through; thicker metal lets less through. A steady (longer half-life) source keeps the gauge calibrated over time. (Naming the radiation type + reasoning earns full credit even without a specific isotope.)
⚖️ PART B · DOSE & SAFETY REASONING (4 items)

Reason carefully — these are about thinking like a responsible scientist, not plugging in a formula.

B1. A report says a patient's tissue absorbed 0.02 J of energy per kilogram, and that this corresponds to a certain biological risk.
(a) Which unit describes the "0.02 J per kilogram absorbed" — the gray or the sievert?
(b) Which unit would you use to express the biological risk, and how is it obtained from the first?
B2. A small amount of an alpha-emitting material is genuinely dangerous if inhaled, yet nearly harmless taped to the outside of your hand. In two or three sentences, explain why the same source can be so different depending on whether it's internal or external.
B3. A patient is nervous about "any radiation at all" from a recommended diagnostic scan. Using cost–benefit reasoning (and the fact that we all receive background radiation), write a short, honest framing of how this decision should be weighed. (Take a defensible position — this is the Responsibility this quarter is about.)
B4. (Synthesis — self-check reasoning.) This week's throughline is that the same nuclear properties that make radiation hazardous are what make it useful. In three or four sentences, defend that idea using two specific examples from this week — one from a use (9.05) and one from an effect (9.06) — and finish by saying why that dual nature makes responsible, evidence-based decisions so important.
▶  Check your thinking — Part B worked answers
B1a. The gray (Gy) — it is defined as 1 joule of energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue (so 0.02 J/kg = 0.02 Gy). This counts energy only.
B1b. The sievert (Sv) expresses biological risk. You get it by multiplying the absorbed dose (in gray) by a quality factor that accounts for how damaging that radiation type is: Sv = Gy × quality factor. (For gamma the factor is ~1, so the numbers are similar; for alpha it's ~20, so the same gray means a much larger sievert.)

B2. Alpha particles are intensely ionizing but barely penetrate — from outside, the dead outer layer of skin stops them, so they never reach living cells. Inhaled, the source sits directly against living tissue with no shielding, so its high ionizing power (quality factor ~20) does serious local damage. Same particle; the hazard depends on radiation type and whether the source is internal or external.

B3. A strong answer notes that “zero radiation” was never the baseline — everyone receives background radiation (radon, cosmic rays, rocks/soil, food) all the time — so a scan adds a small dose, not a first one. Then it weighs that small, real risk against the benefit: the medical information the scan provides (catching or ruling out a serious problem). For a medically indicated scan, the benefit usually outweighs the dose, but it's a genuine trade made with evidence, case by case — not fear, not dismissal. (Any clear, evidence-based position that weighs benefit against risk earns full credit.)

B4. A strong answer picks two concrete pairings and shows the hazard-is-the-use logic in each. For example: gamma radiation's deep penetration is a real external hazard (9.06), yet that same penetration is exactly what lets Tc-99m's gamma rays escape the body to form a medical image, or lets Co-60 reach a tumor (9.05); and radiation's power to break DNA and kill cells is the danger behind cancer risk (9.06), yet that same cell-killing power is how radiation therapy destroys tumor tissue (9.05). Because every use carries the very edge that makes it dangerous, no application is automatically “safe” or “unsafe” — each is a trade to be weighed with evidence (gray vs. sievert, internal vs. external exposure, benefit vs. risk). That is why responsible, evidence-based judgment — not fear and not hype — is the real skill of this module. (Any answer with two valid examples and a clear responsibility point earns full credit.)
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All 5 Part A jobs have an isotope (or radiation type) and a justification from half-life + radiation type + interaction.
☐
All 4 Part B items are answered with clear reasoning (gray vs. sievert; internal vs. external; cost–benefit; and the hazard-is-the-use synthesis).
☐
You attempted each item before checking, and corrected any you missed.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED (COMPLETION)
Criteria Full credit Partial Pts
Part A complete
10 pts		 All 5 jobs have an isotope/radiation type and a property-based justification. Some items missing a choice or a justification. 10
Part B complete
8 pts		 All 4 items answered with clear, correct reasoning. Reasoning missing or unclear on one or more. 8
Honest self-check
2 pts		 Attempted before checking; corrections noted where needed. Little evidence of an honest first attempt. 2
Total: 20 pts
Scored on completion and honest effort — the answer keys above let you confirm accuracy yourself. This is practice, not a test.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M9 W3 Hands-On — Radioisotope Application Analysis
Type your numbered responses directly into the Canvas text-entry box. No separate file is required.
Due: By the end of Week 3, the final content week before the Final Review & Exam.
If you get stuck, submit what you have with a note on where you got stuck — that's useful information, not a penalty.

Module 9 Writing Assignment · Course Capstone
Marie Curie & the Atom Within — A Nuclear Case Study
Word (.docx) · 100 pts · teacher-reviewed · course-closing synthesis
📚 THE TASK
More than a century ago, a young scientist named Marie Curie chased a strange glow that no one understood — and in doing so helped prove that the atom, long thought to be the smallest, indivisible piece of matter, had a turbulent world inside it. This is your course-closing capstone — the last piece of writing in Chemistry I Honors, and your chance to pull the whole year's habits together: investigate a real problem, trace its history, weigh the evidence, and argue responsibly. You will investigate one contemporary nuclear application (nuclear energy, or medical isotopes), trace its scientific development from Becquerel and the Curies to today, evaluate the evidence, connect it to current research, and present a Claim–Evidence–Reasoning (CER) conclusion about its responsible use.
It is a case study joined to a scientific argument: a careful look at the history, then a claim defended with evidence and reasoning and accountable to the trade-offs. Choose one application below to investigate and argue about.
APPLICATION A · NUCLEAR ENERGY
Defend a position on the responsible use of nuclear power — fission reactors today, and/or the pursuit of fusion energy. Ground it in the chemistry: the decay/reaction type, the energy released through E = mc2, and the contrast of fission and fusion. Weigh low-carbon power against waste, accident risk, and the difficulty of fusion.
APPLICATION B · MEDICAL ISOTOPES
Defend a position on the responsible use of medical radioisotopes — imaging and therapy. Ground it in the chemistry: the decay type, the half-life that suits the job (e.g., a short half-life and gamma for imaging), and why a given tissue concentrates an isotope. Weigh real diagnostic and life-saving benefit against radiation dose and risk.
You'll write it in Microsoft Word, organized into the sections listed further down.
⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS
This case study is one of only two teacher-reviewed pieces in Module 9 (the other is your Nuclear Decay & Applications Exhibit VR project), and it is the final assignment of the course — the capstone that asks you to use every habit Chemistry I Honors has built: empirical questioning, evidence over preference, and honest reasoning about how science shapes the world. Your teacher reads it personally and responds to your reasoning — so make it your careful best, and ground the history, the science, and the argument in evidence, not in a guess. This is exactly Quarter 4's question in action: how does chemistry shape our world? — and its virtue, Responsibility: nuclear chemistry's power comes with real risks as well as real goods.
🧮 YOUR TOOLKIT (USE THESE EXACT IDEAS & VALUES)
The discovery of radioactivity: Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 (uranium salts fogged a photographic plate with no sunlight). Marie and Pierre Curie investigated it; Marie Curie coined the term radioactivity and, with Pierre, isolated two new radioactive elements, polonium and radium, in 1898. Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics (1903) and in Chemistry (1911) — the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences.
What it changed: radioactivity is a property of the atom's nucleus, not of its chemistry — evidence that the atom is not an indivisible, unchanging ball. This is the Nature-of-Science idea: models change when the evidence changes.
Decay types & conservation: in a balanced nuclear equation, mass number (A) and atomic number (Z) are each conserved. Alpha (α) emits a 42He nucleus (A−4, Z−2); beta (β−) turns a neutron into a proton + electron (A same, Z+1); gamma (γ) sheds energy (no change in A or Z).
Half-life: t½ is the constant time for half a sample to decay; after n half-lives, (1/2)n remains. Carbon-14 (t½ ≈ 5730 years) dates once-living material.
Fission vs fusion: fission splits a heavy nucleus (e.g., uranium-235) into lighter nuclei + neutrons (a chain reaction); fusion combines light nuclei — 21H + 31H → 42He + 10n — and powers the Sun. Both release energy from a tiny lost mass via E = mc2.
Medical isotopes: technetium-99m (gamma, short ~6-hour half-life) for imaging; iodine-131 for thyroid therapy (the thyroid concentrates iodine).
Dose units: the gray (Gy) measures energy absorbed (1 J/kg); the sievert (Sv) weights that dose by how damaging the radiation type is. They are not the same number.
Where the field is now (broad strokes — verify before citing any specific): scientists are currently pursuing controlled fusion for power (magnetic-confinement tokamaks and inertial/laser approaches; laboratories have recently produced a fusion reaction that released more energy than was delivered to the fuel, though a working power plant is still years away); advanced and small modular fission reactors and better long-term waste strategies; and, in medicine, targeted radionuclide therapies that deliver a radioisotope directly to diseased tissue. Keep these general in your writing unless you can verify a specific figure.
🧠 YOUR REASONING TOOLKIT (how to build the case study)
Use these steps in your own words — don't just copy the headings.
Step 1 — Trace the history accurately, then bring it to now.
Lay out the arc your application rests on: Becquerel's discovery (1896), the Curies (polonium and radium, 1898; that radioactivity comes from the nucleus), and Rutherford (alpha/beta identified; the first transmutation, 1919), through to the present understanding — and then to where scientists are taking the field now. Use the toolkit dates and facts — don't invent quotes or specifics.
Step 2 — Make a claim and back it with the nuclear chemistry.
Pick application A or B and state a clear position on its responsible use. Then ground it in the chemistry that matters for your case — the decay/reaction type, half-life, the energy from E = mc2, fission vs fusion — not just a general opinion.
Step 3 — Weigh the costs honestly, then decide.
No nuclear technology is free of trade-offs: waste, accident risk, and the difficulty of fusion for power; radiation dose and risk for medicine. Name the strongest objection to your position, then answer it — reasoning from evidence, not preference (Honesty).
📝 STRUCTURE: WRITE THESE SECTIONS
Your capstone must include all six sections below. Together they carry the five moves of a full investigation — investigate a contemporary problem, analyze its history, evaluate the evidence, connect to current research, and present a CER conclusion — plus an honest societal cost/benefit.
1
The contemporary problem (investigate). Name the modern nuclear application you're investigating (A nuclear energy, or B medical isotopes) and the real-world problem or question it addresses today — for example, generating low-carbon electricity, or diagnosing and treating disease. Set up why it matters now.
2
Historical development (analyze the history). Trace the arc your application rests on: Becquerel's discovery (1896) → Marie and Pierre Curie (radioactivity named; polonium and radium, 1898; Marie Curie's Nobel Prizes in Physics 1903 and Chemistry 1911) → Rutherford (identified alpha and beta; the first transmutation, 1919) → to the present understanding. Explain the Nature-of-Science idea: radioactivity is a property of the nucleus, which helped overturn the indivisible-atom model — a case of a scientific model changing as evidence improved.
3
Claim & evidence — the nuclear chemistry (evaluate evidence). State a clear, defensible claim about the responsible use of your application (e.g., “Used responsibly, nuclear power is a justified low-carbon energy source,” or “Medical radioisotopes are worth their small radiation risk when the diagnostic benefit is real”). Then evaluate the evidence behind it: the relevant decay or reaction type, the half-life (and why it suits the job), the energy released via E = mc2, and — for energy — how fission and/or fusion work. Use the toolkit values accurately and keep fission and fusion distinct.
4
Connection to current research. Show where the field is going now: for energy, controlled fusion (tokamaks; inertial/laser approaches) or advanced/small modular reactors and waste strategies; for medicine, newer targeted radioisotope therapies. Frame it as “scientists are currently exploring…,” keep specifics general unless you can verify them, and name one open question the field has not yet settled.
5
Societal cost / benefit & responsibility. Weigh the real benefits against the real risks (low-carbon power vs waste and accident risk; diagnostic benefit vs radiation dose). Name the strongest objection to your position and answer it. Reason from evidence, not preference (Honesty thread; Responsibility virtue).
6
CER conclusion (present a Claim–Evidence–Reasoning conclusion). Close with an explicit CER statement: restate your Claim, cite the strongest Evidence (the nuclear chemistry and the cost/benefit), and give the Reasoning that ties them together. End on the big idea: the same nuclear change Curie first glimpsed can heal or harm, power or pollute — and using it well means understanding the chemistry and owning the costs.
✎ LENGTH & STYLE
Aim for roughly 600–800 words across the six sections. Use correct terminology — nucleus, radioactivity, alpha/beta/gamma decay, half-life, fission, fusion, E = mc2, dose. The history, the chemistry, the current-research connection, and the reasoning are what's graded — not polished prose. Ground your claim in the nuclear chemistry, not a hunch, and keep fission and fusion separate.
⚠️ A NOTE ON USING AI TOOLS
An AI tool will happily write you a history of Curie or a paragraph on nuclear power — and it can get things wrong: inventing a date, a half-life, or a dose or energy figure; confusing fission with fusion; or overstating how mature a technology like fusion power really is. If you consult one, treat it as a draft to check, never an answer to paste: verify every historical claim and every nuclear value against this assignment's toolkit and the primary evidence, and re-check the chemistry yourself. The instrument proposes; your reasoning verifies. That is exactly the AI-literacy skill this assignment is built to grow.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Write your case study in Microsoft Word from your school M365 account. Name your file LastName_FirstName_NuclearCaseStudy_CHEM1H, save it to your Optima → Science OneDrive course folder, and submit through Canvas. New here? See the pinned “M365 Setup & File Organization Guide” page in this module.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: structuring a historical case study and an evidence-based argument with headings in Word. If your teacher returns comments for revision, turn on Track Changes before revising.
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED (TEACHER RUBRIC — build natively as a Canvas Rubric)
Criterion Full marks Developing Pts
Historical development (Becquerel → Curie → Rutherford → present) The arc is accurate (Becquerel 1896; the Curies — polonium and radium, 1898; two Nobel Prizes, 1903 & 1911; Rutherford's alpha/beta and 1919 transmutation) and connected to the Nature-of-Science idea that the indivisible-atom model changed as evidence improved. History thin, vague, or contains errors / invented specifics; only a single figure; no link to changing models. 18
Contemporary problem & claim Names a real contemporary problem the chosen application (A or B) addresses, and states a clear, specific, defensible claim about its responsible use. Problem unclear or missing; claim vague, missing, or only restates the prompt. 12
Evidence — nuclear chemistry (evaluated) Correct, relevant nuclear chemistry, evaluated not just listed: the decay/reaction type, half-life and why it suits the job, energy via E = mc2, and (for energy) fission vs fusion kept distinct — with toolkit values used accurately. Chemistry thin, incomplete, or wrong (e.g., fission/fusion confused, half-life logic mis-stated, invented figures). 22
Connection to current research Connects the application to where the field is going now (hedged, e.g. fusion, advanced reactors, or targeted radioisotope therapies) and names an open question — without overstating maturity or inventing specifics. No current-research link, or claims are overstated / fabricated; no open question. 13
Societal cost/benefit & responsibility Weighs genuine benefits and risks, names the strongest objection and answers it, reasoning from evidence not preference (neither dismissing nor exaggerating the risk). Trade-offs missing, generic, or one-sided; no counterargument; risk treated as catastrophic or as zero. 22
CER conclusion & communication Conclusion is an explicit Claim–Evidence–Reasoning statement that ties back to the claim and names the big idea; correct terminology, clear organized writing. Conclusion thin or just restates; not a CER; terms misused; disorganized. 13
Total: 100 pts
The nuclear-chemistry evidence and the cost/benefit reasoning carry the most weight — a confident position with no chemistry behind it, or one that ignores the trade-offs, earns little. Reason from the nucleus up.

Submit your Word .docx through Canvas (OneDrive tab or file upload). If your teacher returns it with comments, revise with Track Changes on and resubmit as a _Revision1 file.

🧘 PREFER NOT TO USE A HEADSET?
A full non-VR alternate — “Nuclear Decay & Applications Exhibit — Narrated Walkthrough (No-Headset Pathway)” — meets the same objectives and is graded on the same rubric. Do one pathway, not both.
📚 THE BIG PICTURE
Across this module you've built a Nuclear Decay & Applications Exhibit in OptimaXR, one week at a time, to answer a single running question: how do unstable nuclei change, how do we measure and date that change, and how do we put nuclear chemistry to use responsibly? Week 1 you built a Decay & Stability model; Week 2 a Half-Life & Energy station; Week 3 a Radioisotope Applications exhibit. Now you bring it all together.
Your task is to record a guided video walkthrough inside the headset — a short tour in which you narrate the chemistry of your build, from what holds a nucleus together and how it decays, through half-life and the enormous energy of fission and fusion, to the real-world isotopes that heal, date, and detect. This recorded explanation, not a static screenshot, is what earns the grade. The build is the stage; your spoken reasoning is the performance.
⭐ WHY THIS MATTERS
This walkthrough is one of only two teacher-reviewed pieces in Module 9 (the other is your Nuclear Case-Study writing assignment on Marie Curie). Your teacher will watch your recording and respond to your reasoning personally — so make it your best thinking, clearly explained.
🥽 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶  A VR headset with the OptimaXR app (or the OptimaXR desktop app).
▶  Your finished build — the Nuclear_Final_YourName snapshot from the Week 3 build, including the Week 1 decay & stability model, the Week 2 half-life & energy station, and the Week 3 radioisotope applications exhibit.
▶  A quiet space and about 30–40 minutes (planning, one or two recording takes, and submitting).
📍 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (or OptimaXR desktop app)
Session type: persistent (your finished build is waiting)
Session ID: see the pinned OptimaXR Sessions list in this module
Session name: Nuclear Science Lab
Location: Nuclear Science Lab
Spawn point: Lab Entrance
🎤 WHAT YOUR RECORDING MUST COVER (aim for 3–5 minutes)
1
Open at the entrance. Introduce your build and state the big question it answers: how do unstable nuclei change, how do we measure and date that change, and how do we use nuclear chemistry responsibly?
2
Decay & stability (Week 1). Walk your decay & stability model. Explain that a nucleus is protons and neutrons (nucleons) held by the strong force, that stable nuclei fall in the band of stability — with no stable nuclei beyond Z = 83 — and walk the three decay types: alpha (α) emits a 42He nucleus, beta (β−) turns a neutron into a proton plus an electron, and gamma (γ) sheds excess energy. Show that mass number (A) and atomic number (Z) are conserved in every equation.
3
Half-life (Week 2). At your half-life model, explain that the half-life (t½) is the time for half of a sample to decay and is constant for a nuclide; after n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)n. Use this to explain carbon-14 dating (t½ ≈ 5730 years): a once-living thing stops taking in 14C at death, and the fraction remaining gives its age.
4
Nuclear energy (Week 2). At your fission-vs-fusion panel, contrast the two: fission splits a heavy nucleus (e.g., uranium-235) into lighter nuclei plus neutrons that can sustain a chain reaction; fusion combines light nuclei (deuterium + tritium → helium-4 + a neutron) and powers the Sun. Explain that both release energy because they move products toward the iron (iron-56) peak of greatest stability, and that the released energy comes from a tiny lost mass via E = mc2.
5
Applications & safety (Week 3). Tour your radioisotope applications exhibit: technetium-99m (imaging), iodine-131 (thyroid therapy), cobalt-60 (radiotherapy/sterilization), carbon-14 (dating), and americium-241 (smoke detectors). For at least two, explain how the choice matches the half-life and radiation type to the job (e.g., a short half-life and penetrating gamma for imaging). Close the station with a cost / benefit & radiation-safety statement — the same properties that make isotopes hazardous make them powerful tools, and using them well means weighing real benefits against real risks (Responsibility).
6
Close by explaining the evidence, then the through-line. Before your final line, make your reasoning explicit — state why mass number (A) and atomic number (Z) must be conserved in a decay equation, what a half-life actually tells you about a sample, why both fission and fusion release energy (products move toward the iron-56 peak; a tiny lost mass becomes energy via E = mc2), and the cost / benefit of one application you chose. Then connect the whole build into one idea: the same hidden change inside an unstable nucleus — measured by half-life and powered by E = mc2 — can heal, date, and power our world, and chemistry's job is to understand it well enough to use it responsibly.
How to record: Use OptimaXR's video recording feature to capture your narrated tour from inside the headset (start the recording from the menu/tablet, walk and talk, then stop and save). If your setup can't capture in-headset audio, record your screen with narration instead. Aim for one clean take; a second take is fine.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
1. Upload your video recording (3–5 minutes) to this Canvas assignment as a media/file upload.
2. In the comment box, list the three weekly builds in one line each (Wk1 decay & stability model, Wk2 half-life & energy station, Wk3 radioisotope applications exhibit) so your teacher can see the iteration behind the final build.
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED (TEACHER RUBRIC — build natively as a Canvas Rubric)
Criterion Full marks Developing Pts
Evidence-based scientific reasoning Explains the evidence, not just the labels: why mass number (A) and atomic number (Z) are conserved in every decay equation; what half-life means and how the (1/2)n logic tracks or dates a sample; why both fission and fusion release energy (products move toward the iron-56 peak; a tiny lost mass becomes energy via E = mc2); and the cost / benefit of at least one chosen application. Reasoning is justified from evidence throughout. States conclusions or names parts without explaining the underlying evidence; reasoning thin or absent. 35
Accurate chemistry The nuclear chemistry is correct at the high-school level: the band of stability (no stable nuclei past Z = 83), α/β/γ decay with the right A & Z changes, a constant half-life, the fission-vs-fusion contrast, and isotope-to-use matching are stated accurately, using the course's verified values. Contains chemistry errors — e.g., fission/fusion confused, broken A/Z conservation, mis-stated half-life logic, or invented values. 25
Clear narration & model The recorded tour is organized and easy to follow; the three builds (decay & stability model, half-life & energy station, radioisotope applications exhibit) are recognizable and support the narration; audio and visuals are usable. Disorganized or hard to follow; builds confusing, missing, or not tied to the narration; key parts unclear or inaudible. 20
Week-by-week iteration The build clearly shows all three weekly stages, and the comment lists the three builds — evidence of a project developed across the module, not assembled at the end. Only some stages present; little sign of building over time. 12
Uncertainty / limits & real-world reflection Closes by weighing a real cost against a real benefit (Responsibility) and naming a limit or uncertainty — e.g., that a model simplifies, that fusion power is not yet mature, or that the same radiation that heals can harm. No honest cost/benefit or limits; the technology is treated as risk-free or as purely dangerous. 8
Total: 100 pts
Both pathways — VR and non-VR — use this identical rubric. A high-school-level model is expected; the depth and accuracy of the evidence-based explanation carry the most weight.

questions.feedback_general: Pressure = force ÷ area. The same force concentrated onto a smaller area produces a larger pressure.

questions.text: At sea level, the mercury column in a barometer stands at about what height, defining one standard atmosphere?
questions.feedback_general: One standard atmosphere supports a mercury column about 760 mm tall — the basis of the units mmHg and torr.

questions.text: Convert 2.0 atm to millimeters of mercury. (1 atm = 760 mmHg)
questions.feedback_general: 2.0 atm × (760 mmHg / 1 atm) = 1520 mmHg. The atm unit cancels, leaving mmHg.

questions.text: Carrying a barometer up a tall mountain makes the mercury column fall, because there is less air overhead pressing down.
questions.feedback_general: At higher altitude less atmosphere sits above you, so the air pushes less on the dish and the column drops. Lower pressure means a shorter column.

questions.text:
Match each pressure value to the equivalent value in another unit (all equal to one standard atmosphere).

Each value below is equal to 1 atm. Select all values that are equivalent to 1 atm.
questions.feedback_general: One standard atmosphere = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 101.3 kPa = 14.7 psi. They are five names for the same sea-level pressure.

questions.text: On the same calm day, two mercury barometers are read: one at a seaside station shows 760 mmHg, and one at a mountain station shows 620 mmHg. What is the best-supported inference?

answers.text: The mountain station is at a higher altitude, where less air sits overhead pressing down.
The seaside station is at a higher altitude than the mountain station.
The air at the mountain station is denser and heavier than the seaside air.
One barometer is broken, because at every location one atmosphere must read exactly 760 mmHg.

questions.feedback_general: A lower barometer reading means less atmosphere is pressing down, which happens at higher altitude — so the 620 mmHg reading points to the mountain station being higher up. (760 mmHg is standard pressure at sea level, not everywhere.)

quizzes.title: Reading Check 5.02 — The Gas Laws & the Ideal Gas Law

questions.text: A gas at 1.0 atm fills 2.0 L. At constant temperature, it is compressed to 0.50 L. What is its new pressure? (Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂)
questions.feedback_general: P₂ = (1.0 atm × 2.0 L) / 0.50 L = 4.0 atm. The volume fell to one-quarter, so the pressure rose four-fold.

questions.text: When applying Charles's law or Gay-Lussac's law, the temperature must be in Kelvin, not degrees Celsius.
questions.feedback_general: The gas laws require absolute (Kelvin) temperature. Using Celsius breaks the proportion. Convert with K = °C + 273.

questions.text: In the ideal gas law PV = nRT, what does n represent?

answers.text: The number of moles of gas

questions.feedback_general: n is the amount of gas in moles. (R is the constant, 0.08206; the number of molecules would be n × Avogadro's number.)

questions.text: What volume does 1.00 mol of an ideal gas occupy at STP (273 K, 1 atm)?
questions.feedback_general: V = nRT/P = (1.00 × 0.08206 × 273) / 1.00 = 22.4 L. This molar volume, 22.4 L/mol at STP, is worth memorizing.

questions.text: Match each gas law to the relationship it describes.

answers.right: P and V are inversely related (constant T)
V and Kelvin T are directly related (constant P)
V is directly related to the number of moles (constant T, P)

distractors: P and V are inversely related
V and Kelvin T are directly related
V is directly related to the number of moles
P and V are directly related
questions.feedback_general: Boyle links P and V (inverse); Charles links V and Kelvin T (direct); Avogadro links V and moles (direct). Together with Gay-Lussac they fold into PV = nRT.

questions.text: Boyle's law reliably predicts that halving a gas's volume doubles its pressure, yet the law itself never says why gases do this. Which statement best captures the relationship between a gas law and the kinetic-molecular theory?

answers.text: The gas law describes the measured pattern; the kinetic-molecular theory explains why the pattern happens.
The gas law explains the underlying cause, and the theory merely restates that cause using numbers.
A scientific law and a scientific theory are the same kind of statement with two different names.
Because Boyle's law was discovered first, the kinetic-molecular theory adds nothing and is unnecessary.

questions.feedback_general: A law is an empirical regularity — it faithfully describes what gases do, measured again and again. A theory (here, the kinetic-molecular theory) explains the mechanism behind it: molecules in constant motion striking the container walls. Laws describe; theories explain; both are genuine scientific knowledge.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 5.03 — Stoichiometry of Gaseous Substances

questions.feedback_general: Equal volumes (same T and P) hold an equal number of molecules, whatever the gas. The masses differ, but the counts are the same.

questions.text: At STP, what volume does one mole of any ideal gas occupy?
questions.feedback_general: The molar volume of an ideal gas at STP (273 K, 1 atm) is 22.4 L/mol — the conversion factor between moles of a gas and its volume.

questions.text: For the reaction 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, all as gases at the same temperature and pressure, how many liters of water vapor form from 5.0 L of O₂ (with H₂ in excess)?
questions.feedback_general: The O₂ : H₂O ratio is 1 : 2, so 5.0 L O₂ × (2 ÷ 1) = 10.0 L H₂O. For gases, the volume ratio equals the mole ratio.

questions.text: Because they have the same volume at the same temperature and pressure, 1 L of helium and 1 L of carbon dioxide have the same mass.
questions.feedback_general: Equal volumes mean equal moles, not equal mass. A mole of CO₂ (44.01 g) is far heavier than a mole of He (4.00 g). Same count, different mass.

questions.text: Match each conversion to the correct factor you would use.

answers.left: Moles of a gas → volume at STP
Moles of reactant → moles of product

questions.feedback_general: Molar mass links mass and moles; molar volume (22.4 L/mol) links moles and gas volume at STP; the balanced equation links moles of one substance to moles of another. Moles are always the hub.

questions.text: At the same temperature and pressure, a 3.0 L sample of methane (CH₄) and a 3.0 L sample of carbon dioxide (CO₂) are found to contain the same number of molecules — even though the CO₂ sample weighs more. Which statement best explains why the counts are equal?

answers.text: The two gases must have the same molar mass.
Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, because a gas is mostly empty space and a molecule's size barely affects how much room it takes up.
The heavier CO₂ molecules pack more loosely, which happens to cancel out the mass difference.
The number of molecules depends only on mass, so equal *masses* would be required for equal counts.

questions.feedback_general: This is Avogadro's law used as reasoning, not recall. Because gas particles are far apart in mostly empty space, molecular size and mass do not change how much volume each particle occupies — so equal volumes (same T, P) mean equal molecule counts, and a volume ratio can stand in for a mole ratio. Mass differs; count does not.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 5.04 — Gas Mixtures & Dalton's Partial Pressures

answers.text: the average of the partial pressures
the sum of the partial pressures of all the gases
the product of the partial pressures

questions.feedback_general: Each gas exerts its pressure independently, so P_total = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + … — the pressures simply add.

questions.text: A sealed tank holds nitrogen at a partial pressure of 0.60 atm and oxygen at a partial pressure of 0.40 atm, with nothing else inside. What is the total pressure?
questions.feedback_general: Add the partial pressures: 0.60 atm + 0.40 atm = 1.00 atm.

questions.text: In that same tank (total 1.00 atm), what is the mole fraction of nitrogen?
questions.feedback_general: A gas's mole fraction is its share of the pressure: x(N₂) = 0.60 atm ÷ 1.00 atm = 0.60. (And x(O₂) = 0.40, so they sum to 1.)

questions.text: A gas is collected over water at 25 °C, where the vapor pressure of water is 23.8 mmHg. If the total pressure is 760 mmHg, what is the pressure of the dry gas alone?
questions.feedback_general: Subtract the water vapor: P_dry gas = 760 − 23.8 = 736.2 mmHg. The collected gas always carries some water vapor that must be removed from the total.

questions.text: When a gas is collected by bubbling it through water, the gas you collect is pure — no correction to the measured pressure is needed.
questions.feedback_general: The collected gas picks up water vapor, so the measured total includes the water's vapor pressure. You must subtract it to find the dry gas: P_dry gas = P_total − P_water vapor.

questions.text: A student collects hydrogen gas over water at 25 °C and forgets to subtract the water vapor pressure before reporting how much hydrogen was produced. Compared with the true value, the student's reported amount of hydrogen will be:

answers.text: too high, because the water vapor's pressure was counted as if it belonged to the hydrogen
too low, because the water vapor takes pressure away from the hydrogen
exactly right, because water vapor does not contribute to the measured pressure
too low, because some of the hydrogen dissolves into the water

questions.feedback_general: By Dalton's law the measured total is P(dry gas) + P(water vapor). Using the full total as if it were all hydrogen counts the water vapor's 23.8 mmHg as product, overstating the hydrogen. This is why the correction matters for an honest result — you report only the gas you actually made.

The temperature of a gas in kelvin
The mass of a gas divided by its volume

questions.text: A weather report gives the pressure as 2.0 atm. Using 1 atm = 760 mmHg, what is this in mmHg?
questions.feedback_general: 2.0 atm × 760 mmHg/atm = 1520 mmHg. The mercury barometer is why pressure is so often quoted in millimeters of mercury.

questions.feedback_general: 380 mmHg ÷ 760 mmHg/atm = 0.50 atm. Half an atmosphere of pressure corresponds to half the standard 760 mm mercury column.

questions.text: A gas occupies 2.0 L at 1.0 atm. It is compressed at constant temperature to 0.50 L. Using Boyle's law (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂), what is the new pressure?

questions.text: When using Charles's law or the ideal gas law, temperature must always be expressed in kelvin, not in degrees Celsius.
questions.feedback_general: True. The gas laws are written in terms of absolute temperature. Using Celsius (which can be zero or negative) gives nonsense; convert first with K = °C + 273.

questions.feedback_general: V₂ = V₁ × T₂ ÷ T₁ = 2.0 L × 600 K ÷ 300 K = 4.0 L. Doubling the absolute temperature doubles the volume — V and T are directly proportional (in kelvin).

questions.text: Using PV = nRT with R = 0.08206 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹, what volume does 1.00 mol of an ideal gas occupy at STP (273 K, 1.00 atm)?
questions.feedback_general: V = nRT ÷ P = (1.00)(0.08206)(273) ÷ 1.00 = 22.4 L. This is the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP — one mole of any ideal gas fills 22.4 L at 273 K and 1 atm.

questions.text: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, all gases at the same temperature and pressure, 5.0 L of O₂ reacts completely. By Avogadro's principle (equal volumes hold equal moles, so volume ratios equal mole ratios), what volume of H₂O vapor forms?
questions.feedback_general: The mole ratio O₂ : H₂O is 1 : 2, so the volume ratio is also 1 : 2. 5.0 L O₂ × (2 vol H₂O / 1 vol O₂) = 10.0 L H₂O vapor. For gases at the same T and P, you can reason directly in volumes.
moles CaCO₃ = 10.0 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 0.0999 mol → 0.0999 mol CO₂ × 22.4 L/mol = 2.24 L at STP. The path is grams → moles (mole bridge from Module 4) → liters of gas at STP.

questions.text: A container holds nitrogen at a partial pressure of 0.60 atm and oxygen at a partial pressure of 0.40 atm. Match each quantity to its correct value (Dalton's law of partial pressures: P_total = ΣP_i).

answers.left: Partial pressure of a gas collected over water at 25 °C when the total is 760 mmHg

questions.feedback_general: The total pressure is the sum of the partials, 0.60 + 0.40 = 1.00 atm. Each gas's mole fraction equals its partial pressure ÷ total pressure, so N₂ is 0.60 ÷ 1.00 = 0.60. When a gas is collected over water, water vapor (23.8 mmHg at 25 °C) is part of the total, so the dry gas's partial pressure is 760 − 23.8 = 736.2 mmHg.

questions.text: A student compresses a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature and records: Which claim is best supported by these data, and why?

answers.text: Pressure and volume are directly proportional, because both quantities change
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional — each time the volume is halved the pressure doubles, and the product P × V stays constant at 4.0 atm·L (Boyle's law)
There is no relationship between pressure and volume
The data must be in error, because pressure cannot change when volume changes

questions.feedback_general: In every row P × V = 4.0 atm·L (1.0×4.0, 2.0×2.0, 4.0×1.0). A constant product means pressure and volume are inversely proportional — Boyle's law — so halving the volume doubles the pressure. Reading the pattern from the data and stating the reasoning is how an empirical gas law is justified from evidence, not just memorized.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 5.05 — Kinetic-Molecular Theory; Effusion & Diffusion

questions.text: According to the kinetic-molecular theory, the average kinetic energy of the particles in a gas depends on which single quantity?

answers.text: The molar mass of the gas

questions.feedback_general: Postulate 5 of the kinetic-molecular theory: average kinetic energy is set by the absolute temperature alone. That is why all gases at the same temperature share the same average kinetic energy.

questions.text: At the same temperature, a helium atom (4.00 g/mol) moves faster on average than an oxygen molecule (32.00 g/mol).
questions.feedback_general: Same temperature means same average kinetic energy. Since kinetic energy is ½mv², the lighter helium atom must move faster than the heavier oxygen molecule to carry the same energy.

questions.text: What is the difference between diffusion and effusion?

answers.text: Diffusion is the spreading of one gas through another; effusion is gas escaping through a tiny pinhole
Diffusion happens only in liquids; effusion happens only in gases
Diffusion is for heavy gases; effusion is for light gases
They are two words for exactly the same process

questions.feedback_general: Diffusion is one gas mixing through another (perfume crossing a room); effusion is gas particles escaping one at a time through a small hole (a balloon slowly deflating). Both go faster for lighter gases.

questions.text: Using Graham's law, rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁), how many times faster does helium (He, 4.00 g/mol) effuse than oxygen (O₂, 32.00 g/mol)?
questions.feedback_general: rate(He)/rate(O₂) = √(M_O₂ / M_He) = √(32.00/4.00) = √8.00 = 2.83. The lighter gas is faster, so the ratio is greater than 1.

questions.text: Match each gas law to why the kinetic-molecular theory says it happens.

answers.right: Particles reach the walls sooner, so more collisions per second

answers.left: Charles's / Gay-Lussac's law (higher temperature → higher pressure or volume)
answers.right: Faster particles strike the walls harder and more often

answers.left: Dalton's law (total pressure = sum of partial pressures)
answers.right: Particles ignore one another, so each gas pushes as if alone

questions.feedback_general: The kinetic theory explains each measured law with a picture of moving particles — that is what makes it a theory (a mechanism) rather than just a law (a pattern).

questions.text: Boyle measured his pressure–volume law more than a century before anyone could picture moving molecules. Which statement best describes the relationship between Boyle's law and the kinetic-molecular theory?

answers.text: Boyle's law is just an unproven guess that the kinetic-molecular theory later replaced
Boyle's law *describes* a measured pattern; the kinetic-molecular theory *explains why* that pattern happens
The kinetic-molecular theory is less certain than Boyle's law because it is "only a theory"
Boyle's law and the kinetic-molecular theory are two names for the same thing

questions.feedback_general: A law reliably describes what happens (pressure doubles when volume halves); a theory supplies the mechanism that explains why — here, particles reaching the walls sooner when crowded. The theory is not a weaker law waiting to be promoted; it does more work, explaining many laws at once.

questions.text: Under which conditions do real gases deviate most from the ideal gas law, PV = nRT?

answers.text: Low pressure and low temperature only
Real gases never deviate from PV = nRT

questions.feedback_general: High pressure crowds the particles together (their own volume matters) and low temperature lets slow particles feel one another's attractions. These are the conditions near where a gas would condense to a liquid.

questions.text: A gas behaves most like an ideal gas when it is spread out at low pressure and warmed to a high temperature.
questions.feedback_general: Far apart and fast-moving, the particles' finite size and mutual attractions are negligible, so PV = nRT is at its most accurate. The model strains in the opposite corner — high pressure and low temperature.

questions.text: Which two assumptions of the ideal-gas model fail in real gases?

answers.text: That particles move and that they collide
That gases fill their container and that they have mass
That particles have no volume and that they have no attraction for one another
That temperature is measured in kelvins and that pressure is measured in atm

questions.feedback_general: The ideal model treats particles as volumeless points that ignore each other. Real particles do take up space (matters at high pressure) and do attract one another (matters at low temperature).

questions.text: The van der Waals corrections to the ideal gas law do which of the following?

answers.text: Replace PV = nRT with a completely unrelated equation
Add a volume correction (for particle size) and a pressure correction (for attractions)
Apply only to ideal gases, never to real gases
Remove the need to convert temperature to kelvins

questions.feedback_general: Van der Waals kept PV = nRT as the backbone and added a volume correction (the space particles occupy) and a pressure correction (for the attractions). Both fade to nearly zero at low pressure and high temperature, so the equation reduces to the ideal gas law there.

questions.text: The fact that the ideal gas law is "not perfectly true" means it is a bad model that scientists should discard.
questions.feedback_general: False. Every model is a simplification. The ideal gas law is excellent over a huge useful range and even tells you in advance where it will fail (high pressure, low temperature). Knowing a model's limits is part of understanding it — not a reason to throw it away.

questions.text: Two gases are held under identical high-pressure, low-temperature conditions. Gas X is made of large molecules with strong attractions for one another; Gas Y is helium (tiny atoms with very weak attractions). Which gas will deviate more from the ideal gas law, and why?

answers.text: Gas Y, because lighter atoms always move faster and break the ideal assumptions
Gas X, because its larger particle volume and stronger attractions make the two failing assumptions matter more
They deviate equally, because deviation depends only on pressure and temperature, not on the gas
Neither — helium and large molecules both behave perfectly ideally under all conditions

questions.feedback_general: Deviation comes from the two real properties the ideal model ignores: particle volume and intermolecular attraction. Gas X has more of both, so its behavior departs further from PV = nRT. Helium's tiny, weakly-attracting atoms need almost no correction — which is exactly why it stays nearly ideal even when crowded and cooled.

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes heat from temperature?

answers.text: Heat and temperature are two words for the same quantity.
Temperature is energy in transit; heat is the average particle motion.
Temperature is the average kinetic energy of particles; heat is energy that flows from a warmer object to a cooler one.
Heat always flows from a cooler object to a warmer one.

questions.feedback_general: Temperature is a property a sample has (average particle motion); heat is energy in transit, always flowing hot → cold until thermal equilibrium.

questions.text: How much heat is needed to warm 50.0 g of water from 20.0 °C to 80.0 °C? (c = 4.184 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹)
A process that absorbs energy from its surroundings, cooling them down, is endothermic.
questions.feedback_general: Endothermic = energy into the system (surroundings cool). Exothermic = energy out of the system (surroundings warm).

questions.text: In a coffee-cup calorimeter, a hot metal is dropped into cool water. By the first law (conservation of energy), the heat lost by the metal is best described as…

answers.text: equal in size to the heat gained by the water (q_metal = −q_water).
always larger than the heat gained by the water.
unrelated to the water's temperature change.

questions.feedback_general: Energy is conserved: whatever heat leaves the metal (negative q) enters the water (positive q), equal in magnitude — heat lost by the metal = heat gained by the water.

questions.text: Match each symbol in q = m·c·ΔT to what it represents.

answers.right: Mass of the sample, in grams

questions.feedback_general: q = m·c·ΔT. Always compute ΔT as final minus initial, and check that grams and degrees cancel, leaving joules.

questions.text: Equal 50.0 g pieces of two different metals, both heated to 100.0 °C, are dropped into identical cups each holding 100.0 g of water at 20.0 °C. Metal X warms its water to a final 28.0 °C; Metal Y warms its water to a final 24.0 °C. Which statement is best supported by this data?

answers.text: Metal Y released more heat to its water than Metal X did.
Metal X has the larger specific heat: for the same mass, it delivered more heat to the water, so by q = m·c·ΔT its c must be greater.
The two metals must have identical specific heats, since the setups were identical.
Conservation of energy was violated in the trial with Metal X.

questions.feedback_general: Both metals cooled from 100 °C by a similar amount, and both masses are equal, so the difference is specific heat. Metal X drove the larger water temperature rise (bigger q_water), so it handed over more energy per gram per degree — the larger specific heat. Energy is conserved in both trials; q_metal = −q_water each time.

questions.text: The enthalpy change (ΔH) of a reaction is best described as…

answers.text: the average kinetic energy of the reactant particles.
the heat released or absorbed by the reaction at constant pressure.
the total mass of the products.

questions.feedback_general: ΔH is the heat of a reaction at constant pressure — the everyday conditions of an open container, which is why a calorimeter can measure it.

questions.text: A reaction has ΔH = −183 kJ. This reaction is…

answers.text: endothermic; it absorbs heat and cools its surroundings.
exothermic; it releases heat and warms its surroundings.
impossible, because ΔH cannot be negative.

questions.feedback_general: A negative ΔH means the reaction releases energy — exothermic. The products sit lower in energy than the reactants, and the surroundings warm up.

It's the reverse. Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic); forming bonds releases energy (exothermic). A reaction is exothermic when forming the product bonds returns more than breaking the reactant bonds cost.

questions.text: Estimate ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl using bond energies: H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 243, H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol.
questions.feedback_general: Broken: 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. ΔH ≈ 679 − 862 = −183 kJ (exothermic).

questions.text: Match each term to its description.

answers.right: ΔH < 0; releases heat; products lower in energy
ΔH > 0; absorbs heat; products higher in energy
Energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond
Estimating a reaction's enthalpy from bond energies

questions.feedback_general: Exothermic = negative ΔH (heat out); endothermic = positive ΔH (heat in); bond energy measures how much energy a bond stores; and you estimate ΔH as bonds broken minus bonds formed.

questions.text: In a certain reaction, breaking all the reactant bonds requires a total of 800 kJ, and forming all the product bonds releases a total of 950 kJ. Without reaching for the specific bonds, what can you conclude?

answers.text: Endothermic, because breaking bonds always outweighs forming them.
Exothermic: forming the product bonds released more (950 kJ) than breaking the reactant bonds cost (800 kJ), so ΔH ≈ 800 − 950 = −150 kJ.
It cannot be classified without knowing which specific bonds are involved.

questions.feedback_general: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) = 800 − 950 = −150 kJ. A negative ΔH means the reaction releases energy overall — exothermic — because forming the products returned more energy than breaking the reactants cost. (C flips the sign; A and D ignore the numbers you were given.)

answers.text: Gas molecules attract one another strongly
Gas molecules collide with the walls of the container, exerting force over an area
Gas molecules have large volumes of their own

questions.feedback_general: P₂ = (1.0)(2.0) ÷ 0.50 = 4.0 atm. Boyle's law: at constant T, pressure and volume are inversely proportional — quarter the volume, quadruple the pressure.

questions.text: Real gases deviate most from ideal-gas behavior (PV = nRT) under conditions of:
questions.feedback_general: At high pressure and low temperature, molecules are crowded and slow, so their own volume and their intermolecular attractions — both ignored by the ideal model — matter most. Under those conditions the ideal-gas law breaks down.
