Because an isotope is chemically (almost) identical to its stable form, so it bonds and reacts the same way — but its radiation can be tracked
Because radiation pulls the atom toward the organ that needs it
Because tracers are made only of gamma rays, which travel in straight lines

questions.feedback_general: Isotopes share the same protons and electrons, so chemistry is unchanged; only the emitted radiation makes the tracer trackable.

questions.text: A medical isotope used for imaging is best if it has a short half-life. Which reasoning best explains why?

answers.text: A short half-life means the isotope is more radioactive forever, giving a brighter image
A short half-life lets it emit enough radiation to make the image, then decay away quickly so the patient's exposure ends soon
A short half-life means it emits only alpha particles, which are safest
A short half-life makes the isotope cheaper to store for years

questions.feedback_general: "Bright then gone" — technetium-99m's ~6-hour half-life images, then clears quickly, limiting lasting dose.

questions.text: The same nuclear properties that make radioisotopes hazardous (penetrating radiation, ability to damage cells) are also what make them useful as tools.
questions.feedback_general: Exactly the module's theme — gamma's penetration lets it image or treat; radiation's cell-killing power treats tumors; both are "hazards" turned to use.

questions.text: Match each radioisotope to its primary use.
questions.feedback_general: Tc-99m (γ, ~6 h) images; I-131 self-targets the thyroid; C-14 (~5730 yr) dates organic material; Am-241 (α) sits in a sealed smoke detector.

questions.text: A factory needs a steady, penetrating radiation source to sterilize medical equipment for years. Which isotope best fits the job?

answers.text: Technetium-99m, because its ~6-hour half-life is convenient
Fluorine-18, because it is used in PET scans
Cobalt-60, a gamma emitter with a multi-year half-life that lasts and penetrates packaging
Carbon-14, because it dates old objects

questions.feedback_general: Sterilizing needs a long-lived, penetrating source — cobalt-60 (γ, ~5.3 yr) fits; a ~6-hour isotope would be gone within a day.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 9.06 — Biological Effects of Radiation

questions.text: What makes radiation ionizing, and why is that the source of its biological danger?

answers.text: It heats tissue until proteins melt
It carries enough energy to knock electrons off atoms, breaking chemical bonds — and when it breaks DNA, it can kill cells, cause mutations, or lead to cancer
It makes atoms radioactive so they spread the radiation to neighbors
It changes the temperature of the body's water

questions.feedback_general: Ionizing radiation breaks bonds; damage to DNA is the most serious effect because it can persist as mutation and lead to cancer.

questions.text: A patient absorbs a certain amount of radiation energy. Which statement about gray (Gy) and sievert (Sv) is correct?

answers.text: The gray and the sievert are two names for the same thing
The gray measures energy absorbed (1 J/kg); the sievert is the gray weighted by a quality factor for how biologically damaging the radiation is
The sievert measures only the number of decays per second
The gray accounts for biological harm; the sievert only counts joules

questions.feedback_general: Gray = energy absorbed per kg; Sv = Gy × quality factor, so the sievert reflects actual biological risk. (1 Gy = 100 rad; 1 Sv = 100 rem.)

questions.text: An alpha-emitting source is generally more dangerous if it is inhaled or swallowed than if it is held against the skin from outside.
questions.feedback_general: From outside, skin stops alpha. Inhaled, the source sits against living cells with no shield, where alpha's high ionizing power (quality factor ~20) does serious damage. Hazard depends on radiation type AND internal vs. external.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a source of the everyday background radiation people normally receive?

answers.text: Naturally radioactive isotopes in rocks, soil, and food
A genetically engineered isotope unique to laboratories

questions.feedback_general: Background radiation comes from natural sources (radon, cosmic rays, rocks/soil, food) plus medical procedures — it is unavoidable, so the question is "how much," not "zero or some."

questions.text: Which statement best reflects responsible, evidence-based cost–benefit reasoning about a recommended diagnostic scan?

answers.text: Refuse all radiation, since any dose at all is unacceptable
Ignore the dose entirely, since radiation is everywhere anyway
Weigh the small radiation risk against the medical information gained, and decide case by case using evidence
Choose whichever option sounds least scary

questions.feedback_general: Responsible decisions weigh real benefits against real risks with evidence — not fear, not wishful thinking. That evidence-over-preference stance is the quarter's Responsibility (and Honesty) in action.

quizzes.title: Module 9 Exam — Nuclear Chemistry & Its Applications (Lessons 9.01–9.06)

questions.text: The protons and neutrons in a nucleus are together called:
questions.feedback_general: Nucleons = protons + neutrons. The atomic number Z counts the protons (and defines the element); the mass number A = protons + neutrons.

questions.text: For an atom written ²³⁵₉₂U, the number of neutrons is:
questions.feedback_general: Neutrons = A − Z = 235 − 92 = 143. The superscript is the mass number (A); the subscript is the atomic number (Z = protons).

questions.text: The strong nuclear force is best described as:

answers.text: A long-range force that pushes protons apart
A very strong, very short-range force that binds nucleons and overcomes proton–proton repulsion
The force that holds electrons in their orbitals

questions.feedback_general: The strong force acts only over sub-nuclear distances but is strong enough there to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between protons, holding the nucleus together.

questions.text: The binding energy per nucleon is greatest for nuclei around iron (mass number ≈ 56). This explains why:

answers.text: Both the fusion of light nuclei and the fission of heavy nuclei release energy — each moves products toward the iron peak of greatest stability
Heavy nuclei are the most stable of all

questions.feedback_general: Nuclei become more stable as they approach the iron-56 peak. Light nuclei reach it by fusing; heavy nuclei reach it by splitting. Both processes release energy because the products are more tightly bound. The missing mass becomes energy via E = mc².

questions.text: There are no stable nuclei beyond Z = 83 (bismuth) — every element heavier than that is radioactive.
questions.feedback_general: True. As nuclei grow, the proton–proton repulsion eventually wins; beyond Z = 83 no combination of neutrons makes a stable nucleus, so all heavier elements undergo radioactive decay.

questions.text: Complete and classify: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ?
questions.feedback_general: Balancing A: 238 = 234 + 4. Balancing Z: 92 = 90 + 2. The missing particle is ⁴₂He — an alpha particle. Alpha decay drops the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2; very heavy nuclei often decay this way.

questions.text: In beta (β⁻) decay, inside the nucleus:

answers.text: A proton becomes a neutron, emitting a positron
A neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron (⁰₋₁e) — A stays the same, Z increases by 1
Two protons and two neutrons leave together
A photon is emitted with no change in A or Z

questions.feedback_general: In β⁻ decay a neutron converts to a proton plus an emitted electron. The mass number is unchanged and the atomic number rises by 1. Example: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e. (Positron emission is the opposite: a proton → neutron, Z − 1.)

questions.text: Which radiation has the greatest penetrating power and requires thick lead or concrete to stop it?
questions.feedback_general: Penetrating power, least to most: alpha (stopped by paper or skin) < beta (a few mm of aluminum) < gamma (highly penetrating; needs thick lead or concrete). Ionizing power runs the other way — alpha is the most ionizing.
True. Gamma is ⁰₀γ — no change in A or Z. It usually accompanies another decay (alpha or beta) as the new nucleus settles to a lower energy state.

questions.text: Radioactivity was first discovered in 1896 by Henri Becquerel; the term radioactivity was coined by, and two new radioactive elements (polonium and radium, 1898) were isolated by:
questions.feedback_general: Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 (uranium salts fogged a photographic plate in the dark). Marie Curie, working with Pierre, coined radioactivity and isolated polonium and radium in 1898. Rutherford identified and named the alpha and beta radiations and showed alpha particles are helium nuclei.

questions.text: Radioactive decay follows first-order kinetics, and the half-life of a given nuclide is constant — it does not depend on sample size, temperature, or chemical form.
questions.feedback_general: True. Decay rate is proportional to the number of nuclei present (rate = kN), so the half-life is fixed for each nuclide (t½ = 0.693/k). This is why half-life is such a reliable clock.

questions.text: After 4 half-lives, the fraction of a radioactive sample remaining is:
A sample begins with 64 g of a nuclide whose half-life is 5 years. How much remains after 15 years?
questions.feedback_general: 15 years ÷ 5 years = 3 half-lives, so (1/2)³ = 1/8 remains: 64 × 1/8 = 8 g. (Mass remaining = initial × (1/2)^(time/t½).)

questions.text: A wooden artifact has 1/4 of the carbon-14 a living tree of the same size would have. Carbon-14's half-life is about 5730 years. The artifact is approximately:
questions.feedback_general: 1/4 = (1/2)² means two half-lives have passed: 2 × 5730 = 11,460 years. Carbon-14 dating works because a living thing keeps a steady ¹⁴C level; after death the ¹⁴C decays and the fraction left gives the age.

questions.text: The becquerel (Bq) is a unit of radioactivity equal to:
questions.feedback_general: 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. The older unit, the curie (Ci) — named for the Curies — equals 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq, so the curie describes a much more intense source.

questions.text: The first artificial transmutation (Rutherford, 1919) was ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + ?
questions.feedback_general: Balancing A: 14 + 4 = 17 + 1. Balancing Z: 7 + 2 = 8 + 1. The missing particle is ¹₁H — a proton. Rutherford fired alpha particles at nitrogen and turned it into oxygen-17, the first deliberate change of one element into another.

questions.text: In nuclear fission of uranium-235, the emitted neutrons can trigger further fission events. The minimum amount of fissile material needed to sustain this chain reaction is the:
questions.feedback_general: A critical mass is the minimum amount needed to sustain a chain reaction. A controlled chain reaction (control rods absorb neutrons; a moderator slows them) powers a reactor; an uncontrolled one is a fission bomb.

True. Fusion (e.g., ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n) powers the Sun. It needs extremely high temperature and pressure to overcome proton repulsion, which is why controlled fusion for power on Earth is so difficult.

questions.text: Both fission and fusion release enormous energy because:

answers.text: Electrons are rearranged into lower orbitals
A tiny amount of mass is converted to energy via E = mc²

questions.feedback_general: In both processes the products have slightly less mass than the reactants; that lost mass becomes energy through E = mc². Because c² is enormous, even a tiny mass change releases a huge amount of energy — far more than any chemical (electron-level) reaction.

questions.text: Why is achieving controlled fusion for power so much harder than running a fission reactor?

answers.text: Light nuclei must be forced together against their mutual electrical repulsion, which requires extremely high temperature and pressure
Fusion only works in particle accelerators

questions.feedback_general: To fuse, positively charged nuclei must come close enough for the strong force to act, which means overcoming their electrostatic repulsion — possible only at the temperatures and pressures found in stars. Scientists are currently pursuing magnetic-confinement (tokamak) and laser/inertial approaches to reach net-energy fusion.

questions.text: Match each radioisotope to its common use.
questions.feedback_general: The isotope is chosen by matching its half-life and radiation type to the task: Tc-99m's short half-life and penetrating gamma suit imaging; the thyroid naturally concentrates iodine, so I-131 targets it; C-14's long half-life dates organic material; Am-241's alpha emission ionizes air in a smoke detector.

questions.text: Why is a short half-life desirable for a radioisotope used in medical imaging?

answers.text: It makes the isotope cheaper to mine
It gives a strong signal for the scan and then decays away quickly, limiting the patient's ongoing radiation exposure
It means the isotope never decays
It changes the patient's blood type

questions.feedback_general: An imaging isotope like Tc-99m must emit enough penetrating radiation to be detected, then clear quickly so the patient isn't exposed for long. A short half-life (≈ 6 hours) does both — strong signal now, little radiation later.

questions.text: Which correctly distinguishes the gray (Gy) from the sievert (Sv)?

answers.text: The gray measures energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue; the sievert weights that absorbed dose by how damaging the radiation type is
The gray measures time; the sievert measures distance
The sievert measures only alpha radiation

questions.feedback_general: 1 Gy = 1 joule absorbed per kilogram (older unit: rad; 1 Gy = 100 rad). The sievert is the equivalent/effective dose — Gy × a quality factor — so it reflects biological harm (older unit: rem; 1 Sv = 100 rem). The same gray of alpha is far more damaging than a gray of gamma, which the sievert captures.

answers.text: The source is held at arm's length
The source is ingested or inhaled, so it deposits its energy directly inside the body
It is blocked by a sheet of paper
It is emitted by a smoke detector across the room

questions.feedback_general: From outside the body, alpha is stopped by skin or clothing. But if an alpha emitter is taken inside (ingested or inhaled), its high ionizing power and large quality factor (~20) make it very damaging to nearby tissue. Gamma, by contrast, is mainly an external hazard because it penetrates deeply. So the danger depends on radiation type and whether the source is internal or external — one reason decisions about nuclear medicine and power require an honest weighing of benefits against risks.

questions.text: A nuclide lies above the band of stability on a neutron-versus-proton plot — it has too many neutrons for its number of protons. The most likely way for it to move toward stability is:

answers.text: Beta (β⁻) decay — a neutron becomes a proton, lowering the neutron-to-proton ratio

questions.feedback_general: A neutron-rich nuclide sits above the band. Beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton (A unchanged, Z + 1), which lowers the N/Z ratio and moves the nuclide down toward the band of stability. (Proton-rich nuclides below the band tend to use positron emission or electron capture instead.)

questions.text: A decay curve shows a sample starting at 100 g and falling to 25 g after 10 days. From the graph, the half-life of the nuclide is:
questions.feedback_general: 25 g is 1/4 of 100 g, and 1/4 = (1/2)², so two half-lives have passed in 10 days: t½ = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 days. Reading the fraction remaining off a decay curve and converting it to a number of half-lives is the key skill.

questions.text: On a graph of binding energy per nucleon versus mass number, the curve rises steeply for the lightest nuclei, peaks near iron-56, then declines slowly for the heaviest nuclei. This shape best explains why:

answers.text: Only heavy nuclei can release energy
Fusing very light nuclei releases even more energy per nucleon than fissioning heavy nuclei, because light nuclei sit farthest below the iron peak
Both fission and fusion absorb energy

questions.feedback_general: Energy is released when the products end up more tightly bound — higher on the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve. Light nuclei start far below the iron-56 peak, so fusing them upward gives a large gain per nucleon; heavy nuclei are only slightly past the peak, so fission gives a smaller (still enormous) gain. Both processes move products toward iron-56.

questions.text: A hospital must pick an isotope for a diagnostic scan. Isotope X emits gamma rays and has a 6-hour half-life; Isotope Y emits alpha particles and has a 30-year half-life. The better choice, and why, is:

answers.text: Isotope Y, because alpha radiation is easy to detect outside the body
Isotope X, because its gamma rays escape the body to be imaged and its short half-life clears quickly, limiting the patient's dose
Isotope Y, because a long half-life gives more time to scan

questions.feedback_general: A diagnostic isotope must be detectable from outside the body (gamma penetrates; alpha does not) and should decay quickly so ongoing exposure is small. Isotope X does both. Isotope Y would be a poor and hazardous choice — alpha can't be imaged from outside, and a 30-year alpha emitter left inside the body would deposit damaging dose for decades. This is a cost/benefit judgment weighing signal against risk.

questions.text: A gas at 1.0 atm occupies 6.0 L. Compressed at constant temperature to 2.0 L, its pressure becomes (Boyle's law, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂):
questions.feedback_general: P₂ = (1.0)(6.0) ÷ 2.0 = 3.0 atm. At constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional — shrink the volume to one-third, triple the pressure.

questions.text: Using PV = nRT (R = 0.08206), how many moles of gas occupy 2.0 L at 1.0 atm and 273 K?
questions.feedback_general: n = PV ÷ RT = (1.0)(2.0) ÷ [(0.08206)(273)] = 2.0 ÷ 22.4 = 0.0893 mol. The mole — the counting unit you met in Module 4 — is what links a measured volume of gas to a number of particles.

questions.text: A rigid sealed canister of gas is left in a hot car and its temperature climbs. Predict what happens to the pressure inside, and why:

answers.text: Pressure drops, because the molecules slow down
Pressure rises, because the molecules move faster and strike the walls harder and more often
Pressure stays the same, because the volume cannot change
Pressure rises, because the gas gains mass

questions.feedback_general: In a rigid container (constant V), raising the temperature speeds the molecules up, so they hit the walls harder and more frequently — pressure rises with absolute temperature (Gay-Lussac). No mass is added; the molecules just move faster.

questions.text: A gas is collected over water at 25 °C; the total pressure is 760 mmHg. The water vapor pressure at 25 °C is 23.8 mmHg. The partial pressure of the dry collected gas is:
questions.feedback_general: The collected gas is mixed with water vapor, so by Dalton's law P_dry gas = P_total − P_water = 760 − 23.8 = 736.2 mmHg. You must subtract the water vapor's contribution.

questions.text: Using Graham's law (rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁)), compare the effusion of helium (4.00 g/mol) and oxygen (32.00 g/mol):

answers.text: They effuse at the same rate

questions.feedback_general: rate_He / rate_O₂ = √(32.00 ÷ 4.00) = √8 = 2.83. The lighter gas effuses faster, so helium escapes through a small opening about 2.83 times faster than oxygen.

questions.text: Real gases deviate most from ideal-gas behavior (PV = nRT) under conditions of:
questions.feedback_general: At high pressure and low temperature, molecules are crowded and slow, so their own volume and their intermolecular attractions — both ignored by the ideal model — matter most. A model is useful precisely where its assumptions hold.

questions.text: Using q = mcΔT (c_water = 4.184 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹), how much heat is needed to warm 50.0 g of water from 20.0 °C to 80.0 °C?
questions.feedback_general: q = (50.0 g)(4.184 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹)(80.0 − 20.0 °C) = 50.0 × 4.184 × 60.0 = 12,552 J ≈ 12.6 kJ. Heat scales with mass, specific heat, and the temperature change.

questions.text: For H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl, estimate ΔH from bond energies (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol) using ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed):
questions.feedback_general: Bonds broken: 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. ΔH ≈ 679 − 862 = −183 kJ. A negative ΔH means the reaction releases energy — it is exothermic.

questions.text: Which substance has only London dispersion forces acting between its molecules?
questions.feedback_general: CH₄ (methane) is nonpolar, so its only intermolecular force is London dispersion. H₂O, NH₃, and HF all hydrogen-bond (H bonded to O, N, or F).

questions.text: Three substances have similar molar masses but boiling points of −89 °C, −19 °C, and +78 °C. The substance boiling at +78 °C most likely:

answers.text: Can form hydrogen bonds (e.g., it contains an –OH group)
Is the lightest of the three

questions.feedback_general: The highest boiling point points to the strongest intermolecular forces. Among molecules of similar mass, hydrogen bonding (as in an alcohol's –OH group) is strongest, so it requires the most energy to boil.

questions.text: A liquid boils when:

answers.text: Its temperature reaches exactly 100 °C in every case
Its vapor pressure equals the external (atmospheric) pressure
Its density equals that of air

questions.feedback_general: Boiling occurs when a liquid's vapor pressure rises to match the surrounding pressure. Because that external pressure is lower at high altitude, water boils below 100 °C on a mountain.

questions.text: A solid is very hard, does not conduct electricity, and melts at an extremely high temperature (like diamond or quartz). It is best classified as a:
questions.feedback_general: In a covalent network solid, atoms are joined by a continuous web of covalent bonds (diamond, quartz, silicon carbide). Breaking it means breaking covalent bonds, so it is extremely hard and very high-melting.

questions.text: Match each solute to its electrolyte behavior in water.
questions.feedback_general: Soluble ionic salts and strong acids/bases are strong electrolytes; weak acids/bases (like vinegar's acetic acid) partly ionize; molecular compounds like sugar dissolve but form no ions, so they don't conduct.

questions.text: Using ΔT_f = i·K_f·m with K_f(water) = 1.86 °C/m, the freezing point of a 1.00 m NaCl solution (i = 2) is about:
questions.feedback_general: ΔT_f = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 3.72 °C, so the solution freezes at 0 − 3.72 = −3.72 °C. The two ions per formula unit double the depression — which is why salt is spread on icy roads.

questions.text: A beam of light shone through a glass of milk reveals a visible path, but the same beam through salt water does not. This difference identifies milk as a:

answers.text: Colloid (it scatters light — the Tyndall effect)

questions.feedback_general: Colloids have particles large enough to scatter light (the Tyndall effect), so the beam's path is visible (milk, fog, gelatin). True solutions like salt water have particles too small to scatter light, so no beam shows.

questions.text: Which process is expected to increase the entropy of the system?

answers.text: Water vapor condensing on a window
A solid dissolving to form a solution
A gas being cooled and compressed

questions.feedback_general: Dissolving disperses particles and energy, raising entropy. Condensing, compressing/cooling a gas, and freezing all reduce particle freedom and lower entropy. Entropy rises in the order solid < liquid < gas.

questions.text: The Gibbs free energy change is given by:
questions.feedback_general: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (T in kelvin) combines enthalpy and entropy into a single spontaneity criterion: ΔG < 0 is spontaneous, ΔG > 0 is nonspontaneous, ΔG = 0 is at equilibrium.

questions.text: For a reaction at 298 K with ΔH = −100 kJ and ΔS = +50 J/K (+0.050 kJ/K), the value of ΔG is:
questions.feedback_general: TΔS = 298 × 0.050 = 14.9 kJ, so ΔG = −100 − 14.9 = −114.9 kJ — spontaneous. Watch the unit conversion: ΔS in J/K must become kJ/K to subtract from ΔH in kJ.

questions.text: Match each sign combination to its temperature dependence for spontaneity.
questions.feedback_general: When ΔH and ΔS push the same direction (−/+ or +/−), temperature can't change the outcome. When they conflict (−/− or +/+), the −TΔS term decides: low T favors enthalpy, high T favors entropy.

questions.text: The Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), is exothermic (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol). Which set of conditions would, by Le Châtelier's principle alone, maximize the equilibrium yield of NH₃?
questions.feedback_general: High pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles (4 mol → 2 mol of NH₃). Because the reaction releases heat, low temperature also shifts toward product. In practice industry uses a moderate temperature plus an iron catalyst, since very low temperature makes the reaction far too slow — a real-world compromise between yield and rate.

questions.text: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, which statement about the equilibrium constant K is correct?

answers.text: Pure solids and liquids are included in the K expression
K = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b), and a large K means products are favored
K changes whenever a catalyst is added

questions.feedback_general: K is products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient; pure solids and liquids are omitted. A large K (≫ 1) favors products, a small K (≪ 1) favors reactants. A catalyst does not change K.

questions.text: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), at equilibrium [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.20 M and [HI] = 1.60 M. The value of Kc is:
questions.feedback_general: Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]) = (1.60)² / (0.20 × 0.20) = 2.56 / 0.04 = 64. The HI concentration is squared because of the coefficient 2 in the balanced equation.

questions.text: Under the Brønsted-Lowry definitions, an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. In HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, the base is:
questions.feedback_general: Water accepts the proton donated by HCl, so water is the Brønsted-Lowry base here and HCl is the acid. Water is amphoteric — it can donate or accept a proton depending on its partner.

questions.text: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M. Its pH, and whether it is acidic or basic, is:
questions.feedback_general: pH = −log[H₃O⁺] = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3.00. A pH below 7 (at 25 °C) is acidic. The pOH would be 14.00 − 3.00 = 11.00.

questions.text: In a titration, 25.0 mL of HCl is exactly neutralized by 30.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. Using M_aV_a = M_bV_b, the concentration of the HCl is:
questions.feedback_general: mol NaOH = 0.0300 L × 0.100 M = 0.00300 mol = mol HCl (1 : 1); M_HCl = 0.00300 mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.120 M. The strong acid–strong base equivalence point is pH 7.

questions.text: In any redox reaction, reduction is:

answers.text: The loss of electrons (oxidation number increases)
The gain of electrons (oxidation number decreases)

questions.feedback_general: OIL RIG — Reduction Is Gain of electrons; the oxidation number goes down. The species reduced is the oxidizing agent; the species oxidized is the reducing agent. (Redox first appeared as a reaction type back in Module 4.)

questions.text: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻? (Oxygen is usually −2.)
questions.feedback_general: Four oxygens at −2 give −8. For the ion to total −2, sulfur must be +6: (+6) + (−8) = −2. A free element is 0, oxygen is usually −2, and the oxidation numbers sum to the species' charge.

questions.text: In a galvanic cell, the anode is the electrode where:

answers.text: Reduction occurs and it is the positive terminal
Oxidation occurs and it is the negative terminal

questions.feedback_general: Oxidation always happens at the anode; in a galvanic cell the anode is the negative terminal (it releases electrons). Reduction happens at the cathode, the positive terminal. Electrons travel anode → cathode through the wire.

questions.text: Using E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, with Cu the cathode and Zn the anode, E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode is:
questions.feedback_general: E°cell = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous, so the Daniell cell is galvanic. E° is intensive — doubling the coefficients does not change it.

questions.text: For the Daniell cell, n = 2 and E°cell = +1.10 V. Using ΔG° = −nFE°cell (F = 96,485 C/mol), ΔG° is approximately:
questions.feedback_general: ΔG° = −(2)(96,485)(1.10) = −212,267 J ≈ −212 kJ. A positive E°cell always gives a negative ΔG° and K > 1 — the three travel together. This is the same free-energy story you met in Module 7, now read off a voltmeter.

questions.text: A zinc coating protects the steel beneath it even if the coating is scratched, because zinc:

answers.text: Is less reactive than iron, so it stays intact
Is more easily oxidized than iron, so it corrodes first and spares the iron
Conducts heat away from the steel

questions.feedback_general: Galvanizing relies on the same principle as a sacrificial anode: zinc is more active (more easily oxidized) than iron, so it gives up electrons preferentially and corrodes first, protecting the steel even where the coating is broken. A more-active metal sacrificing itself is cathodic protection.

questions.text: A current of 2.00 A flows for 3600 s through CuSO₄ solution, depositing copper by Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. With Q = I·t and mol e⁻ = Q/F (F = 96,485 C/mol; Cu ≈ 63.5 g/mol), the mass of copper deposited is about:
questions.feedback_general: Q = 2.00 × 3600 = 7200 C; mol e⁻ = 7200 ÷ 96,485 = 0.0746 mol; because Cu²⁺ needs 2 e⁻, mol Cu = 0.0373 mol; mass = 0.0373 × 63.5 ≈ 2.37 g. Forgetting to divide by 2 double-counts and gives ~4.74 g.

questions.text: For rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, an experiment shows that doubling [A] (with [B] fixed) multiplies the rate by 4. The order with respect to A is:
questions.feedback_general: Doubling [A] and seeing the rate ×4 means rate ∝ [A]² — second order in A (2² = 4). By the method of initial rates: ×1 → zero order, ×2 → first order, ×4 → second order. Reaction orders are found experimentally, not from the balanced coefficients.

questions.text: A catalyst speeds up a reaction because it:

answers.text: Is consumed in the reaction, supplying energy
Provides an alternate pathway with a lower activation energy (Eₐ), without being used up and without changing ΔG or the products
Raises the activation energy so fewer collisions are needed
Shifts the equilibrium toward the products

questions.feedback_general: A catalyst offers an alternate route with a lower Eₐ, so more collisions succeed and the reaction goes faster. It is not consumed, it speeds the forward and reverse directions equally, and it does not change ΔG, K, the equilibrium position, or the products — only the rate.

questions.text: For an atom written ²³⁵₉₂U, the number of neutrons is:
questions.feedback_general: Neutrons = A − Z = 235 − 92 = 143. The superscript is the mass number (A); the subscript is the atomic number (Z = protons).

questions.text: Complete and classify: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ?
questions.feedback_general: Balancing A: 238 = 234 + 4. Balancing Z: 92 = 90 + 2. The missing particle is ⁴₂He — an alpha particle. Alpha decay drops the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

questions.text: Which radiation has the greatest penetrating power and requires thick lead or concrete to stop it?
questions.feedback_general: Penetrating power, least to most: alpha (stopped by paper or skin) < beta (a few mm of aluminum) < gamma (highly penetrating; needs thick lead or concrete). Ionizing power runs the other way — alpha is the most ionizing.

questions.text: A wooden artifact has 1/4 of the carbon-14 a living tree of the same size would have. Carbon-14's half-life is about 5730 years. The artifact is approximately:
questions.feedback_general: 1/4 = (1/2)² means two half-lives have passed: 2 × 5730 = 11,460 years. Carbon-14 dating works because a living thing keeps a steady ¹⁴C level; after death the ¹⁴C decays and the fraction left gives the age.

questions.text: Both nuclear fission and fusion release enormous energy because:

answers.text: Electrons are rearranged into lower orbitals
A tiny amount of mass is converted to energy via E = mc²

questions.feedback_general: In both processes the products have slightly less mass than the reactants; that lost mass becomes energy through E = mc². Because c² is enormous, even a tiny mass change releases a huge amount of energy — far more than any chemical (electron-level) reaction.

answers.text: The source is held at arm's length
The source is ingested or inhaled, so it deposits its energy directly inside the body
It is blocked by a sheet of paper
It is emitted by a smoke detector across the room

questions.feedback_general: From outside the body, alpha is stopped by skin or clothing. But if an alpha emitter is taken inside, its high ionizing power and large quality factor make it very damaging to nearby tissue. So the danger depends on radiation type and on whether the source is internal or external — one reason decisions about nuclear medicine and power require an honest weighing of benefits against risks.
